Let $N \cap W = \{x \in N : \ell_i(x) = 0\ \forall i\}$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · nullSpace⟧ and $Q_\Sigma = (\ell_i)_{i \in \Sigma} : N \to \mathbb R^\Sigma$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · sigmaCoord⟧.

**Lemma 3.65.** A good complement satisfies $\ell_i(p) = 0$ for $p \in P$, $i \in \Sigma$: take $a \in Q \setminus 0$ with $\ell_i(a) = 0$, scale $p$ so that $|p| \le \varepsilon|a|$; $a \in C$ gives $a + p \in C$, so $\ell_i(p) = \ell_i(a + p) \ge 0$; the same for $-p$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · lemma_3_65⟧. *Consequences.* $Q_\Sigma$ is onto: for $k \in \mathbb R^\Sigma$ pick $v$ with $\ell_i(v) = k_i$ and split $v = n + p$; then $Q_\Sigma(n) = k$ (the text's (55), p. 125) ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · sigmaCoord_surjective⟧. If an interior point $y$ of $Q$ has $\ell_i(y) = 0$, then $\ell_i = 0$ on $N$ ($y \pm tu \in Q$) ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · restrFun_eq_zero_of_interior⟧.

**Proposition 3.22, the normal form.** There are $k$, a subspace $N_0$ and a linear isomorphism $e : N \to \mathbb R^k \times N_0$ with $Q = e^{-1}([0, \infty)^k \times N_0)$, $k = \dim N - \dim(N \cap W)$, the $\mathbb R^k$-component of $e$ vanishing exactly on $N \cap W$, and the vanishing coordinates of $e(x)$ as many as the vanishing $\ell_i(x)$ for $x \in Q \setminus N \cap W$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · QuadrantNormalForm⟧ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · exists_quadrantNormalForm⟧. Three cases. *Case A, $Q = N$*: every $\ell_i$ is $\ge 0$ on a vector space, hence $0$; $k = 0$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · quadrantNormalForm_of_eq_univ⟧ (a case the text's case distinction does not single out). *Case B, $Q \ne N$, $\Sigma = \emptyset$*: an interior point $y$ is nonzero with all $\ell_i(y) > 0$; for $u \in N$ the set $\{t : u + ty \in Q\}$ is closed, contains all large $t$ and is bounded below; at its minimum $t^*$ some $\ell_i(u + t^*y) = 0$, so $u + t^*y = 0$: $N$ is the line $\mathbb Ry$ and $Q$ a half-line ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · quadrantNormalForm_of_vanIdx_empty⟧ (the text's Lemma 3.68, second case). *Case C, $\Sigma \ne \emptyset$*: first $Q = \{x \in N : \ell_i(x) \ge 0 \text{ for } i \in \Sigma\}$ — move from such an $x$ towards an interior point $y$ along $x + sy$; at the first parameter $s^*$ with $x + s^*y \in Q$, if $s^* > 0$ the point $z = x + s^*y$ is nonzero (else $\ell_i(x) < 0$ for $i \in \Sigma$), so it has $\ell_i(z) > 0$ for all $i$ ($\ell_i(z) \ge s^*\ell_i(y) > 0$ in $\Sigma$, by definition of $\Sigma$ outside), and finitely many strict inequalities survive a small step back, contradicting minimality ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · mem_quadCone_of_vanIdx⟧. This replaces the text's extreme rays (Lemmas 3.62–3.64, cited from [21], and 3.66–3.68). Then a linear right inverse $g$ of $Q_\Sigma$ gives $e(x) = (Q_\Sigma x, x - gQ_\Sigma x) \in \mathbb R^\Sigma \times \ker Q_\Sigma$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · splitEquiv⟧, and $\ker Q_\Sigma = N \cap W$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · quadrantNormalForm_of_vanIdx⟧. For a partial quadrant in good position this applies in a presentation ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · IsInGoodPosition.quadrantNormalForm⟧, and choosing a basis of $N_0$ makes $(N, N \cap C)$ isomorphic to $(\mathbb R^{\dim N}, [0, \infty)^k \oplus \mathbb R^{\dim N - k})$ through an sc-isomorphism of constant structures ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · scIsoOfLinearEquiv⟧ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · preimage_eq_of_normalForm⟧: **$N \cap C$ is a partial quadrant in $N$** ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · proposition_3_22⟧.

**Lemma 3.45 (linear form).** A continuous linear isomorphism $S : E_0 \to E'_0$ with $x \in C \iff Sx \in C'$ carries a good complement $P$ of $N$ to one of $S(N)$, with $\varepsilon' = \varepsilon/(\|S\|\|S^{-1}\| + 1)$: for $|Sp| \le \varepsilon'|Sn|$, $|p| \le \|S^{-1}\|\varepsilon'\|S\||n| \le \varepsilon|n|$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · IsGoodComplement.map⟧; and the interior condition is transported by the homeomorphism $S|_N$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · IsInGoodPosition.map⟧. The text states it for $T\varphi(0)$; since the coordinate change of Theorem 3.38 is linear, this is the form §§III.18–III.23 need.

**Proposition 3.69.** In the model $\mathbb R^n \oplus W$, for $x \in N \cap C$: $d_{N \cap C}(x) = d_C(x)$ if $x \notin N \cap W$, and $d_{N \cap C}(x) + \dim(N \cap W) = \dim N$ if $x \in N \cap W$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPosition · proposition_3_69⟧ — read off the normal form ($d_{N \cap C}$ does not depend on the presentation, Lemma 1.24).

### III.15 The degeneracy index along a graph: Lemma 3.70

**Lemma 3.70.** In the model, for $N$ in good position with good complement $Y$ and $\tau : N \to E$ with values in $Y$, $C^1$ on $N \cap C$, $\tau(0) = 0$, $D\tau(0) = 0$: there is $\rho > 0$ such that for $v \in N \cap C$, $|v| < \rho$, $v + \tau(v) \in C$, and $d_{N \cap C}(v) = d_C(v + \tau(v))$ if $v \notin N \cap W$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGraph · lemma_3_70⟧. The text distinguishes $\dim N = 1$ (a contradiction argument with $\tau(v) = o(|v|)$) and $\dim N \ge 2$ (the sign of a directional derivative). The formal proof unifies them.

*Ray decomposition.* From the normal form, $u_i = e^{-1}(\mathbf e_i, 0)$ are finitely many nonzero points of $Q$, and every $v \in Q \setminus N \cap W$ has some $i$ and $s > 0$ with $v - su_i \in Q$ and $s|u_i| \le c|v|$ (take $s = \lambda_i > 0$ for $e(v) = (\lambda, n_0)$) ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGraph · exists_rayDecomp⟧ — the text's basis $e^j$ of $\widetilde N$. *Smallness.* $D\tau(0) = 0$ and continuity of $D\tau$ on the convex $Q$ make $\tau$ $\eta$-Lipschitz on $Q \cap B(\rho)$ for every $\eta$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGraph · exists_lipschitz_small⟧ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGraph · quadCone_convex⟧. *The margin.* Choose $\eta \le \varepsilon$ with $\eta\|\ell_j\||u_i| < \ell_j(u_i)$ for all $i$ and $j \notin \Sigma$ — a positive lower bound of finitely many positive numbers ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGraph · exists_pos_le_of_forall_pos⟧. *Conclusion* ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGraph · lemma_3_70_core⟧. For $|v| < \rho/(1 + c)$: $|\tau(v)| \le \varepsilon|v|$, so $v + \tau(v) \in C$ (good complement). For $j \in \Sigma$, $\ell_j(\tau(v)) = 0$ (Lemma 3.65). For $v \notin N \cap W$, $w = v - su_i \in Q$, the segment $[w, v]$ lies in $Q \cap B(\rho)$ — which is why the radius is $\rho/(1 + c)$, the text's "close to $0$" — and for $j \notin \Sigma$,
$$\ell_j(v + \tau(v)) = \ell_j(w + \tau(w)) + s\ell_j(u_i) + \ell_j(\tau(v) - \tau(w)) \ge 0 + s\ell_j(u_i) - \|\ell_j\|\eta s|u_i| > 0.$$
So $v$ and $v + \tau(v)$ have the same vanishing coordinates, and Proposition 3.69 (1) gives the lemma in the model, with the coordinate functionals ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGraph · coordCLM⟧. (The level $Y_1$ of the text's $\tau$ plays no role.)

### III.16 The quadrant inverse function theorem (Theorem 3.72, Proposition 3.73, Lemmas 3.74, 3.77, Corollary 3.75)

*Interior points.* For the model quadrant, $x$ is interior iff all its half-line coordinates are positive ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · interior_quadrant⟧, so $d_C(x) = 0$ exactly at interior points ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · degIndex_eq_zero_iff⟧. A linear isomorphism $S$ with $S(C) = C$ preserves $d_C$ (Lemma 1.24 for the presentation $T \circ S$) ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · ScIso.ofCLE⟧ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · degIndex_map_eq⟧. A linear map carrying a set with nonempty interior onto itself is onto ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · surjective_of_image_eq⟧ — the text's "$\mathbb R^n = C - C$".

**Proposition 3.73.** The hypotheses (`InvData`): $U$ relatively open and convex in the partial quadrant $C$ of a finite-dimensional $V$; $f : U \to C$ of class $C^j$, $j \ge 1$; $\|Df(x) - 1\| \le \tfrac12$; and $x$ interior iff $f(x)$ interior — the only consequence of $d_C(x) = d_C(f(x))$ the proof uses ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData⟧. The text's $0 \in U$, $f(0) = 0$ are not needed. Conclusion: $f(U)$ is relatively open in $C$, $f$ is injective on $U$, with an inverse of class $C^j$ on $f(U)$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · proposition_3_73⟧.

**Lemma 3.74.** $x \mapsto x - f(x)$ is a $\tfrac12$-contraction on the convex $U$ (mean value inequality) ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData.norm_sub_sub_le⟧, which gives (70): $\tfrac12|x - x'| \le |f(x) - f(x')| \le \tfrac32|x - x'|$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData.half_norm_le⟧ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData.norm_sub_le⟧, and injectivity ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData.injOn⟧. *Openness*: if $B(x', 3r) \cap C \subseteq U$ then $B(f(x'), r) \cap C \subseteq f(U)$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData.ball_inter_subset_image⟧. The set $A = f(\bar B(x', 2r) \cap C)$ is compact ($\bar B(x', 2r) \cap C \subseteq U$ is compact in finite dimensions). Interior points first: for an interior $y_1 \in B(y', r)$ choose an interior $x_0 \in U$ with $f(x_0) \in B(y', r)$ — the text takes any interior $x_0 \in B(x', 3r) \cap C$, which does not suffice — and follow the segment $y_t$ from $f(x_0)$ to $y_1$, which stays interior. $\{t : y_t \in A\}$ is closed and contains $0$; at its maximum $t^* < 1$, $y_{t^*} = f(x^*)$ with $x^*$ interior and $|x^* - x'| < 2r$, and at the interior point $x^*$, $Df(x^*)$ is a unit ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData.isUnit_deriv⟧ and $U$ a neighbourhood ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData.U_mem_nhds⟧, so the classical inverse function theorem maps neighbourhoods onto neighbourhoods ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData.map_nhds_eq⟧, pushing $t^*$ further — a contradiction. The compactness of $A$ replaces the text's Cauchy sequence and also gives the remaining points by density. So $f(U)$ is relatively open ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData.image_relOpen⟧. **Corollary 3.75**: $f$ and its inverse ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData.inv⟧ (2-Lipschitz by (70) ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData.norm_inv_sub_le⟧) are continuous and inverse to each other ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · corollary_3_75⟧.

**Lemma 3.77.** The inverse $g$ is differentiable within $f(U)$ with $Dg(y) = [Df(g(y))]^{-1}$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData.hasFDerivWithinAt_inv⟧: with $x_0 = g(y_0)$, $x_0 + \delta = g(y_0 + h)$, the quotient $|g(y_0 + h) - g(y_0) - Df(x_0)^{-1}h|/|h|$ is $|\delta|/|h|$ (bounded by (70)) times the remainder quotient of $f$ at $x_0$. The lemma's extra hypotheses (relatively open image, homeomorphism, invertible derivative) are consequences of those of Proposition 3.73. *Regularity (the text: Lemma 3.76 on the iterated tangent maps $T^kf$).* $x \mapsto [Df(x)]^{-1}$ is $C^{j-1}$ (inversion is smooth on units) ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData.contDiffOn_inverse_deriv⟧, so $Dg = [Df]^{-1} \circ g$ and $g \in C^i$, $i < j$, give $g \in C^{i+1}$: $g$ is $C^j$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · InvData.contDiffOn_inv⟧. Lemma 3.76 is not needed.

**Theorem 3.72.** $U$ a relatively open neighbourhood of $0$ in $C$, $f$ of class $C^j$ with $f(U) \subseteq C$, $f(0) = 0$, $Df(0)C = C$, $d_C(x) = d_C(f(x))$ on $U$: then $f$ is a $C^j$-diffeomorphism between relatively open neighbourhoods $U'$, $V'$ of $0$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantInverse · theorem_3_72⟧. *Proof.* $Df(0)$ is onto, hence invertible, with $Df(0)^{-1}C = C$; $\tilde f = Df(0)^{-1}f$ maps into $C$, $D\tilde f(0) = 1$, and preserves $d_C$ ($d_C \circ Df(0)^{-1} = d_C$), hence interior points. On $U' = B(0, \rho) \cap C$ with $\|D\tilde f - 1\| \le \tfrac12$, Proposition 3.73 applies, and $V' = Df(0)\tilde f(U')$ is relatively open since $Df(0)$ is a linear homeomorphism preserving $C$. The text's hypothesis (2) is used only through interior points; some such hypothesis is needed ($f(x, y) = (x, y + x^2)$ on $[0, \infty)^2$ satisfies (1) but $f(C)$ is not a neighbourhood of $0$ in $C$).

### III.17 The implicit function theorem in partial quadrants (Theorem 3.78, Lemmas 3.79–3.82)

**Theorem 3.78.** $U$ a relatively open neighbourhood of $0$ in the partial quadrant $C$ of a finite-dimensional $V$, $f : U \to F$ of class $C^j$, $j \ge 1$, with $f(0) = 0$, $Df(0)$ onto, $K = \ker Df(0)$ in good position with good complement $Y$. Then there are a relatively open $V' \ni 0$ in $K \cap C$, $\tau : K \to Y$ of class $C^j$ on $V'$ and $\varepsilon, \sigma > 0$ with (1) $\tau(0) = 0$, $D\tau(0) = 0$, and $k + \tau(k) \in U$, **$f(k + \tau(k)) = 0$** for $k \in V'$; (2) $|\tau(k)| \le \sigma$ for $|k| \le \varepsilon$; (3) if $k \in V'$, $|k| \le \varepsilon$, $y \in Y$, $|y| \le \sigma$, **$k + y \in U$** and $f(k + y) = 0$, then $y = \tau(k)$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · theorem_3_78⟧. The two bold clauses are not in the text; the first is the content of the theorem (its proof has $\tau(k) = B(k, \tau(k))$), the second is needed for $f(k + y)$ to make sense.

*Normalization (71)–(72).* With $L = (Df(0)|_Y)^{-1}$, in coordinates $x = k + y \in K \oplus Y$, $Lf(k + y) = y - B(k, y)$ with $B(k, y) := y - Lf(k + y)$, $B(0, 0) = 0$, $DB(0, 0) = 0$. The data after normalization: on $K \times Y$ a convex set $C_p$ with nonempty interior, a relatively open $U_p \ni 0$, $B$ of class $C^j$ on $U_p$ with $B(0) = 0$, $DB(0) = 0$, the good-position estimate and the interior condition ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · ContractionData⟧. Only convexity and interior are used; the quadrant enters through good position.

*Lemmas 3.79, 3.80: the constants* ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii⟧ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · ContractionData.exists_radii⟧. With $\varepsilon$ the good-position constant and $c_0 = \varepsilon/(2(1 + \varepsilon)) \le \tfrac12$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.c₀⟧, continuity of $DB$ at $0$ gives $a, b$ with $\varepsilon a \le b$, the region $R = \{|k| \le a, |y| \le b\} \cap C_p \subseteq U_p$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.R⟧ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.R_sub_U⟧ and $\|DB\| \le c_0$ on $R$. $R$ is convex ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.R_convex⟧, so the mean value inequality gives $|B(q) - B(p)| \le c_0|q - p|$ on $R$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.norm_sub_le⟧ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.norm_B_sub_le_snd⟧ and $|B(p)| \le c_0|p|$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.norm_B_le⟧. For $k \in V_0 = \{k \in K \cap C : |k| < a\}$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.V₀⟧ and $|y| \le \varepsilon|k|$: good position puts $(k, y) \in C_p$, $|y| \le \varepsilon a \le b$, so $(k, y) \in R$ and $|B(k, y)| \le c_0(1 + \varepsilon)|k| = \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}|k|$. So $B(k, \cdot)$ maps $X_k = \bar B_Y(\varepsilon|k|)$ into itself ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.mapsTo_ball⟧ and has a fixed point $\tau(k)$ there ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.exists_fixed⟧ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.τ⟧; any fixed point $y$ with $(k, y) \in R$ equals $\tau(k)$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.eq_τ⟧. (In Lemma 3.80 the maximum is over $B((1 + \varepsilon)a) \cap C$, where $DB$ is defined.)

*Lemma 3.81: continuity.* $|\tau(k)| \le \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}|k|$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.norm_τ_le⟧. If $|k_0| \le 2|k|$, then $(k, \tau(k_0)) \in R$ and $|\tau(k) - \tau(k_0)| \le \tfrac12|\tau(k) - \tau(k_0)| + c_0|k - k_0|$, so $|\tau(k) - \tau(k_0)| \le \varepsilon|k - k_0|$ — the text's estimate, whose argument needs $(k, \tau(k_0))$ in the domain. If $|k_0| > 2|k|$, then $|k - k_0| \ge \tfrac12|k_0|$ and $|\tau(k) - \tau(k_0)| \le \tfrac{\varepsilon}{2}(|k| + |k_0|) \le \tfrac{3\varepsilon}{2}|k - k_0|$. In all cases the constant is $1 + 2\varepsilon$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.norm_τ_sub_le⟧, and $\tau$ is continuous ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.continuousOn_τ⟧. Since $X_k$ depends on $k$, the parametrized fixed point theorem of §III.8 does not apply, and continuity is proved by hand, as in the text.

*Lemma 3.82: regularity.* With $D_1B = DB \circ \mathrm{inl}$, $D_2B = DB \circ \mathrm{inr}$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.D₁⟧ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.D₂⟧, $\|D_2B\| \le \tfrac12$ on $R$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.norm_D₂_le⟧, $M = (1 - D_2B)^{-1}$ (Neumann) ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.M⟧ and $\Phi = MD_1B$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.Φ⟧: from the fixed-point identities and the little-o composition of $B$ with the Lipschitz $k' \mapsto (k', \tau(k'))$, $\tau$ is differentiable within $V_0$ with $D\tau(k) = \Phi(k, \tau(k))$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.hasFDerivWithinAt_τ⟧ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.fderivWithin_τ⟧. $\Phi$ is $C^{j-1}$ on $R$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.contDiffOn_Φ⟧, so $\tau \in C^i$, $i < j$, gives $D\tau = \Phi \circ (\mathrm{id}, \tau) \in C^i$ and $\tau \in C^{i+1}$: $\tau$ is $C^j$ on all of $V_0$ ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · Radii.contDiffOn_τ⟧. The text iterates $f \mapsto f^{(1)}$ (the finite-dimensional model of Lemma 3.31) and concludes "on a possibly smaller neighbourhood"; in finite dimensions there are no levels to shift and no shrinking is needed. *Assembly* ⟦Chapter3/QuadrantIFT · ContractionData.exists_solution⟧: $V' = V_0$, $\sigma = b$, $\varepsilon$ below $a$; (1) $Lf(k + \tau(k)) = \tau(k) - B(k, \tau(k)) = 0$ and $L$ is injective; (3) $f(k + y) = 0$ means $B(k, y) = y$ with $(k, y) \in R$.

### III.18 Weak stability of basic germs: Theorem 3.38

**Theorem 3.38** (text): for a basic germ $f$ and the principal part $s$ of an sc⁺-section with $s(0) = 0$ there is a strong bundle isomorphism $\Phi$ covering an sc-diffeomorphism $\varphi$ such that $(\Phi_*(f + s))^1$, with the levels raised by one, is a basic germ, and $n - N = n' - N'$. The text's proof: with $A = P_W \circ D_2s(0)$, $1 + A$ is sc-Fredholm of index $0$, with sc-splittings $W = C \oplus X = R \oplus Z$, $C = \ker(1 + A)$, $R = \mathrm{range}(1 + A)$; $P_W \circ s(a, w) = Aw + S(a, w)$ with $S$ a small contraction in $w$ on every level $m \ge 1$; and with $L = (1 + A)|_X : X \to R$ the equation becomes $x - L^{-1}P_2\bar B(a, c + x) = 0$ in the new parameters $(a, c)$ and the new fibre variable $x$. The formal proof follows it with two observations: the coordinate change is *linear*, and the index raise is a *change of sc-structure*.

*The linear part of $s$.* For an sc¹-germ $s$ into $W^1$, $A = D_2s(0)$ is an sc⁺-operator whose level-$m$ map is the level operator of Proposition 1.16 at $0 \in U_{m+1}$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · scPlusOfDeriv⟧. The remainder $S(a, w) = s(a, w) - Aw$ on level $m + 1$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · scPlusRemainder⟧ is, for $a$ and $w$ small depending on $m$ and $\varepsilon$, an $\varepsilon$-contraction in $w$: $D_2S(0) = 0$ on level $m + 1$, the derivative of $s : U_{m+1} \to W_{m+1}$ is continuous in the operator norm (§III.1), and the mean value inequality on a ball for fixed $a$ concludes ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · scPlusRemainder_contraction⟧. The partial derivative of $S$ in $a$ does not vanish and plays no role. The text gives this one sentence ("$S$ is … an arbitrary small contraction on every level $m \ge 1$").

*The data and the splitting.* The data of the theorem are the germ $G$, the $W$-component $s$ of the sc⁺-germ with $s(0) = 0$, and an sc-Fredholm splitting $W = C \oplus X = R \oplus Z$ of $T = 1 + A$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData⟧. Such data exist: the identity is sc-Fredholm of index $0$ (the trivial splitting) ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · isScFredholm_id⟧ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · scIndex_id⟧, so $1 + A$ is sc-Fredholm by Proposition 1.10 ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.exists_of_scPlus⟧. With the projections $P_1 : W_m \to X_m$ along $C_m$, $P_2 : W_m \to R_m$ along $Z_m$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.projX⟧ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.projR⟧, $L = T|_X : X_m \to R_m$ is bijective ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.Lm_bijective⟧, a topological isomorphism by the open mapping theorem ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.Lequiv⟧, and $L^{-1}P_2$ is an sc-operator $W \to X$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.LinvPOp⟧. The finite-dimensional $C$, $Z \subseteq W_\infty$ lift to every level ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · ScBanach.finLift⟧.

*The coordinate changes.* On the index-raised spaces, the new source is $E' = (P \oplus C) \oplus X^1$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.E'⟧ and the new target $F' = (Q \oplus Z) \oplus X^1$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.F'⟧ — the text's $\tau : Z \to C$, making the new finite-dimensional target $\mathbb R^N \oplus C$, is not applied. The base change $\psi(a, w) = ((a, (1 - P_1)w), P_1w)$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.split⟧ and its inverse $\psi^{-1}((a, c), x) = (a, c + x)$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.glue⟧ are sc-operators inverse to each other ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.glue_split⟧ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.split_glue⟧; so are the fibre change $\Psi(q, w) = ((q, (1 - P_2)w), L^{-1}P_2w)$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.fiber⟧ and $\Psi^{-1}((q, z), x) = (q, z + (1 + A)x)$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.fiberInv⟧ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.fiber_fiberInv⟧ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.fiberInv_fiber⟧, and $\Psi$ vanishes only at $0$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.fiber_eq_zero_iff⟧. No general strong bundle isomorphism is needed.

*The push-forward.* The perturbed germ is $f + \iota s$ with the inclusion $W^1 \to Q \oplus W$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · ScBanach.inrOp⟧ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.fsum⟧, sc-smooth by the pairing and operator rules ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.fsum_isScSmoothGerm⟧. Its germ of neighbourhoods on $E'$ is $\psi(U_{m+1})$, the preimage of $U_{m+1}$ under $\psi^{-1}$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.pushGerm⟧ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.glue_mapsToGerm⟧, and the push-forward is $(\Phi_*(f + s))^1 = \Psi \circ (f + \iota s)^1 \circ \psi^{-1}$ with the level-shifted operators ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · ScOperator.shiftOp⟧ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.pushMap⟧. It is sc-smooth: $(f + \iota s)^1$ is sc-smooth on the shifted germ (Proposition 1.17 for germs) and $\Psi$, $\psi^{-1}$ are sc-operators ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.pushMap_isScSmoothGerm⟧. With $\bar B = B - S$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.Bbar⟧, the $W$-component of $(f + \iota s)^1$ at a level-$1$ point is $(1 + A)w - \bar B(a, w)$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.snd_levelMap_fsum⟧, so the $X$-component of the push-forward is $x - \hat B((a, c), x)$ with $\hat B((a, c), x) = L^{-1}P_2\bar B(a, c + x)$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.pushB⟧ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.snd_pushMap⟧ — the text's "desired formula". $\hat B$ is an sc⁰-contraction germ on the index-raised structure: on level $m$ of $E'$, i.e. level $m + 1$ of $W$, $B$ contracts by Definition 3.7 and $S$ by the remainder estimate, and $L^{-1}P_2$ is bounded ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.levelMap_pushB⟧ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.pushB_isSc0ContractionGerm⟧. So **the push-forward is a basic germ with contraction map $\hat B$** ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · theorem_3_38⟧. Its zeros correspond to those of $f + \iota s$ under $\psi$, since $\Psi$ is a linear isomorphism ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.pushMap_eq_zero_iff⟧. *The index*: $\mathrm{ind}(1 + A) = \mathrm{ind}(1) = 0$ (Proposition 1.10 with its index), i.e. $\dim C = \dim Z$, so $n' - N' = (n + \dim C) - (N + \dim Z) = n - N$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.finrank_Cs_eq_finrank_Zs⟧.

*The same on level $0$.* For §§III.19–III.20 the coordinate changes are also needed before the index raise: $\psi$, $\psi^{-1}$, $\Psi$, $\Psi^{-1}$ on every level ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.split₀⟧ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.glue₀⟧ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.fiber₀⟧, the germ $\psi(U_m)$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.pushGerm₀⟧, and $g = \Phi_*(f + s) = \Psi \circ (f + \iota s) \circ \psi^{-1}$ on level $0$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.pushMap₀⟧, sc-smooth ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.pushMap₀_isScSmoothGerm⟧, whose level-$1$ map is the index-raised push-forward ⟦Chapter3/BasicClass · StabilityData.pushMap_eq_levelMap_pushMap₀⟧.

### III.19 The linearization at nearby solutions: Corollary 3.41

**Corollary 3.41.** For the data of Theorem 3.38 with $f := h$ basic and $D(h + \iota s)(0)$ surjective, there is $r > 0$ such that every zero $x$ of $h + \iota s$ in $U_0$ with $|x|_0 < r$ is $\iota(x_1)$ with $x_1 \in U_1$, and $D(h + \iota s)(x_1) : E_0 \to F_0$ is a surjective Fredholm operator of index $\dim P - \dim Q$ ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · StabilityData.corollary_3_41⟧. The text's sc⁺-map $s$ has an $\mathbb R^N$-component; it can be absorbed into the basic germ (as in §III.23), so the data carry only the $W$-component.

*The derivative on $U_1$.* For $x \in U_1$, $D(h + \iota s)(x) = Dh(x) + \iota Ds(x)$ — uniqueness of the derivative within $U_1$, then density of $E_1$ ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · StabilityData.Dfs'_eq⟧ — and $\mathrm{pr}_W Dh(x) = \mathrm{pr}_W - DB(x)$, from $\mathrm{pr}_W h = \mathrm{pr}_W - B$ on $U_0$ ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · StabilityData.snd_Df_eq⟧; $D_2B(0) = 0$ ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · StabilityData.DB_zero_snd⟧. *The decomposition.* $D(h + \iota s)(x) = D(h + \iota s)(0) + S(x) + K(x)$ with $S(x)(\alpha, \zeta) = (0, -D_2B(x)\zeta)$ ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · StabilityData.Sop⟧ ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · StabilityData.Dfs'_eq_add⟧ of norm $\le \varepsilon$ for $x \in U_1$ small on level $1$, by Lemma 3.9 (c) ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · StabilityData.exists_norm_Sop_le⟧, and $K(x)$ ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · StabilityData.Kop⟧ compact: the sum of finite-rank operators through $Q$ and through $P$ and of $\iota(Ds(x) - Ds(0))$ through the compact inclusion $W_1 \to W_0$ ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · StabilityData.Kop_isCompactOperator⟧.

*Fredholm with index $n - N$ at every small $x \in U_1$.* $D(h + \iota s)(0)$ is Fredholm of index $n - N$: $Dh(0)$ is (Proposition 3.10 for the basic germ, §III.5) and $\iota Ds(0)$ is compact ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · StabilityData.isFredholm_Dfs⟧. A small perturbation of a Fredholm operator is Fredholm: if $v$ is a quasi-inverse of $u$ and $\|v\|\|s\| < 1$, then $(1 + vs)^{-1}v$ is a quasi-inverse of $u + s$ (Neumann series) ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · isFredholm_add_of_norm_lt⟧, with the same index ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · isFredholm_fredholmIndex_add_of_norm_lt⟧; a compact perturbation does not change the index ⟦Chapter1/FredholmIndex · fredholmIndex_add_isCompactOperator⟧. So $D(h + \iota s)(x)$ is Fredholm of index $n - N$ for *every* $x \in U_1$ small on level $1$, not only at solutions ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · StabilityData.exists_isFredholm_Dfs'⟧.

*Surjectivity: the compactness argument.* Let $N$ be a closed complement of $\ker D(h + \iota s)(0)$. Then $\ker D(h + \iota s)(x) \cap N = 0$ for $x \in U_1$ small on level $1$ ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · StabilityData.exists_ker_Dfs'_inf_eq_bot⟧. Otherwise there are $x_k \to 0$ in $E_1$ and unit vectors $(\alpha_k, \zeta_k) \in N$ in the kernels; the $W$-component of the equation reads $\zeta_k = D_1B(x_k)\alpha_k + D_2B(x_k)\zeta_k - \iota Ds(x_k)(\alpha_k, \zeta_k)$. $\alpha_k$ has a convergent subsequence ($P$ finite-dimensional); $Ds(x_k)(\alpha_k, \zeta_k)$ is bounded in $W_1$ (the derivatives near $0$ are uniformly bounded ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · IsSc1GermWith.exists_norm_deriv_le⟧), so its image in $W_0$ has a convergent subsequence; $D_1B(x_k)\alpha_k \to D_1B(0)\alpha$ by the joint continuity of the tangent map ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · IsSc1GermWith.tendsto_deriv⟧; and $\|D_2B(x_k)\| \to 0$. So $\zeta_k$ converges, $(\alpha_k, \zeta_k) \to (\alpha, z_0) \in N$ of norm $1$ in $\ker D(h + \iota s)(0)$ — a contradiction. (The text uses the Neumann series $\zeta_k = \sum(D_2B(x_k))^l z_k$; here $|\zeta_k - z_k| \le \varepsilon_k \to 0$ suffices.) Then $\dim\ker D(h + \iota s)(x) \le \dim\ker D(h + \iota s)(0) = n - N = \mathrm{ind}$, and an operator of finite index with $\dim\ker \le \mathrm{ind}$ is onto ⟦Chapter3/SolutionLinearization · HasFiniteIndex.surjective_of_finrank_ker_le⟧ — instead of the text's "$Df(x)|_N$ has index $0$ and is injective". *Zeros are on level $1$ and small there*: by the lifts of Theorem 3.40, continuous at $0$ (§III.12); the text's detour through "bounded on level $2$, hence convergent on level $1$" is not needed.

### III.20 Local solvability: Lemma 3.46, Theorem 3.43, Lemmas 3.42, 3.44, Corollary 3.47

**Lemma 3.46** (Appendix 3.8.2). If $K' = \{(\alpha, L\alpha) : \alpha \in \widetilde K\}$, the image of the graph map ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · graphMap⟧ (with $(\alpha, L\alpha) \in \widetilde C \oplus W$ iff $\alpha \in \widetilde C$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · graphMap_mem_prod_iff⟧), has a good complement $Y'$ with respect to $\widetilde C \oplus W$, then $\widetilde K$ has a good complement $Z$ with respect to $\widetilde C$ such that $Z \times W$ is a good complement of $K'$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · lemma_3_46⟧. *Proof.* $Z' := \mathrm{pr}_P(Y')$ satisfies $P = \widetilde K + Z'$; choose $Z \subseteq Z'$ with $P = \widetilde K \oplus Z$ and a linear right inverse $\rho : Z' \to Y'$ of the projection (bounded, finite dimensions); for $|z| \le \varepsilon'|\alpha|$, $\varepsilon' = \varepsilon/(\|\rho\| + 1)$, $y = \rho(z) = (z, w) \in Y'$ has $|y| \le \varepsilon|(\alpha, L\alpha)|$, so $(\alpha, L\alpha) \in C'$ iff $(\alpha, L\alpha) + y \in C'$, i.e. $\alpha \in \widetilde C$ iff $\alpha + z \in \widetilde C$. The text's intermediate complement $Y_0$ is not needed. Good position of $K'$ gives good position of $\widetilde K$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · lemma_3_46_isInGoodPosition⟧.

**Projecting solutions into the quadrant.** A gap in the text's proof of Theorem 3.43 (3): a solution $a = k + z$ ($k \in \widetilde K$, $z \in Z$) of $H(a) = 0$ is matched with the solution of Theorem 3.78 by its uniqueness clause, which needs $k \in \widetilde C$ — not verified in the text. It holds because $z$ is small compared with $k$: from $H(a) = 0 = H(0)$ and $DH(0)k = 0$, $|DH(0)z| = o(|a|)$; $DH(0)$ is injective on $Z$, hence bounded below there ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · exists_norm_le_of_injOn⟧; so $|z| \le \varepsilon|k|$ near $0$, and the good-complement property gives $k \in \widetilde C$ from $k + z = a \in \widetilde C$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · exists_proj_mem_of_eq_zero⟧.

**The data of Theorem 3.43.** The text states it for $g = \Phi_*(f + s)$; the formal statement is for any sc-smooth germ $g$ on $G$ with $g(0) = 0$ whose index-raised germ $g^1$ on the shifted germ is a basic germ with contraction map $B$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData⟧. Its solution germ $\delta$ (of the working form of $B$) takes values in $W_1$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.δ⟧, with $\mathrm{pr}_W g(a, \delta(a)) = 0$ on level $0$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.snd_g_sol⟧ and uniqueness in the contraction region ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.eq_δ⟧. Put $H(a) = \mathrm{pr}_Q\,g(a, \delta(a))$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.H⟧. *Regularity of $H$* (the text: "$H$ restricted to $U'_i$ is of class $C^{i-1}$"): for every $j \ge 1$ there is a relatively open $V \ni 0$ in $\widetilde C$ on which $H$ is $C^j$ — by Corollary 3.34 for $g^1$, $\delta$ lifts to a $C^j$ map into $W_{2j}$, and $g : E_{2j} \to F_j$ is $C^j$ by Proposition 1.18 for germs ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.H_contDiffOn⟧. A single $C^1$ neighbourhood $V_1$ carries the derivative data ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Deriv⟧ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.exists_deriv⟧: $D\delta(0) : P \to W_1$, $L = \iota D\delta(0)$, and $DH(0) = \mathrm{pr}_Q Dg(0)(\alpha, L\alpha)$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Deriv.DH₀⟧ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Deriv.hasFDerivWithinAt_H⟧, by the chain rule for $a \mapsto g(a, \delta(a))$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Deriv.hasFDerivWithinAt_comp⟧.

**Lemma 3.44.** "Recalling from Lemma 3.9 that $D_2B(0) = 0$": Lemma 3.9 gives this for $g^1$, on level $1$; the kernel of $Dg(0)$ is computed on level $0$. So first the $W$-component of $Dg(0)(0, \zeta)$ is $\zeta$ for $\zeta \in W_1$, by Lemma 3.9 (b) for $g^1$, and then for all $\zeta \in W_0$ by density ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Deriv.snd_Dg_inr⟧. Differentiating $\mathrm{pr}_W g(a, \delta(a)) = 0$ at $0$ gives $\mathrm{pr}_W Dg(0)(\alpha, L\alpha) = 0$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Deriv.snd_Dg_graph⟧. Hence $Dg(0)(\alpha, \zeta) = 0$ iff $\zeta = L\alpha$ and $DH(0)\alpha = 0$: $\ker Dg(0) = \{(\alpha, D\delta(0)\alpha) : \alpha \in \ker DH(0)\}$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Deriv.ker_Dg_eq⟧, and $DH(0)$ is onto when $Dg(0)$ is ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Deriv.DH₀_surjective⟧.

**Theorem 3.43** ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · theorem_3_43⟧. Hypotheses: $\widetilde C$ a partial quadrant, $Dg(0)$ onto, $K' = \ker Dg(0)$ in good position to $\widetilde C \oplus W$, and *the regularity of Lemma 3.42 as an explicit hypothesis*: for every $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $r > 0$ such that every zero $x$ of $g$ in $U_0$ with $|x|_0 < r$ has $W$-component $\iota(w_1)$, $|w_1|_1 < \varepsilon$. *The choices* ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Sol⟧ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.exists_sol⟧: $\widetilde K = \ker DH(0)$ with $K'$ its graph (Lemma 3.44); the good complement $Z$ of $\widetilde K$ with $Z \oplus W$ good for $K'$ (Lemma 3.46); and the solution $\sigma : V' \to Z$ of $H(k + \sigma(k)) = 0$ with its uniqueness constants, from Theorem 3.78 applied to $H$ (§III.17). Then $\tau(y) = (\sigma(v), \delta(v + \sigma(v)) - Lv)$ for $y = (v, Lv)$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Sol.τ⟧ on $V = \pi^{-1}(V')$, relatively open in $K' \cap C'$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Sol.V⟧ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Sol.V_relOpen⟧, with values in $Z \oplus W$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Sol.τ_mem_Y⟧, so that $y + \tau(y) = (a, \delta(a))$ with $a = v + \sigma(v)$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Sol.coe_add_τ⟧. (3), first half: $y + \tau(y)$ lies in $U_0$ and is a zero, since $\mathrm{pr}_W g(a, \delta(a)) = 0$ and $\mathrm{pr}_Q g(a, \delta(a)) = H(a) = 0$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Sol.sol_mem_and_eq_zero⟧. Regularity: $\tau$ is $C^1$ on $V$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Sol.τ_contDiffOn⟧ with $W$-component on level $1$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Sol.snd_τ_mem_range⟧, and $D\tau(0)\eta = -D\delta(0)\pi(\eta) + D\delta(0)\pi(\eta) = 0$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Sol.hasFDerivWithinAt_τ⟧ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Sol.fderivWithin_τ⟧ — (2). (3), second half ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Sol.exists_eq_add_τ⟧: a zero $x = (a, w)$ near $0$ has, by the regularity hypothesis, $w$ on level $1$ and small there, so $w = \delta(a)$ by the uniqueness of the solution germ on level $1$, so $H(a) = 0$; write $a = k + z$ with the projection along $Z$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Sol.projK⟧; then $k \in \widetilde K \cap \widetilde C$ (the gap above) and $z = \sigma(k)$ by the uniqueness clause of Theorem 3.78; so $x = y + \tau(y)$ for $y = (k, Lk)$. *Clause (1), "$\tau$ is an sc-smooth germ"*, is proved level-wise: for every $k \ge 1$ there are a relatively open $V_k \subseteq V$ containing $0$ and a $C^k$ map $\tau_k : V_k \to E_k = P \oplus W_k$ with $\iota_k\tau_k = \tau$ on $V_k$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · ShiftedBasicData.Sol.exists_contDiffOn_level⟧ — the reading of Corollary 3.34 and Definition 3.25 (ii). The proof applies Theorem 3.78 to $H$ at regularity $k$ on the neighbourhood of its regularity lemma, and identifies the $C^k$ solution $\sigma_k$ with $\sigma$ near $0$ through the uniqueness clause (3) of Theorem 3.78 — which needs $\sigma$ continuous at $0$ with $\sigma(0) = 0$, so that $|\sigma(y)|$ is below the uniqueness constant for $y$ small; the text says nothing about why the solutions produced for the different $k$ coincide. The $W$-component $\iota\delta(a) - L\pi(y)$, $a = \pi y + \sigma(\pi y)$, lifts to $W_k$ through the $C^k$ lift of $\delta$ into $W_{2k}$, with $L$ the derivative of that lift at $0$ composed with the inclusion (uniqueness of the derivative of $\iota\delta$ at $0$). The full statement is ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · theorem_3_43_sc_smooth⟧; the statement without (1) is kept for Theorem 3.54.

**Lemma 3.42.** For the push-forward $g = \Phi_*(f + s)$ of Theorem 3.38 — packaged as the data of Theorem 3.43, $g$ on level $0$ with index-raised basic germ $(\Phi_*(f + s))^1$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · StabilityData.toShiftedBasicData⟧ — the regularity hypothesis holds: a zero $x'$ of $g$ in $\psi(U_0)$ with $|x'|_0$ small has $\psi^{-1}(x')$ a zero of $f + \iota s$, which by the lifts of Theorem 3.40, continuous at $0$, lies on level $1$ and is small there; $\psi$ is linear on level $1$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · StabilityData.lemma_3_42⟧.

**Corollary 3.47** ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · theorem_3_47_sc_smooth⟧ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · theorem_3_47⟧. For a basic germ $f$ and the data of Theorem 3.38 with $D(f + \iota s)(0)$ surjective and kernel $K$ in good position to $C = \widetilde C \oplus W$: a good complement $Y$, $V$ relatively open in $K \cap C$, $\sigma : V \to Y$ of class $C^1$ with values on level $1$, $\sigma(0) = 0$, $D\sigma(0) = 0$, the graph consisting of zeros of $f + \iota s$, an open $U'' \ni 0$ in which every zero lies on the graph, and for every $k$ a $C^k$ lift of $\sigma$ into $E_k$ near $0$. *Proof.* Theorem 3.43 for $g = \Phi_*(f + s)$, with Lemma 3.42 for its regularity hypothesis. Since the coordinate change is linear, $Dg(0) = \Psi \circ D(f + \iota s)(0) \circ \psi^{-1}$ (chain rule for sc-operators) ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · StabilityData.scDerivGerm_pushMap₀⟧, so surjectivity and the kernels correspond, $\ker Dg(0) = \psi(K)$; good position of $\psi(K)$ follows by Lemma 3.45 (finite dimensionality of $K$ from Lemma 3.44); and the conclusion is transported back by $\psi^{-1}$: $Y = \psi^{-1}(Y')$, $V = \psi^{-1}(V')$, $\sigma = \psi^{-1}\tau\psi$. The text transports the solution set back with the nonlinear $\varphi$ and justifies the good position with the degeneracy index (Lemma 3.70, Theorem 3.72); with $\psi$ linear neither is needed. The transport uses that $\widetilde C \oplus C$ is a partial quadrant for finite-dimensional $C$ ⟦Chapter3/LocalSolvability · IsPartialQuadrant.const_prod_univ⟧.

### III.21 The linearization at a zero (Proposition 3.52) and good position of a germ (Definition 3.53)

**Proposition 3.52** (text): if $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section of a tame strong bundle and $f(x) = 0$, then $Tf(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ is an sc-Fredholm operator. Formalized in the chart of Definition 3.11 centred at a zero $x_0$, with the level-$0$ Fredholm property ⟦Chapter3/FredholmGermLinearizationG · proposition_3_52⟧ ⟦Chapter3/FredholmGermLinearizationG · proposition_3_52_local⟧: $Dg(0) : E_0 \to F_0$ and $Tf(x_0) = Dg(0)|_{T_0O} : T_0O \to K_0$ are Fredholm with $\mathrm{ind}\,Tf(x_0) = \mathrm{ind}\,Dg(0)$. Here $Dg(0)$ is the value at $0$ of a derivative family $Dg$ of the filling germ on a germ $G$ with $G_0 \subseteq U$, the same for every family and every germ (§III.4); the statement exposes $G$ and $Dg$, where the whole-chart statement ⟦Chapter3/FredholmGermLinearization · proposition_3_52_wholeChart⟧ has the derivative on $U$, a junk value for a germ. (The sc-Fredholm property of $Tf(x)$ would need $T_0O = Dr(0)E$ and $K_0 = \rho(0)F$ as sc-Banach spaces, not set up. The statements quantify the index as "$n - N$ for some natural numbers $n$, $N$", which every integer satisfies; the identification with $\dim P - \dim Q$ of the conjugating basic germ is made inside the proof, by `proposition_3_10_basic_level_zero`, and not exported.)

*Step (a): the derivative of the conjugation* ⟦Chapter3/FredholmGermLinearizationG · IsConjugateToBasicGerm.scDeriv_isFredholm⟧. Let $k = g - \iota s$, an sc¹-germ on $G_g \cap G_s$ (§III.48) with $k(0) = 0$ ($s(0) = g(0)$ in Definition 3.11, $g(0) = \mathbf f(0) = 0$ by the filler) and $(\Psi(u, k(u)))_2 = h(\psi(u))$ near $0$. Linearizing needs: the chain rule for the germ $h \circ \psi$ on a germ small enough that $\psi$ maps it into the germ of $h$ (§III.1, `ScNbhdGerm.preimage`); the derivative of $u \mapsto \Gamma(u)k(u)$ at $0$, where $\Gamma(u) = (\Psi(u, \cdot))_2$ is a bounded operator ⟦Chapter3/FredholmGermLinearization · IsStrongBundleMap.fiberCLM⟧ and $D(\mathrm{pr}_{F'} \circ \Psi)(0, 0)(h, k) = \Gamma(0)k$ (as in §III.4) ⟦Chapter3/FredholmGermLinearization · IsStrongBundleMap.scDeriv_fiber_zero⟧, so the derivative is $\Gamma(0)Dk(0)$ because $k(0) = 0$ ⟦Chapter3/FredholmGermLinearization · IsStrongBundleMap.scDeriv_fiber_comp⟧ — for the germ $k$ by the chain rule with the whole-chart outer map $\mathrm{pr}_{F'} \circ \Psi$, the two derivative families agreeing at $0$ on $G_k \cap \psi^{-1}(G)$ ⟦Chapter3/FredholmGermLinearizationG · IsStrongBundleIso.fiberCLM_comp_deriv_zero_eq_germ⟧, so no shrinking of the basic germ is needed at $0$; and the invertibility of $D\psi(0)$ and $\Gamma(0)$ (inverses $D\psi'(0)$, $\Gamma'(0)$, chain rule for $\psi' \circ \psi = \mathrm{id}$). Then $\Gamma(0)Dk(0) = Dh(0)D\psi(0)$, so $Dk(0) = \Gamma(0)^{-1}Dh(0)D\psi(0)$ is Fredholm with the index of $Dh(0)$: Fredholm operators and their index are stable under composition with isomorphisms on both sides ⟦Chapter3/FredholmGermLinearization · isFredholm_equiv_comp_equiv⟧, and $Dh(0)$ is Fredholm by Proposition 3.10 for the basic germ ⟦Chapter3/FredholmGermLinearization · proposition_3_10_basic_level_zero⟧. *Step (b)*: $Dg(0) = Dk(0) + \iota Ds(0)$ — for germs this is algebra at $0$: $g - \iota s$ has the derivative family $Dg - \iota Ds$ on $G_g \cap G_s$ ⟦Chapter3/FredholmGermLinearizationG · IsSc1GermWith.sub_toBase_shift⟧ ⟦Chapter3/FredholmGermLinearizationG · IsSc1GermWith.deriv_zero_eq_add_scPlus⟧ (on $U$ it was the uniqueness of the derivative within $U_1$ and density) — a compact perturbation since $\iota Ds(0)$ is the level-$0$ map of an sc⁺-operator ($s$ is an sc¹-germ into $F^1$ and $0$ is smooth); the index is unchanged (Part I, §I.9). *Step (c)*: Proposition 3.5 (§III.4) transfers both to $Tf(x_0)$; it needs $g(0) = 0$.

**Definition 3.53** (text): $(f, x)$ with $f(x) = 0$ is in good position if (1) $f'(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ is onto and (2) if $d_X(x) \ge 1$, $\ker f'(x)$ is in good position to the partial cone $C_xX$ in $T_xX$. In the chart: Definition 3.21 *inside a subspace* $T \subseteq E_0$ — $N \subseteq T$, interior of $N \cap C$ in $N$ nonempty, and a good complement $P \subseteq T$ of $N$ in $T$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGerm · IsInGoodPositionIn⟧ (for $T = E_0$ it is Definition 3.21 ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGerm · isInGoodPositionIn_top_iff⟧); and the germ is in good position if $Tf(0) = Dg(0)|_{T_0O}$ is onto and $\ker Dg(0)$ is in good position to $T_0O \cap C$ inside $T_0O = Dr(0)E$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGerm · IsGoodPositionAt⟧ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGerm · IsGoodPositionAt.surjective_fillerRestrict⟧. Here $\ker Dg(0) \subseteq T_0O$, because $(1 - \rho(0))Dg(0)$ is injective on $\ker Dr(0)$ (filler (3)) and $(1 - \rho(0))Dg(0)Dr(0) = 0$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGerm · IsFillerOf.ker_deriv_le_range⟧, and it is the kernel of $Tf(0)$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGerm · IsFillerOf.map_ker_fillerRestrict⟧ — the text's "$\ker Tf(0) \oplus \{0\} = \ker Dg(0)$ by the properties of the filler". The case distinction $d_X(x) \ge 1$ is dropped: at an interior point the partial cone is the whole tangent space and (2) holds for every subspace. For a filling germ the condition is one on the operator $Dg(0)$ (the text's $f'(x)$ is defined through the filler at the centre only), which the chart notion takes as a parameter ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGermG · IsGoodPositionAtGerm⟧ — the notion above is the case of the derivative on $U$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGermG · isGoodPositionAt_iff_germ⟧ — and the two kernel facts hold with the same proofs ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGermG · IsFillingGerm.ker_deriv_le_range⟧ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGermG · IsFillingGerm.map_ker_fillerRestrict⟧. For a section, $(f, x_0)$ is in good position if it has the data of Definition 3.11 at $x_0$ and a derivative family $Dg$ of the filling germ on a germ inside $U$, with the germ in good position at $Dg(0)$ in that chart ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGermG · StrongBundle.IsGoodPositionGerm⟧; as $Dg(0)$ does not depend on the family, "for some family" and "for every family" agree ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGermG · StrongBundle.IsGoodPositionGerm.forall_isGoodPositionAtGerm⟧; it is then an sc-Fredholm germ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGermG · StrongBundle.IsGoodPositionGerm.isScFredholmGerm⟧. The definition is in a chart, not in $T_xX$; the transport of $C_xX$ to $T_xX$ (Definition 2.38) is not formalized.

### III.22 Good position along a graph: Lemma 3.55

**Lemma 3.55** (text, Appendix 3.8.3): for $N$ in good position to $C$ with good complement $Y$, $V \subseteq N \cap C$ relatively open and $\tau : V \to Y_1$ of class $C^1$ with $\tau(0) = 0$, $D\tau(0) = 0$, for $v$ near $0$: (1) $v + \tau(v) \in C_1$; (2) $Y$ is a topological complement of $N_v = \{n + D\tau(v)n\}$; (3) for some $\gamma_v > 0$, $n \in C_x \iff n + y \in C_x$ for $n \in N_v$, $y \in Y$, $|y|_0 \le \gamma_v|n|_0$, $x = v + \tau(v)$. *Formalized* ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionOpen · lemma_3_55⟧ in the model $\mathbb R^n \oplus W$, with the core in coordinates for any $C$ cut out by functionals ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionOpen · lemma_3_55_core⟧: for $N$ in good position with good complement $Y$, **$Y$ closed**, and $\tau : N \to E$ with values in $Y$, $C^1$ on $N \cap C$, $\tau(0) = 0$, $D\tau(0) = 0$: there is $\rho > 0$ such that for $v \in N \cap C$, $|v| < \rho$, $v + \tau(v) \in C$ and $Y$ is a good complement of $N_v$ (the subspace $\{n + Ln\}$ for $L = D\tau(v)$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionOpen · graphSpace⟧) with respect to the partial quadrant $C_{v + \tau(v)}$.

*The added hypothesis.* The step "$D\tau(v)n \in Y$ for all $n \in N$" needs $Y$ closed: the derivative within $N \cap C$ at a point of unique differentiability of a map with values in a closed subspace takes values there, because the tangent cone of a subset of a closed subspace lies in it ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionOpen · tangentConeAt_subset_of_subset_closed⟧ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionOpen · fderivWithin_mem_of_mapsTo⟧; for a non-closed algebraic complement it fails. The text's $Y = Y_0$ is a topological complement, hence closed. With $Y$ closed, (2) is linear algebra: $E_0 = N_v \oplus Y$ whenever $E_0 = N \oplus Y$ and $L$ takes values in $Y$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionOpen · graphSpace_isCompl⟧, and $N_v$ is closed (finite-dimensional) ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionOpen · graphSpace_isClosed⟧.

*The estimate.* (1) is Lemma 3.70's smallness: $|\tau(v)| \le \varepsilon|v|$ near $0$ and good position. For (3), take $\varepsilon_0 = \min(\varepsilon, 1)$ and the neighbourhood where $\|D\tau(v)\| \le \varepsilon_0/4$; then $\gamma = \varepsilon_0/4$ works *for every $v$*, since $\gamma(1 + \varepsilon_0/4) + \varepsilon_0/4 \le \varepsilon_0$ (the text: $\gamma_v(1 + \varepsilon) + \varepsilon < \gamma$, with $\gamma_v$ chosen after $v$). If $v \in N \cap W$, $C_x = C$ and the estimate transfers the good-complement property from $N$ to $N_v$. If $v \notin N \cap W$, no normal form is needed: if $\ell_i(v) = 0$ then $i \in \Sigma$, so $\ell_i$ vanishes on $Y$ (Lemma 3.65), and $\ell_i(v + \tau(v)) = 0$ iff $\ell_i(v) = 0$ (Lemma 3.70); so $\ell_i(h + y) = \ell_i(h)$ for every coordinate $i$ that defines $C_x$, and (3) holds for every $\gamma$. The text's cases $\dim N = 1$, $\dim N > 1$ are not needed, and the sc-level of the values of $\tau$ plays no role. The formal $\tau$ is given on all of $N \cap C$ rather than on a neighbourhood $V$; the conclusion is local.

### III.23 Theorem 3.54: the linear part and the graph description of the solution set

**Theorem 3.54** (text): for an sc-Fredholm section $f$ of a tame strong bundle with $f(x) = 0$ and $(f, x)$ in good position there is an open $V \ni x$ such that $S = \{y \in V : f(y) = 0\}$ satisfies (1) $(f, y)$ is in good position at every $y \in S$, and (2) $S$ is a sub-M-polyfold with the structure of a manifold with boundary with corners. The proof: the linear part (surjectivity and good position transported from $T_xX$ to the chart and the push-forward); (3), the graph description of $S$ from Corollary 3.47 for $\Psi_*(g) = h + t$; then Corollary 3.41 and Lemma 3.55 for (1), and Theorem 3.27 for (2). Formalized: the linear part and (3).

*The linear part* ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGermG · theorem_3_54_linear⟧. In the chart, with the germ in good position and $(1 - Dr(0))E \subseteq E_0$ (the minimal subspace at the corner $0$; Proposition 2.35 for the tame retraction $r$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGermG · theorem_3_54_linear_of_isTameWith⟧ ⟦Chapter2/TameRetracts · proposition_2_35⟧): $Dg(0)$ is onto (Proposition 3.5 for the filling germ, §III.4, from the surjectivity of $Tf(0)$), and $\ker Dg(0)$ is in good position to $C$ in $E$; only the filler at $0$ enters, and $r$ is whole-chart, so $Dr(0)$ is a genuine derivative. The latter is the *transport lemma*: for a bounded idempotent $\pi$ with $(1 - \pi)E_0$ inside the minimal subspace at $0$, good position inside $\pi E_0$ gives good position in $E_0$, with the good complement $P \oplus (1 - \pi)E_0$ and the constant $\varepsilon/(\|\pi\| + 1)$ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGerm · IsInGoodPositionIn.isInGoodPosition⟧. Two points the text passes over: for $p = z + k$ with $|p| \le \varepsilon'|n|$ the $T_0O$-component is $z = Dr(0)p$, so $|z| \le \|Dr(0)\|\varepsilon'|n|$ — the splitting must be topological; and $\ker Dr(0) \subseteq E_0$ is used only as "the $\mathbb R^n$-coordinates of $k$ vanish, so $n + z + k \in C \iff n + z \in C$". *This inclusion is the only place where tameness enters.*

*$C' = T\psi(0)C$.* Not part of the data of a conjugation (§III.6); it is a theorem: for an sc-diffeomorphism $\psi$ between relatively open subsets of partial quadrants with $\psi(0) = 0$, $x \in C \iff D\psi(0)x \in C'$, by the one-sided sign argument for $\psi$ and $\psi^{-1}$ (Part II, §II.12) ⟦Chapter2/Boundary · IsSc1With.mapsTo_partialQuadrant⟧, since $C_0 = C$ at the corner ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGerm · partialQuadrantAtWith_zero⟧ ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGerm · scDeriv_mem_iff_of_inverse⟧.

*The push-forward.* $\Psi_*(g)(u') = (\Psi(\psi^{-1}(u'), g(\psi^{-1}(u'))))_2$ ⟦Chapter3/GermPushforward · pushforward⟧ is an sc-smooth germ on the germ of the points that $\psi^{-1}$ maps into the germ of $g$ ⟦Chapter3/GermPushforward · IsStrongBundleIso.pullGerm⟧ ⟦Chapter3/GermPushforward · IsStrongBundleIso.pushforward_isScSmoothGerm⟧ (chain rules with the whole-chart $\Psi$ and $\psi^{-1}$, §III.48), with $\Psi_*(g)(0) = 0$ and $D(\Psi_*g)(0) = \Gamma(0)Dg(0)D\psi(0)^{-1}$ for its explicit derivative family ⟦Chapter3/GermPushforward · IsStrongBundleIso.pushforwardDeriv_zero⟧ ($Dk(0) = \Gamma(0)Dg(0)$ for $k(u) = (\Psi(u, g(u)))_2$) ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGermG · IsStrongBundleIso.pushforward_linearization⟧; so it is onto ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGermG · IsStrongBundleIso.pushforward_surjective⟧, its kernel $D\psi(0)(\ker Dg(0))$ is in good position to $C'$ (Lemma 3.45) ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGermG · IsStrongBundleIso.pushforward_ker_isInGoodPosition⟧, and it is Fredholm (transported from $Dg(0)$, Proposition 3.52) — the hypotheses of Corollary 3.47, for *any* conjugating isomorphism ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGermG · theorem_3_54_pushforward⟧, and in bundle form ⟦Chapter3/GoodPositionGermG · theorem_3_54_pushforward_section⟧. The text instead obtains the Fredholm property of $D(h + t)(0)$ from Propositions 3.10 and 1.10.

**The graph description** ⟦Chapter3/GlobalIFTG · theorem_3_54_graph⟧. Let the charts of the bundle have tame base retractions (`htame`, the hypothesis of the first formalization; it cannot be met, and it is replaced by good position in a tame chart, §III.47), $f(x_0) = 0$, $(f, x_0)$ in good position. The proof, in the order of the Lean.

1. *The chart and the identities.* Take the chart of Definition 3.53 centred at $x_0$, filling germ $g$ on $G_g$, sc⁺-germ $t_0$ on $G_s$ and conjugation $\Psi$ covering $\psi$, with inverse $\Psi'$ covering $\psi'$. *Shrink the basic germ* to the germ $G''$ of the points of $G$ that $\psi'$ sends into $G_g \cap G_s$ level by level: same $\Psi$, $h$, $B$ and conjugation identity ⟦Chapter3/BasicGermShrink · ConjugationData.shrink⟧ (§III.48); below, $G$ denotes $G''$. There is an open $N_1 \ni 0$ on which $\mathbf f = g$ on $O$, zeros of $g$ in $U$ lie in $O$, and $\Psi(u, (g - \iota t_0)(u))_2 = h(\psi(u))$ (filler (1), (2) and the conjugation).
2. *The sc⁺-germ $t$.* $t(u') = \Psi[1](\psi'(u'), t_0(\psi'(u')))_2$ is an sc-smooth germ into $(Q \oplus W)^1$ on $G$: $t_0 \circ \psi'$ is a germ on the preimage of $G_s$, which contains $G = G''$, and the whole-chart $\Psi[1]$ is composed on the outside (§III.48). (With $t_0$ sc-smooth on $U$, $t$ was sc-smooth on all of $U'$.) On $U \cap N_1$, $\Psi_*(g)(\psi(u)) = h(\psi(u)) + \iota t(\psi(u))$, by the linearity of the fibre maps.
3. *Absorbing the $\mathbb R^N$-component.* The data of Theorem 3.38 carry only the $W$-component of an sc⁺-germ. Let $t_Q$, $t_W$ be the two components of $t$, through the sc-operators $(q, w) \mapsto (q, 0)$ and $(q, w) \mapsto w$ ⟦Chapter3/GlobalIFT · ScBanach.qPartOp⟧ ⟦Chapter3/GlobalIFT · ScBanach.wPartOp⟧. Then $h' = h + (t_Q, 0)$ is again a basic germ with the same contraction $B$ (Definition 3.7 constrains only the $W$-component), and with the data $\mathcal S$ of Theorem 3.38 for $s = t_W$ (they exist, §III.18) one has $\mathcal S.\mathrm{fsum}\,h' = h' + \iota t_W = h + \iota t$.
4. *The hypotheses of Corollary 3.47.* Tameness gives $(1 - Dr(0))E \subseteq E_0$ (Proposition 2.35), so the push-forward step applies: $D(\Psi_*g)(0)$ is surjective with kernel in good position. Since $\mathcal S.\mathrm{fsum}\,h' = \Psi_*(g)$ only on a neighbourhood $W'$ of $0$, the two derivatives at $0$ are identified by the uniqueness of the derivative within $G''_1$ and density of $E_1$ ⟦Chapter3/GlobalIFT · scDeriv_eq_of_eqOn_nhds⟧; $\Psi_*(g)$ is a germ on the preimage of $G_g$, which contains $G''$.
5. *Corollary 3.47 for $h + t$* gives $Y$, $V_0$, $\sigma$ (good complement, $C^1$, level $1$, $\sigma(0) = 0$, $D\sigma(0) = 0$), the graph consisting of zeros, and $U''$ in which every zero lies on the graph.
6. *The neighbourhoods* (the text does not say which $V$). Let $\Omega = U'' \cap W'$ and $V' = V_0 \cap (1 + \sigma)^{-1}(\Omega)$, relatively open in $K \cap C'$ because $v \mapsto v + \sigma(v)$ is continuous. Let $V_x = \{y \in \mathrm{dom}\,\varphi : \varphi(y) \in N_1,\ \psi\varphi(y) \in \Omega \cap G_0\}$, open and containing $x_0$ by continuity of $\psi \circ \varphi$. $D\sigma(0) = 0$ persists on the smaller $V'$ (unique differentiability at $0$ of $V'$).
7. *The conclusions.* $\psi \circ \varphi$ is injective on $V_x$ ($\varphi$ is, and $\psi' \circ \psi = \mathrm{id}$ on $U$). For $y \in V_x$: $f(y) = 0 \iff \mathbf f(\varphi y) = 0 \iff g(\varphi y) = 0 \iff (h + \iota t)(\psi\varphi y) = 0$ (items 1–2). If $f(y) = 0$, then $\psi\varphi(y)$ is a zero in $U'' \cap G_0$, hence $v + \sigma(v)$ with $v \in V_0$, and $v \in V'$ since $v + \sigma(v) \in \Omega$. Conversely, for $v \in V'$, $u = \psi'(v + \sigma(v))$ lies in $U \cap N_1$, $g(u) = 0$, so $u \in O$ and $u = \varphi(y)$ for some $y$, which lies in $V_x$ and is a zero.

So $\psi\varphi(\{y \in V_x : f(y) = 0\}) = \{v + \sigma(v) : v \in V'\}$. When this section was written, (1) and (2) were not formalized; they are now: the kernel and good position at the nearby zeros in §§III.32–III.33 (the surjectivity of $f'(y)$ under an added hypothesis), the data of Definition 3.25 at every zero in §§III.34–III.36, and the theorem in §III.37. The graph description also records, since then, that $Y$ is closed, that the kernel is a smooth subspace and the level-wise lifts of $\sigma$ (Corollary 3.47 (1)), and it is a corollary of the version with a good complement whose projection maps $C'$ into itself (§III.29).

**Theorems 3.56 and 3.57, the step from the tangent germ property.** With $S = \{f = 0\}$ ⟦Chapter3/GlobalIFT · solutionSet⟧: if $S \ne \emptyset$ has at every point regular data of Definition 3.25 (§III.24), then $S$ is a sub-M-polyfold whose induced structure is tame and an $n$-dimensional manifold with boundary with corners (Theorem 3.27) ⟦Chapter3/GlobalIFT · theorem_3_57_of_tangentGerm⟧; if $X$ has no boundary, the induced structure is without boundary, since $d_S \le d_X = 0$ (Lemma 2.26) ⟦Chapter2/SubMPolyfold · lemma_2_26⟧ ⟦Chapter3/GlobalIFT · theorem_3_56_of_tangentGerm⟧. The first step of the text's proof — good position at every zero gives the tangent germ property — was not formalized when this section was written; the theorems with the text's hypotheses are in §III.37.

### III.24 The tangent germ property: Definition 3.25 and Theorem 3.27

**Definition 3.25.** The data at $x \in M$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart⟧: a chart $\varphi : (U, x) \to (O, 0)$ onto a tame retract $(O, C, E)$; an $n$-dimensional smooth $N \subseteq E$ in good position to $C$ with a good complement $Y$, **$Y$ closed**; a relatively open $V \ni 0$ in $N \cap C$; $\delta : V \to E$ continuous with values in $Y$; (i) $\varphi(M \cap U) = \{v + \delta(v) : v \in V\}$; (ii) $\delta(0) = 0$, $D\delta(0) = 0$ and $\delta$ an sc^∞-germ, read as: for every $m$, $k$ a relatively open $V_{m,k} \ni 0$ in $N \cap C$ with $\delta(V_{m,k}) \subseteq E_m$ and $\delta : V_{m,k} \to E_m$ of class $C^k$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · IsScInftyGermAt⟧. This $k$-dependent reading is what the germ implicit function theorem delivers (§III.11); the reading "sc-smooth on one fixed germ" implies it by Proposition 1.18 for germs ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · IsScSmoothGerm.isScInftyGermAt⟧, as does sc-smoothness on $V$ as a set ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · IsScSmooth.isScInftyGermAt⟧, so the theorem covers all three. $M$ has the property if $M \subseteq X_\infty$ and every point has such data ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.HasTangentGermProperty⟧. With these data: $N \cap C$ is a partial quadrant in $N$ (Proposition 3.22) ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.isPartialQuadrant⟧, and $N$, $Y$ are topological complements — this is where $Y$ closed is used — so the projection $\pi : E \to N$ along $Y$ is continuous ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.isTopCompl⟧ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.π⟧; with $\Gamma(v) = v + \delta(v)$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.Γ⟧, $\pi\Gamma = \mathrm{id}$ and $\varphi(y) = \Gamma(\pi\varphi(y))$ for $y \in M \cap U$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.exists_eq_Γ⟧.

**Proposition 3.26** ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · proposition_3_26⟧. For an sc-diffeomorphism $\psi : X \to X'$ (sc-smooth on all of $X$ with sc-smooth inverse $\psi'$ on all of $X'$) and $\psi(M) = M'$, $M'$ has the $n$-dimensional tangent germ property iff $M$ has it. One direction suffices, applied to $\psi$ and $\psi'$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · proposition_3_26_image⟧: $\psi(M) \subseteq X'_\infty$ because sc-smooth maps preserve the levels, and the data at $\psi(x)$ are the transported chart $\varphi \circ \psi^{-1}$ ⟦Chapter2/DegeneracyIndex · transportChart⟧, whose model is that of $\varphi$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.transportChart_model_O⟧, with the same $N$, $Y$, $V$, $\delta$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.transport⟧: condition (i) is transported because $\varphi\psi^{-1}(\psi(M) \cap \psi(U)) = \varphi(M \cap U)$. As in the text; tameness of $X$ plays no role.

**Two gaps in the text's proof of Theorem 3.27, and the conditions that close them** ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.IsRegular⟧. (a) The text asserts that $\delta$ is an sc^∞-germ near every $v_0 \in V$, by linearizing at $v_0$ and claiming that a certain map $N' \to N$ is an isomorphism. That needs $\delta$ differentiable at $v_0$, known only near $0$, and fails: in $X = \mathbb R^2$ take $M$ the graph of $g$ with $g(s) = s^2$ near $0$ and $g(s) = 4 + (s - 2)^{1/3}$ near $2$, a smooth embedded curve with a vertical tangent at $(2, 4)$; with $\varphi = \mathrm{id}$, $N$ the horizontal axis, $Y$ the vertical one and $\delta = g$, the data at $0$ satisfy Definition 3.25, $M$ has the tangent germ property (at $(2, 4)$ use a rotated chart), but $\delta$ is not differentiable at $2$ and the chart $\pi\varphi$ on all of $M \cap U$ is not smoothly compatible with the chart at $(2, 4)$. So condition (a): $\delta$ is sc-smooth on $V$ as a map on a set. (b) The text's $\Sigma = \{v + y \in C : v \in V, y \in Y\}$ is claimed relatively open in $C$, so that $t(v + w) = v + \delta(v)$ is defined near $0$ in $O$. False: $E = \mathbb R^3$, $C = [0, \infty)^3$, $N = \mathbb R(1, 1, 1)$, $Y = \{x + y - z = 0\}$ is a good complement, and $\pi(x, y, z) = (x + y - z)(1, 1, 1)$, so $\pi z \in C$ iff $x + y \ge z$; $\Sigma$ is not open at $(1, 0, 1)$ and points $(\varepsilon, 0, \varepsilon + \varepsilon^2) \notin \Sigma$ approach $0$. So condition (b): $\pi(O) \subseteq C$; then $\Sigma \cap O = \{z \in O : \pi z \in V\}$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.Sig⟧ is relatively open in $O$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.Sig_eq⟧. (A good complement with $\pi'(C) \subseteq N \cap C$ always exists, via the normal form, but then $M \cap U$ must be rewritten as a graph along it with the quadrant inverse function theorem, and the regularity problem of (a) returns; this is not done.)

**Theorem 3.27** ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · theorem_3_27⟧. If $M \ne \emptyset$ has at every point data satisfying (a), (b), then:

*$M$ is a sub-M-polyfold* ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · theorem_3_27_isSubMPolyfold⟧, with the text's retraction. $t(v + w) = v + \delta(v)$, i.e. $t = \Gamma \circ \pi$ on $\Sigma \cap O$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.t⟧, is idempotent with image $\Gamma(V)$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.t_t⟧ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.t_eq_self_of_mem⟧. It is sc-smooth: $\pi$ is a continuous linear map into a finite-dimensional space, hence sc-smooth (Corollary 1.20) ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.π_isScSmooth⟧; $\Gamma = \iota + \delta$ is sc-smooth on $V$ by (a) and because the inclusion of a smooth finite-dimensional subspace is sc-smooth, its level maps being the linear lifts $N \to E_m$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · finSmoothLift⟧ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · isScSmooth_subtype_val⟧ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.Γ_isScSmooth⟧; and for a retraction $R$ onto $\Sigma \cap O$, $t \circ R = \Gamma \circ \pi \circ R$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.t_isScSmoothRetractMap⟧. The text says nothing about either. On $U_0 = \varphi^{-1}(\Sigma \cap O)$, open ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.U₀⟧ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.isOpen_U₀⟧, the map $s = \varphi^{-1} \circ t \circ \varphi$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.s⟧ is an sc-smooth retraction ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.s_s⟧ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.s_isScSmoothOn⟧ onto $M \cap U_0$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.image_s⟧ — Definition 2.20 at $x$.

*The charts $\pi \circ \varphi$.* On $M \cap U_0$, $y \mapsto \pi\varphi(y)$ is a chart with model $(V, N \cap C, N)$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.model⟧, a tame retract (the identity retraction) ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.model_isTameRetract⟧, with inverse $v \mapsto \varphi^{-1}(v + \delta(v))$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.chartInv⟧ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.chart⟧, a finite-dimensional corner chart of dimension $n$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.chart_isCorner⟧ containing $x$ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.mem_chart_source⟧. It is compatible with every chart $\varphi'|_{W \cap M}$ of the induced structure of Proposition 2.21: the transition maps are $\varphi' \circ \varphi^{-1} \circ \Gamma$ and $\pi \circ \varphi \circ \varphi'^{-1}$, compositions of sc-smooth maps between retracts ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.Γ_isScSmoothRetractMap⟧ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.π_isScSmoothRetractMap⟧ ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.TangentGermChart.chart_compatible_subChart⟧. So it is a chart of the induced structure — **Theorem 3.27 (2)** ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.theorem_3_27_isChart⟧ ⟦Chapter2/SubMPolyfold · subPolyfold⟧; these charts are pairwise compatible by locality ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.tangentCharts_compatible⟧ and form an atlas ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.germAtlas⟧ equivalent to the induced one ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.theorem_3_27_atlas_equiv⟧, with tame models: **the induced structure is tame** ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.theorem_3_27_isTame⟧, and **sc-smoothly equivalent to an $n$-dimensional manifold with boundary with corners** ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.theorem_3_27_isManifoldWithCorners⟧. "Manifold with boundary with corners" belongs to Chapter 4; here it is an equivalent atlas of charts on relatively open subsets of $n$-dimensional partial quadrants ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.IsManifoldWithCorners⟧, whose transition maps are classically smooth because sc-smooth maps between finite-dimensional constant structures are $C^\infty$ ⟦Chapter1/ExpositionLemmas · isScSmooth_iff_contDiffOn_const⟧. Tameness of $X$ is not used: the text's "since $O$ is a tame retract, there exists … a tame sc-smooth retraction $r$" is Proposition 2.10 (1) for any retract. *The degeneracy index*: since $\pi\varphi$ has a tame model, $d_M(y) = d_{N \cap C}(\pi\varphi(y))$ (Proposition 2.36) ⟦Chapter3/TangentGerm · MPolyfold.theorem_3_27_degIndex⟧; Lemma 3.70 relates this to $d_C(v + \delta(v)) = d_X(y)$ in the model $\mathbb R^n \oplus W$ only.

### III.25 Lemmas 3.59–3.61: towards the basic germ criterion

**Lemmas 3.59 and 3.60, abstract form.** In the proof of Theorem 3.58 the family $L(b) = P_Y \circ Df(b)|_X : X \to Y$ is shown to be injective for $b$ near $0$ (Lemma 3.59) and to satisfy uniform lower bounds $|L(b)h|_m \ge c_m|h|_m$ (Lemma 3.60) — the hypotheses of Lemma 3.61. Both are sequence arguments, and all they use of the compactness condition (2) of Theorem 3.58 is a property of the family itself: if $b_j \to b$, $(h_j)$ is bounded in $X_m$ and $L(b_j)h_j \to 0$ in $Y_m$, then $(h_j)$ has a convergent subsequence in $X_m$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicGermCriterion · FamilyCompactness⟧. (For $L = P_Y \circ Df|_X$ it follows from (2), since $Df(b_j)h_j - L(b_j)h_j = (1 - P_Y)Df(b_j)h_j$ lies in the finite-dimensional smooth complement $A$ and is bounded on every level.) The two lemmas are formalized for an abstract family of sc-operators with jointly continuous level maps. *Lemma 3.59*: if $L(0)$ is injective, so is $L(b)$ for $b$ near $0$ — otherwise $b_j \to 0$ and unit vectors $h_j$ with $L(b_j)h_j = 0$ give, by the compactness property, a limit $h$ with $|h| = 1$ and $L(0)h = 0$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicGermCriterion · lemma_3_59⟧. *Lemma 3.60*: on a compact parameter set $K$ on which every $L(b)_m$ is injective there is $c_m > 0$ with $c_m|h|_m \le |L(b)h|_m$ — otherwise $b_j \in K$ and unit $h_j$ with $|L(b_j)h_j|_m \to 0$ give, after subsequences, $b_j \to b \in K$, $h_j \to h$, $|h|_m = 1$, $L(b)h = 0$ ⟦Chapter3/BasicGermCriterion · lemma_3_60⟧. The text's step "$P_Y \circ Df(b)|_X$ is an injective sc-Fredholm operator of index $0$, hence an sc-isomorphism" is needed only to feed Lemma 3.61. The setting of Theorem 3.58 (the splitting as coordinates, the complement $A$, the index computation), the strong bundle map $\Phi((b, x), (c, y)) = ((b, x), (c, L(b)^{-1}y))$ and the contraction estimate from condition (3) were not formalized when this section was written; they are now, in the coordinates of the text's proof, and there the hypotheses of the two lemmas are derived from those of the theorem (§III.38).


**Lemma 3.61** (quoted by the text from [25, Proposition 4.8] without proof). Let $V$ be a germ of relatively open neighbourhoods of $0$ in a partial quadrant $\widetilde C$ of a finite-dimensional $G$, $V \oplus E$ the product germ with levels $V_m \times E_m$ ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · ScNbhdGerm.prodFull⟧, and $L(v) : E \to F$ sc-isomorphisms such that $\Phi(v, h) = L(v)h$ ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · famMap⟧ is an sc-smooth germ on $V \oplus E$ and $c_m|h|_m \le |L(v)h|_m$ for $v \in V_0$. Then $\Lambda(v, k) = L(v)^{-1}k$ ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · famInv⟧ is an sc-smooth germ on $V \oplus F$ ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · lemma_3_61⟧. Operator-norm continuity of $v \mapsto L(v)$ is not assumed.

*sc⁰.* On level $m$, with $h_0 = L(v_0)^{-1}k_0$, $|L(v)^{-1}k - L(v_0)^{-1}k_0|_m \le c_m^{-1}(|k - k_0|_m + |(L(v_0) - L(v))h_0|_m)$, and $v \mapsto L(v)h_0$ is continuous ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · famInv_isSc0Germ⟧.

*Differentiability* ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · famInv_hasFDerivWithinAt⟧. The candidate is $D\Lambda(v, k)(\delta v, \delta k) = L(v)^{-1}(\delta k - D_1\Phi(v, L(v)^{-1}k)\delta v)$ ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · famInvDeriv⟧. With $h = \Lambda(v, k)$ and $w = D\Lambda(v, k)(\delta v, \delta k)$, $\Lambda(v', k') - \Lambda(v, k) - w = L(v')^{-1}[(L(v) - L(v'))w] - L(v')^{-1}r$, where $r = \Phi(v', h) - \Phi(v, h) - D_1\Phi(v, h)\delta v = o(|\delta v|)$ is the remainder of $\Phi$ along $(\delta v, 0)$ with $h$ fixed, so that only the finite-dimensional variable moves. The term $(L(v) - L(v'))w$ is $o(|(\delta v, \delta k)|_1)$ *because the increment is measured on level $1$*: $w/|(\delta v, \delta k)|_1$ lies in the compact set $D\Lambda(v, k)(\iota(B_1))$ ($\iota : F_1 \to F_0$ compact), and $(L(v) - L(v'))u \to 0$ uniformly for $u$ in a compact set — a tube lemma for jointly continuous maps vanishing on $\{x_0\} \times K$ ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · exists_forall_norm_le_of_isCompact⟧. Strong continuity plus the compactness of $F_1 \to F_0$ replace the operator-norm continuity; the differentiability of $\Lambda$ as a map $(V \oplus F)_0 \to E_0$ would need the latter and is not claimed.

*The tangent map and the induction.* $T\Lambda((v, k), (\delta v, \delta k)) = (\Lambda(v, k), \Lambda(v, \delta k - (T\Phi((v, \Lambda(v, k)), (\delta v, 0)))_2))$, a composition of $\Lambda$, $T\Phi$ and sc-operators (the projections ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · tangentBaseOp⟧ ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · tangentInlOp⟧ ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · tangentFiberOp⟧ and subtraction ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · ScBanach.subOp⟧); it is sc⁰ ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · famInv_tangent_isSc0⟧, so $\Lambda$ is sc¹ ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · famInv_isSc1GermWith⟧; and if $\Phi$ is sc^{k+1}, then $\Lambda$ (sc^k by induction) and $T\Phi$ (sc^k) make $T\Lambda$ sc^k, so $\Lambda$ is sc^{k+1} ⟦Chapter3/InverseFamily · famInv_isSckGerm⟧. The sc¹ step uses no quadrant hypothesis; the induction uses the composition rules for germs.

### III.26 What the formalization taught us

1. **The germ implicit function theorem holds with the text's hypotheses**, but on shrinking germs: the solution germ is sc^k on the germ shifted by $2^k - 1$ levels. In the text's reading of germs (up to shrinking) this is the theorem; read with fixed germs, "if $f$ is sc-smooth so is its solution germ" holds for every $k$ on a germ depending on $k$. Every later "sc-smooth germ" (Definition 3.25 (ii), Theorem 3.43 (1), Corollary 3.47 (1)) must be read the same way. Whether the shrinking is intrinsic is open.
2. **Theorem 3.30 has a short proof**, which the text cites from [21]: an approximate fixed point and the $\tfrac12$-contraction on level $0$, at parameters where the level-$1$ operators exist.
3. **The contraction regions must be explicit** for "from the uniqueness we conclude $\delta^{(1)} = T\delta$" (Lemma 3.31) to be true.
4. **Several "immediate consequences" are proofs of their own**: the compactness of Theorem 3.12 (not in Theorem 3.40), the induction of Theorem 3.40 (lifts, bounds and continuity together), the sc-smoothness and regularizing property in Theorem 3.15, the sc⁺ property in Proposition 3.10, the projection of solutions into the quadrant in Theorem 3.43.
5. **Three added hypotheses**: $Y$ closed in Lemma 3.55 and Definition 3.25; and the two regularity conditions of Theorem 3.27, each with a counterexample to the step of the text's proof it replaces.
6. **Tameness is nearly unused**: not in §3.1 at all, and in §3.6 only through $(1 - Dr(0))E \subseteq E_0$ and, for the tangent germ property of the solution set, the tameness of the model of the chart $\psi \circ \varphi$ (§III.27).
7. **Linear coordinate changes** in Theorem 3.38 make the text's degeneracy-index argument for Corollary 3.47 unnecessary.
8. **The extreme-ray lemmas and the iterated tangent maps are not needed**: Proposition 3.22 by a segment argument, the regularity in Theorems 3.72 and 3.78 by bootstrapping, without shrinking.
9. **What remained of Theorem 3.54** when this list was written — the re-centring of good position at the nearby zeros, and the level-wise regularity of the solution map in the data of Definition 3.25 at every zero — is done in §§III.31–III.37, with one added hypothesis for Theorem 3.54 (1); see §III.39.

### III.27 Tameness is carried by sc-diffeomorphisms, and by open subsets

The text never states that tameness is invariant under sc-diffeomorphisms, or that an open piece of a tame retract is a tame retract, but it uses both. In the proof of Theorem 3.54 the chart $\psi \circ \varphi$ onto $\psi(O)$ must be a chart of the tame M-polyfold $X$ for Definition 3.25 to apply; in the proof of Proposition 3.26 it writes "$X' = \psi(X)$ is tame"; and wherever a chart is restricted to a smaller domain (the shrinking of the data of Definition 3.25 in §§III.36–III.37) the model of the restricted chart must again be a tame retract. Both facts are proved here, with Definition 2.34 as the formalization states it (Part II).

**The objects.** An sc-diffeomorphism between relatively open subsets $U \subseteq C$, $U' \subseteq C'$ of partial quadrants is a pair $\psi : U \to U'$, $\psi' : U' \to U$ of sc-smooth maps, each mapping its domain into the other's, inverse to each other on $U$ and on $U'$ ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · IsScDiffeoQuadrant⟧ (its inverse is again one ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · IsScDiffeoQuadrant.symm⟧). A retraction $r : U \to U$ is *tame* for a presentation $T$ of $C$ if (1) $d_C(r(x)) = d_C(x)$ for $x \in U$ and (2) at every smooth point $x$ of $O = r(U)$ on level $1$ the tangent space $T_xO = Dr(x)E$ has an sc-complement $A$ contained in the minimal subspace $E_x$ ⟦Chapter2/Tame · ScRetraction.IsTameWith⟧; it is tame if it is tame for every presentation ⟦Chapter2/Tame · ScRetraction.IsTame⟧, and $(O, C, E)$ is a tame retract if $O$ is the image of a tame retraction ⟦Chapter2/Tame · IsTameRetract⟧.

**The transported retraction.** For an sc-smooth retraction $r$ with domain $U$, put $r' = \psi \circ r \circ \psi' : U' \to U'$ ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · IsScDiffeoQuadrant.transport⟧. It maps $U'$ into $U'$ because $\psi'(U') \subseteq U$, $r(U) \subseteq U$ and $\psi(U) \subseteq U'$; it is sc-smooth by the chain rule applied twice; and it is idempotent, $r'(r'(u')) = \psi(r(\psi'\psi(r(\psi'u')))) = \psi(r(r(\psi' u'))) = r'(u')$, since $\psi'\psi = \mathrm{id}$ on $U$ and $r$ is idempotent. Its image is $\psi(O)$ ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · IsScDiffeoQuadrant.transport_retract⟧: $r'(u') = \psi(r(\psi'u'))$ with $r(\psi'u') \in O$; conversely, for $z \in O$, $r'(\psi z) = \psi(r(z)) = \psi(z)$.

*Condition (1).* The degeneracy index is preserved by $\psi$, $d_{C'}(\psi(u)) = d_C(u)$ for $u \in U$: this is Theorem 1.25 ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · IsScDiffeoQuadrant.degIndex_eq⟧ ⟦Chapter2/DegeneracyIndex · theorem_1_25⟧. Then for $u' \in U'$: $d_{C'}(r'(u')) = d_C(r(\psi'u')) = d_C(\psi'u') = d_{C'}(\psi\psi'u') = d_{C'}(u')$, the middle step being condition (1) for $r$.

*The derivative of $r'$.* On level $0$, $D\psi'(\psi(x)) \circ D\psi(x) = 1$ for $x \in U_1$ and $D\psi(\psi'(y)) \circ D\psi'(y) = 1$ for $y \in U'_1$, by the chain rule for $\psi' \circ \psi = \mathrm{id}$ and $\psi \circ \psi' = \mathrm{id}$ ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · IsScDiffeoQuadrant.deriv_inv_deriv⟧ ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · IsScDiffeoQuadrant.deriv_deriv_inv⟧ ⟦Chapter2/DegeneracyIndex · scDeriv_comp_eq_self⟧. If $y \in U'_1$ and $\psi'(y) \in O$, then with $x = \psi'_1(y)$,
$$Dr'(y) = D\psi(x) \circ Dr(x) \circ D\psi'(y)$$
⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · IsScDiffeoQuadrant.scDeriv_transport⟧. The chain rule is applied to $\psi \circ (r \circ \psi')$ and then to $r \circ \psi'$ ⟦Chapter2/TameFaces · scDeriv_comp_apply_of_isScDomain⟧; the outer derivative of $\psi$ is taken at the level-$1$ point of $r \circ \psi'$ over $y$, and this point is $x$ because $r$ fixes $\psi'(y) \in O$. Without $\psi'(y) \in O$ the formula would involve $Dr$ at $\psi'(y)$ and $D\psi$ at the different point $r(\psi'(y))$.

*Sc-isomorphisms carry sc-splittings.* Let $D : E \to E'$ be an sc-operator with an sc-operator inverse $D'$. Its level maps are topological linear isomorphisms $E_m \cong E'_m$ ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · scIsoLevel⟧ (inverse to each other by the injectivity of the inclusions into level $0$); they carry $A_m = A \cap E_m$ onto $(DA)_m$ ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · levelSub_map_eq⟧ and smooth points to smooth points ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · mem_smoothLvl_of_isScOperator⟧. Hence an sc-subspace $A$ (closed, with the smooth points of $A_m$ dense in $A_m$ for every $m$) is carried to the sc-subspace $DA$: $DA = (D')^{-1}(A)$ is closed, and the image of the closure of the smooth points of $A_m$ lies in the closure of the image ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · IsScSubspace.map⟧. An sc-splitting $E = F \oplus A$ (sc-subspaces, complementary on every level) is carried to the sc-splitting $E' = DF \oplus DA$, since an isomorphism of each level carries complements to complements ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · IsScSplitting.map⟧.

*Condition (2)* ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · IsScDiffeoQuadrant.isTameWith_transport⟧. Let $T$, $T'$ be presentations of $C$, $C'$, $r$ tame for $T$, and $y$ a smooth point of $\psi(O)$ on level $1$. Then $x = \psi'_1(y)$ lies on level $1$ of $O$ (if $y = \psi(z)$ with $z \in O$, then $\psi'(y) = z$) and is smooth, because sc-smooth maps carry smooth points to smooth points. Tameness of $r$ at $x$ gives an sc-splitting $E = T_xO \oplus A$ with $A \subseteq E_x$. Because $x$ and $y$ are smooth points, $D\psi(x)$ and $D\psi'(y)$ are sc-operators (the remark after Proposition 1.16) ⟦Chapter1/Properties · IsSc1With.scOperator_deriv⟧ — at a point that is only on level $1$ they need not be — and they are inverse to each other. From the formula for $Dr'(y)$ and $D\psi'(y)D\psi(x) = 1$: $T_y\psi(O) = \mathrm{range}\,Dr'(y) = D\psi(x)(\mathrm{range}\,Dr(x)) = D\psi(x)(T_xO)$. So $E' = T_y\psi(O) \oplus D\psi(x)A$ is an sc-splitting. Finally $D\psi(x)A \subseteq E'_y$: the derivative of an sc¹-map between relatively open subsets of partial quadrants maps the minimal subspace $E_x$ into $E'_{\psi(x)}$ (the one-sided sign argument, and density) ⟦Chapter2/DegeneracyIndex · IsSc1With.mapsTo_minimalSubspace⟧, which needs $\psi(U) \subseteq C'$, and $\psi(x) = y$. Since $T'$ was arbitrary and the presentation $T$ of $C$ is available, the transported retraction of a tame retraction is tame ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · IsScDiffeoQuadrant.isTame_transport⟧, and **the image $(\psi(O), C', E')$ of a tame retract under an sc-diffeomorphism is a tame retract**, with retraction $\psi \circ r \circ \psi^{-1}$ ⟦Chapter2/TameInvariance · IsScDiffeoQuadrant.isTameRetract_image⟧.

**Open subsets.** For an open $W \subseteq E_0$, the restriction of $r$ to $U \cap r^{-1}(W)$ is an sc-smooth retraction onto $O \cap W$ (Proposition 2.10 (1)) ⟦Chapter2/Retracts · ScRetraction.restrict⟧.
