Throughout, $E$ and $F$ are real Banach spaces, $T : E \to F$ is bounded, $R(T)$ is its range and $\operatorname{coker}T = F/R(T)$; $T$ is Fredholm if $\ker T$ and $\operatorname{coker}T$ are finite-dimensional, with index $\dim\ker T - \dim\operatorname{coker}T$. A *line* is a one-dimensional real space. $P : Y \to X$ is a strong bundle over an M-polyfold, both paracompact and Hausdorff, and from §VI.10 on $X$ is tame with sc-smooth bump functions and $f$ is an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data (Definition 3.51), the reading of Chapter 5 (Part V). A strong bundle chart $c$ has base chart $\varphi$, retraction $r$ on an open set $U$ of a partial quadrant $C$, retract $O = r(U)$, and fibre projections $\rho(u)$; the *principal part* of a section is its fibre coordinate in the chart. $\mathbb R^1$ is the M-polyfold of the parameter $t$, with $t$ the point of $\mathbb R^1$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · pt1⟧, and $(\tau, t)$ the point of $\mathbb R^2$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · pt2⟧; $\kappa$ is Mathlib's smooth transition function, $0$ on $(-\infty, 0]$, $1$ on $[1, \infty)$.

### VI.1 Definition 6.1: the space $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$

§6.1 (pp. 200–201) works at a smooth point $x$. Since $f(x)$ is a smooth point of the fibre, there is an sc⁺-section $s$ with $s(x) = f(x)$ — in a chart, $s(y) = R(y, f(x))$ — and $(f - s)'(x) : T_xX \to Y_x$ is sc-Fredholm. Definition 6.1 collects these linearizations, perturbed by sc⁺-operators, into $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$; the index is the index of any member, and Proposition 6.2 says that it is constant along sc-smooth paths.

**The chart point** (V6.1). A chart point of $x$ is a strong bundle chart $c$ of the atlas whose base chart contains $x$, with the level-$1$ point $z$ of the model over $\varphi(x)$ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint⟧. In it $T_xX$ is $T_zO = Dr(z)E$, the range of the derivative of the retraction ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.T⟧, and $Y_x$ is $K_z = \rho(z)F$, the range of the fibre projection over $z$ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.K⟧; both are closed, as ranges of continuous projections, hence Banach spaces. An sc⁺-operator $T_xX \to Y_x$ is level $0$ of an sc⁺-operator between these sc-subspaces ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.IsScPlusOp⟧.

**Definition 6.1** (V6.1). $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$, at the chart point $p$, is the set of the operators $(f + s)'(x) + a : T_zO \to K_z$ for an sc⁺-section $s$ with $(f + s)(x) = 0$ and an sc⁺-operator $a$ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.linSet⟧ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.mem_linSet_iff⟧. The linearization of $f + s$ at its zero $x$ is the derivative at $z$ of the principal part composed with $r$, restricted to $T_zO$ — the $\mathrm{Lin}(z)$ of Part III. Replacing the text's $s$ by $-s$ turns $f - s$ with $s(x) = f(x)$ into $f + s$ with $(f + s)(x) = 0$.

**Two sections differ by an sc⁺-operator.** For two sections $s$, $t$ with $(f + s)(x) = (f + t)(x) = 0$, the principal parts of $f + s$ and $f + t$ differ by that of the sc⁺-section $s - t$, whose derivative at $z$, followed by $\rho(z)$, is level $0$ of an sc⁺-operator: the derivative of an sc⁺-map is sc⁺ on the shifted levels. So $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is $(f + s)'(x)$ plus all the sc⁺-operators, for any one $s$ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.exists_isScPlusOp_linAt_eq⟧, and two members differ by an sc⁺-operator ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.isScPlusOp_sub_of_mem_linSet⟧. The paragraph before the definition puts this as "$(f - s)'(x)$ is an sc-Fredholm operator if and only if $(f - s)'(x)$ is"; it is read with $(f - t)'(x)$ in the second place (possible misprint; Findings, Chapter 6, item 41).

**Not empty.** The text makes its section locally, in a chart. The formalization uses global sc⁺-sections: $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is not empty when $P$ has sc⁺-sections through the smooth points of its fibres, one through $-f(x)$ giving a member ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.linSet_nonempty⟧, and bump functions give such sections ⟦Chapter3/IndexLocallyConstantLocal · MPolyfold.AdmitsBumpFunctions.hasScPlusSectionsThrough⟧. This is the hidden hypothesis of the definition: an sc⁺-section through $f(x)$.

**Fredholm, of one index.** Every member is Fredholm on level $0$, with the index $\mathrm{ind}(f, x)$ of the germ at $x$ (§III.49) ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.isFredholm_isIndexAt_of_mem_linSet⟧ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.exists_index_linSet⟧ ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.fredholmIndex_of_mem_linSet⟧. The proof: $f + s$ has germ data at $x$ (an sc-Fredholm germ plus an sc⁺-germ is one), so its linearization at the zero $x$ is Fredholm of the index of the germ, through the conjugation to a basic germ (Proposition 3.52, §III.30); adding an sc⁺-operator, compact on level $0$, keeps the Fredholm property and the index; and the index of the germ does not depend on the choices. That the members are sc-Fredholm on every level, as the text says, is not stated: the determinant lines use level $0$ only (gap G.64; Findings, Chapter 6, item 40).

**Convex** ⟦Chapter6/LinSet · ChartPoint.convex_linSet⟧. $(1 - \tau)(L + a) + \tau(L + b) = L + ((1 - \tau)a + \tau b)$, and the sc⁺-operators form a vector space. The text notes this on p. 219, where Proposition 6.26 needs it.

**Proposition 6.2** (V3.98). The constancy of the index along sc-smooth paths was formalized with Chapter 3 and is retold in §III.49: for paths on $\mathbb R$, with the text's hypotheses — tame germ data, no bump functions, the locally defined sc⁺-sections of Definition 6.1. It is not repeated here. The facts on paths recalled before it on p. 201 — an M-polyfold is locally path connected, and two smooth points in one path component are joined by an sc⁺-smooth path — are formalized only inside a chart (§VI.18; gap G.56; Findings, Chapter 6, item 42).

### VI.2 Determinant lines, Definition 6.3, Proposition 6.4

**$\lambda(E)$ and $\lambda^*(E)$** (V6.2). For a finite-dimensional real space $E$, $\lambda(E) = \Lambda^{\max}E$ is the top exterior power ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · maxPow⟧ and $\lambda^*(E)$ its dual ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · maxPowDual⟧; both are lines ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · finrank_maxPow⟧, $\lambda(\{0\}) = \mathbb R$ being the zeroth exterior power. A family $a_1, \dots, a_n$ with $n = \dim E$ has its wedge $a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n$ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · wedge⟧. Two rules carry every computation of the chapter. A change of basis multiplies the wedge by its determinant ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · wedge_eq_det_smul⟧, also when only one block of a two-block wedge $a \wedge b$ is changed ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · wedge_append_basis_left⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · wedge_append_basis_right⟧; and adding to the vectors of one block vectors of the span of the other does not change the wedge ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · wedge_append_add_left⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · wedge_append_add_right⟧. For $v \ne 0$ in a line, $v^*$ is the functional with $v^*(v) = 1$ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · dualVec⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · dualVec_self⟧, and that value determines it ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · eq_dualVec_of_apply_eq_one⟧. For $\dim E = \dim F$ and $\Phi : E \to F$, $\lambda(\Phi)(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) = \Phi a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \Phi a_n$ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · maxPowMap⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · maxPowMap_wedge⟧, with $\lambda(\Psi\Phi) = \lambda(\Psi)\lambda(\Phi)$ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · maxPowMap_comp⟧, and $\lambda(\Phi) \ne 0$ iff $\Phi$ is bijective ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · maxPowMap_ne_zero_iff⟧; $\lambda^*(\Phi)$ is its dual ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · maxPowDualMap⟧ (pp. 203–204).

**Definition 6.3** (V6.3). $\iota : \lambda(E^*) \to \lambda^*(E)$ is $\iota(e_1^* \wedge \dots \wedge e_n^*)(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) = \det(e_i^*(a_j))$ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · iotaDual⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · iotaDual_wedge_wedge⟧. The formula is alternating and multilinear in both families, so it descends to the exterior powers; that is the text's well-definedness. $\iota$ is a nonzero map of lines ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · iotaDual_ne_zero⟧, and for a basis with its dual basis $\iota(e_1^* \wedge \dots \wedge e_n^*) = (e_1 \wedge \dots \wedge e_n)^*$ ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · iotaDual_wedge_dualBasis⟧, since the matrix is the identity. The text's matrix $(e_i^*(a_j))$ is the transpose of the one of Mathlib's pairing, with the same determinant (p. 204).

**Proposition 6.4** (V6.4) ⟦Chapter6/DetLine · proposition_6_4⟧. For an isomorphism $\Phi : E \to F$, $\lambda^*(\Phi) \circ \iota = \iota \circ \lambda(\Phi^*)$. Both sides, evaluated at $f_1^* \wedge \dots \wedge f_n^*$ and $a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n$, give $\det(f_i^*(\Phi a_j))$: the left side by the definition of $\lambda^*(\Phi)$, the right side because $(\Phi^*f_i^*)(a_j) = f_i^*(\Phi a_j)$ (p. 205).

### VI.3 Four-term exact sequences: $\Phi_E$, Lemma 6.5, Proposition 6.6

**The data of (91)** (V6.5). Let $\mathbf E : 0 \to A \xrightarrow{\alpha} B \xrightarrow{\beta} C \xrightarrow{\gamma} D \to 0$ be an exact sequence of finite-dimensional spaces ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact⟧. A *choice* ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.Choice⟧ consists of a complement $Z$ of $\alpha(A)$ in $B$, a complement $V$ of $\beta(B)$ in $C$, bases $a$ of $A$, $d$ of $D$, $b'$ of $Z$, and the $\gamma$-preimages $c$ in $V$ of the basis $d$. Then $\alpha(a), b'$ is a basis of $B$, and $c, \beta(b')$ is one of $C$, because $\beta$ maps $Z$ isomorphically onto $\beta(B)$ and $\gamma$ maps $V$ isomorphically onto $D$. Formula (91) assigns to the choice the value $(\alpha(a_1) \wedge \dots \wedge \alpha(a_n) \wedge b'_1 \wedge \dots \wedge b'_{m-n}) \otimes (c_1 \wedge \dots \wedge c_l \wedge \beta(b'_1) \wedge \dots \wedge \beta(b'_{m-n}))^*$ as the image of $(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) \otimes (d_1 \wedge \dots \wedge d_l)^*$, with the text's two ordering conventions ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.Choice.value⟧. $\Phi_E : \lambda(A) \otimes \lambda^*(D) \to \lambda(B) \otimes \lambda^*(C)$ is the linear map of lines defined by one fixed choice ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.canonicalChoice⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.phi⟧; it is nonzero ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.phi_ne_zero⟧, hence an isomorphism ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.phiEquiv⟧ (p. 206).

**Lemma 6.5** (V6.6) ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.lemma_6_5⟧. The text: $\Phi_E$ does not depend on the choices. The formalization proves the strongest form: $\Phi_E$, defined from one choice, maps the source element $(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) \otimes (d_1 \wedge \dots \wedge d_l)^*$ of *any other* choice to the right-hand side of (91) computed with that choice. This is the form every later computation uses — $\gamma^P_T$ is always evaluated in bases adapted to the problem at hand (Findings, Chapter 6, item 1). The proof is §6.7.1 (§VI.28).

**Proposition 6.6** (V6.7). With the contraction $\bar\iota(v \otimes b \otimes \varphi) = \varphi(v)\,b$ ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · contractDual⟧, (92) defines $\Psi_E(c \otimes h) = \bar\iota(c \otimes \Phi_E(h))$ ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.psi⟧. The proposition ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.proposition_6_6⟧: $\Psi_E$ maps the wedge of the basis $c, \beta(b')$ of $C$, tensored with $(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) \otimes (d_1 \wedge \dots \wedge d_l)^*$, to $\alpha(a_1) \wedge \dots \wedge \alpha(a_n) \wedge b'_1 \wedge \dots \wedge b'_{m-n}$. By Lemma 6.5 in its strong form, $\Phi_E$ of the source is the value of (91) for this choice, and the dual wedge evaluated on the wedge is $1$. The wedge in $C$ is taken in the order of (91); the statement exchanges the names of its two blocks (possible misprint; Findings, Chapter 6, item 2) (p. 207).

### VI.4 Determinants of Fredholm operators, good left-projections, and Lemma 6.10

**Definition 6.7** (V6.8). $\det(T) = \lambda(\ker T) \otimes \lambda^*(F/R(T))$ ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · linDet⟧ ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · fredholmDet⟧, a line for $T$ Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · finrank_fredholmDet⟧. Equal operators have identified determinants ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · linDetEquivOfEq⟧: $PQT$ and $PT$ are the same operator when $P \le Q$, but not the same expression, and Proposition 6.12 compares their determinants. The alternative definition $\lambda(\ker T) \otimes \lambda(\operatorname{coker}(T)^*)$ mentioned after the definition is not formalized (gap G.57) (p. 208).

**Definition 6.8** (V6.9). An orientation of $T$ is a ray of $\det(T)$ ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · FredholmOrientation⟧; there is one ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · nonempty_fredholmOrientation⟧, and exactly two ⟦Chapter6/FredholmDet · exists_two_fredholmOrientation⟧ (p. 208).

**Definition 6.9 and the facts after it** (V6.10). A *good left-projection* for $T$ is a bounded projection $P : F \to F$ with $\dim F/R(P) < \infty$ and $R(PT) = R(P)$ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj⟧; $\Pi_T$ is their set ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · goodLeftProjs⟧. $P \le Q$ iff $P = PQ = QP$ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · ProjLE⟧, a partial order ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · ProjLE.refl⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · ProjLE.antisymm⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · ProjLE.trans⟧. A good left-projection is Fredholm of index $0$ — $\ker P$ is a complement of $R(P)$, of dimension $\dim F/R(P)$ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj.isFredholm⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj.fredholmIndex_eq_zero⟧ — so $PT$ is Fredholm with $\mathrm{ind}(PT) = \mathrm{ind}(T)$ when $T$ is, by the index of a composite ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj.isFredholm_comp⟧ ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj.fredholmIndex_comp⟧. For $P, P' \in \Pi_T$, $R(P) \cap R(P')$ has finite codimension ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · IsGoodLeftProj.finiteDimensional_quotient_inf⟧. And $\Pi_T \ne \emptyset$ for $T$ Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · exists_isGoodLeftProj⟧ — the projection onto $R(T)$ along a finite-dimensional complement is one — which the text uses from Lemma 6.11 on without stating it (Findings, Chapter 6, item 3) (p. 208).

**Lemma 6.10** (V6.11) ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · lemma_6_10⟧. *For $P, P' \in \Pi_T$ there is $P'' \in \Pi_T$ with $P'' \le P$ and $P'' \le P'$*, for any bounded $T$. The text's $P''$ projects onto $R(P) \cap R(P')$ along a complement assembled from $\ker P$, $\ker P'$ and a further piece, and $P'' = P''P$ needs $\ker P \subseteq \ker P''$. As we read it, this does not hold in general: on $\mathbb R^2$ with $T = 1$, let $P$ project onto the $x$-axis along the $y$-axis and $P'$ along the diagonal; $R(P) \cap R(P')$ is the $x$-axis, and a projection onto it below both would equal both ⟦Chapter6/GoodProjections · lemma_6_10_text_reading⟧. The lemma holds with a smaller range. *Step 1.* $K = \ker P + \ker P'$ is finite-dimensional, each kernel having the dimension of a finite-dimensional quotient. *Step 2.* $K$ has a closed complement $N$ (finite-dimensional subspaces are complemented, by Hahn–Banach), and $R'' = R(P) \cap R(P') \cap N$ is closed, of finite codimension, and meets $K$ only in $0$. *Step 3.* $R''$ has a complement $C \supseteq K$, topological because the quotient by $R''$ is finite-dimensional; $P''$ is the projection onto $R''$ along $C$. *Step 4.* $\ker P \subseteq C = \ker P''$ gives $P''P = P''$, and $R'' \subseteq R(P)$ gives $PP'' = P''$; the same for $P'$. *Step 5.* $R(P''T) = P''(R(PT)) = P''(R(P)) = R''$, since $P''$ is the identity on $R'' \subseteq R(P)$. Nothing uses that $T$ is Fredholm. The 2017 version drops the lemma and remarks that a common lower bound need not exist; with the order of Definition 6.9, used by both versions, it always exists, as we read it, so the preprint's route to Lemma 6.25 is sound and is the one formalized (Findings, Chapter 6, item 4) (pp. 208–209).

### VI.5 Lemma 6.11, $\gamma^P_T$, Proposition 6.12 and Corollary 6.13

**Lemma 6.11** (V6.12). For $P \in \Pi_T$, the sequence $\mathbf E(T, P) : 0 \to \ker T \to \ker(PT) \to F/R(P) \to \operatorname{coker}T \to 0$, with the inclusion ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · projSeqJ⟧, $x \mapsto Tx + R(P)$ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · projSeqPhi⟧ and $y + R(P) \mapsto (I - P)y + R(T)$ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · projSeqPi⟧, is exact ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · lemma_6_11⟧, a four-term exact sequence of §VI.3 ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · projSeq⟧. The four checks use only $P^2 = P$ and $R(PT) = R(P)$. At $\ker(PT)$: if $PTx = 0$ and $Tx \in R(P)$, then $Tx \in R(P) \cap \ker P = 0$. At $F/R(P)$: the last map is well defined because $(I - P)R(P) = 0$; it kills $[Tx]$ for $x \in \ker(PT)$, since $(I - P)Tx = Tx$; and if $(I - P)y = Tx$, then $PTx = 0$ and $y - Tx = Py \in R(P)$. Onto: $Py = PTe$ for some $e$, and then $(I - P)(y - Te) = y - Te$, which has the class of $y$ in $\operatorname{coker}T$ (p. 209).

**The isomorphism $\gamma^P_T$** (V6.13). $\gamma^P_T : \det(T) \to \det(PT)$ is $\Phi_{\mathbf E(T,P)}$ followed by the identification of $\lambda^*(F/R(P))$ with $\lambda^*(F/R(PT))$ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · gammaProj⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · gammaProj_tmul⟧ — the text's "recalling $R(P) = R(PT)$" (Findings, Chapter 6, item 5). By Lemma 6.5 it is given on wedges by (91) for any choice ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · gammaProj_wedge_tmul⟧ (p. 210).

**Proposition 6.12** (V6.14). *For $P \le Q$ in $\Pi_T$, $QT$ is Fredholm, $P \in \Pi_{QT}$, and $\gamma^P_{QT} \circ \gamma^Q_T = \gamma^P_T$*, up to the identification of $\det(P(QT))$ with $\det(PT)$ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · proposition_6_12⟧. $P \in \Pi_{QT}$ because $R(PQT) = R(PT) = R(P)$ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · IsGoodLeftProj.of_projLE⟧. The identity is a computation in adapted bases ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · comp_comp_eq_of_projLE⟧, the proof of §6.7.2, retold in §VI.29 (p. 211).

**Corollary 6.13** (V6.15) ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · corollary_6_13⟧. For $P \le S$ and $P \le R$ in $\Pi_T$, $(\gamma^P_{RT})^{-1} \circ \gamma^P_{ST} = \gamma^R_T \circ (\gamma^S_T)^{-1}$. Proposition 6.12 twice gives $\gamma^P_{ST}\gamma^S_T = \gamma^P_T = \gamma^P_{RT}\gamma^R_T$; rearranging gives the claim. So the left side, the comparison of two local frames through a common lower bound, does not depend on the lower bound (p. 211).

### VI.6 The stabilization: Lemma 6.14, formula (94), Proposition 6.15, Definition 6.16

**Lemma 6.14** (V6.16). For $T$ Fredholm and $\varphi : \mathbb R^n \to F$ with $T_\varphi(e, r) = Te + \varphi r$ onto, the sequence $0 \to \ker T \xrightarrow{j} \ker T_\varphi \xrightarrow{\pi} \mathbb R^n \xrightarrow{[\varphi]} F/R(T) \to 0$, with $j(e) = (e, 0)$ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabJ⟧, $\pi(e, r) = r$ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabPi⟧ and $[\varphi](r) = \varphi(r) + R(T)$ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabClass⟧, is exact ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · lemma_6_14⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabSeq⟧. $j$ is injective; $\ker\pi \cap \ker T_\varphi$ is $\{(e, 0) \mid Te = 0\} = j(\ker T)$; for $(e, r) \in \ker T_\varphi$, $\varphi r = -Te \in R(T)$, and conversely $\varphi r = -Te$ puts $(e, r)$ in $\ker T_\varphi$; $[\varphi]$ is onto because $T_\varphi$ is. A stabilizing $\varphi$ exists for every Fredholm $T$ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · exists_surjective_coprod⟧: send a basis of $\mathbb R^n$ to representatives of a basis of the cokernel. The proof writes $j(e) = (0, e)$, read as $(e, 0)$ (possible misprint; Findings, Chapter 6, item 8) (pp. 211–212).

**Formula (94)** (V6.17). $\psi : \lambda^*(\mathbb R^n) \to \lambda^*(\{0\})$ maps $(e_1 \wedge \dots \wedge e_n)^*$ to $1^*$ for the standard basis ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stdWedge⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabOne⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabPsi⟧. Then $\psi((c_1 \wedge \dots \wedge c_n)^*) = \det[c_1, \dots, c_n]^{-1}\,1^*$ for every basis ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabPsi_dualVec⟧: $c_1 \wedge \dots \wedge c_n = \det[c]\,e_1 \wedge \dots \wedge e_n$, and the dual vectors scale inversely (p. 212).

**Proposition 6.15** (V6.18). Since $T_\varphi$ is onto, $\det(T_\varphi) = \lambda(\ker T_\varphi) \otimes \lambda^*(\{0\})$, and $\iota_\varphi = (1 \otimes \psi) \circ \Phi_{\mathbf E}$, for the sequence $\mathbf E$ of Lemma 6.14, is an isomorphism $\det(T) \to \det(T_\varphi)$ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabIota⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stabIota_bijective⟧. The formula ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · proposition_6_15⟧: for a basis $a$ of $\ker T$, vectors $\bar c_1, \dots, \bar c_m$ with $[\varphi](\bar c_i)$ a basis of $F/R(T)$, and $\bar b_i = (b_i, r_i)$ completing $(a, 0)$ to a basis of $\ker T_\varphi$, $\iota_\varphi(h) = \det(\bar c, r)^{-1}\,((a_1, 0) \wedge \dots \wedge (a_k, 0) \wedge \bar b_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \bar b_l) \otimes 1^*$. These data are a choice of (91) for $\mathbf E$ — $Z$ the span of the $\bar b_i$, $V$ the span of the $\bar c_j$ — so Lemma 6.5 gives $\Phi_{\mathbf E}(h) = ((a, 0) \wedge \bar b) \otimes (\bar c \wedge r)^*$, and (94) turns the second factor into $\det(\bar c, r)^{-1}1^*$. To form $\det(\bar c, r)$ one needs $m + l = n$: the statement takes it as a hypothesis, and it is proved to hold always ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · stab_card_eq⟧; that the $r_i$ and $\bar c_j$ form a basis of $\mathbb R^n$, which the text notices, is proved — the $r_i$ span $\pi(\ker T_\varphi) = \ker[\varphi]$, and the $\bar c_j$ a complement of it ⟦Chapter6/Stabilization · isCompl_range_stabPi_span⟧. The statement calls $\psi$ "$\varphi$" (possible misprint). The identification (95) and the maps $V \otimes \lambda(\mathbb R^n) \to V$, $V \otimes \lambda^*(\mathbb R^n) \to V$ after the proposition are not formalized; the formalized statements use only (94) (gap G.58; Findings, Chapter 6, items 9, 10) (p. 213).

**Definition 6.16** (V6.19). For Fredholm $T$, $S$, the operator $T \oplus S$ has $\ker(T \oplus S) \cong \ker T \times \ker S$ and $\operatorname{coker}(T \oplus S) \cong \operatorname{coker}T \times \operatorname{coker}S$, through the inclusions of the factors ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · kerInl⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · kerInr⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · cokerInl⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · cokerInr⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · kerProdEquiv⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · cokerProdEquiv⟧; the dimensions add ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · finrank_ker_prodMap⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · finrank_coker_prodMap⟧, so $T \oplus S$ is Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · isFredholm_prodMap⟧. The map $\det(T) \otimes \det(S) \to \det(T \oplus S)$, $h \otimes h' \mapsto (a \wedge a') \otimes (d \wedge d')^*$, is defined by the formula in one choice of bases ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · directSumVec⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · directSumDet⟧, satisfies it for every choice ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · directSumVec_eq_smul⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · definition_6_16⟧ — a change of bases multiplies source and target by the same product of determinants, the block wedges by the block determinants — and is an isomorphism ⟦Chapter6/DirectSumDet · directSumDet_bijective⟧. "Natural" is read as the formula for every choice, as in Lemma 6.5 (Findings, Chapter 6, item 11) (p. 214).

### VI.7 Local determinant bundles: Lemmas 6.17–6.19, Proposition 6.20, Lemma 6.21

**Lemma 6.17** (V6.20). The Fredholm operators form a subspace of $L(E, F)$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · FredholmOp⟧. *For a bounded $T$, $P \in \Pi_T$ and a topological complement $Y$ of $\ker(PT)$, there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that for $\|S - T\| < \varepsilon$, $P \in \Pi_S$ and $PS|_Y : Y \to R(P)$ is a topological isomorphism* ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · lemma_6_17⟧. *Step 1.* $PT|_Y$ is injective, since $Y \cap \ker(PT) = 0$, and onto $R(P)$, since $PT(E) = PT(Y)$ and $R(PT) = R(P)$; as a bijection between the Banach spaces $Y$ and $R(P)$ (both closed) it is an isomorphism by the open mapping theorem. *Step 2.* $\|PS|_Y - PT|_Y\| \le \|P\|\,\|S - T\|$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · projRestrict⟧, and the invertible operators form an open set. *Step 3.* $R(PS) \supseteq PS(Y) = R(P)$, so $P \in \Pi_S$. That $T$ is Fredholm is not used (Findings, Chapter 6, item 20); a topological complement is an algebraic complement with a continuous projection (p. 214).

**Lemma 6.18** (V6.21). A *local determinant chart* is the data $(T, P, Y, \varepsilon)$ of Lemma 6.17 with its conclusions ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart⟧. For $k \in \ker(PT)$, $y(k, S) = -(PS|_Y)^{-1}PSk$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.ySol⟧ is continuous in $(k, S)$, inversion being continuous, and $k + y(k, S) \in \ker(PS)$. The map $(S, k) \mapsto (S, k + y(k, S))$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.kerMap⟧ is onto $\bigcup_{\|S - T\| < \varepsilon}\{S\} \times \ker(PS)$, inverted by the continuous projection onto $\ker(PT)$ along $Y$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.kerProj⟧: for $w \in \ker(PS)$ write $w = k + y$ with $y \in Y$; then $PSy = -PSk$, so $y = y(k, S)$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.lemma_6_18⟧. "Is a trivial vector bundle" is stated as this trivialization and its inverse (Findings, Chapter 6, item 21) (p. 215).

**Lemma 6.19 and Proposition 6.20** (V6.22). For a basis $k$ of $\ker(PT)$, $k_i(S) = k_i + y(k_i, S)$ is a continuous frame of the kernels ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.kerFrame⟧, and with a constant basis $e$ of $F/R(P) = F/R(PS)$, $\omega(S) = (k_1(S) \wedge \dots \wedge k_n(S)) \otimes (e_1 \wedge \dots \wedge e_l)^*$ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.frame⟧ is a nowhere-zero frame ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.frame_ne_zero⟧ of $\mathrm{DET}(T, P, \varepsilon) = \bigcup_S\det(PS)$. The frames of two charts with the same $P$ differ by a continuous nowhere-zero factor ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · proposition_6_20⟧: the determinant of the matrix expressing one kernel frame in the other, continuous because both frames are continuous in $S$, times the constant change of the bases of $F/R(P)$. Lemma 6.19 — exterior powers, duals, sums and tensor products of topological vector bundles — is not formalized in general (gap G.59): it is applied only to trivial bundles, and Proposition 6.20 is proved with the explicit frames; "in a natural way" is read as this relation between frames (Findings, Chapter 6, item 22) (p. 216).

**Lemma 6.21** (V6.23). *For $Q \le P$, $\gamma^Q_{PS}$ maps the $P$-frame at $S$ to a continuous nowhere-zero multiple of the $Q$-frame, on the common ball of any two local determinant charts* ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · LocalDetChart.gammaProj_frame_eq⟧ ⟦Chapter6/LocalDetBundle · lemma_6_21⟧. The text's sketch — extend the kernel sections of $PS$ to sections spanning $\ker(QS)$ — is the proof. For a basis $f_1, \dots$ of $R(P) \cap \ker Q$, $z_m(S) = (PS|_Y)^{-1}f_m$ is continuous and $PSz_m(S) = f_m$; the $k_i(S)$ and $z_m(S)$ span $\ker(QPS) = \ker(QS)$; and in the choice of (91) for $\mathbf E(PS, Q)$ these vectors go with the *constant* classes $[f_m]$. So $\gamma^Q_{PS}(\omega_P(S))$ is $(k(S) \wedge z(S)) \otimes (e \wedge [f])^*$, continuous in $S$, and its ratio to the $Q$-frame of the other chart is the determinant of a continuous change of basis. The lemma is stated for two charts with different centres and radii, the form Lemma 6.25 uses (Findings, Chapter 6, item 23) (pp. 216–217).

### VI.8 $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$: Definition 6.22, Propositions 6.23 and 6.24, Lemma 6.25

**The prebundle** (V6.24). The fibre over a Fredholm $S$ is $\det(S)$ ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · DetFiber⟧. A local determinant chart gives the pretrivialization $(S, h) \mapsto (S, \omega(S)^*(\gamma^P_Sh))$ over its ball, with model fibre $\mathbb R$ ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · LocalDetChart.pretriv⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · LocalDetChart.coord⟧ — the text's $\gamma_{(T,P,\varepsilon)}$ read in the frame of Proposition 6.20 (Findings, Chapter 6, item 24). Every Fredholm operator is the centre of one ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · exists_localDetChart⟧: $\Pi_T \ne \emptyset$ (§VI.4) and the finite-dimensional $\ker(PT)$ has a topological complement. The charts form a Mathlib vector prebundle ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · detPrebundle⟧, which needs exactly that the coordinate changes be continuous, Lemma 6.25 below; its topology and bundle structure are those of $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ (p. 217).

**Lemma 6.25** (V6.28), proved first. *The transition between two charts is $(S, t) \mapsto (S, g(S)t)$ with $g$ continuous and nowhere zero on the common ball* ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · lemma_6_25_local⟧ ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · lemma_6_25⟧. The proof is the text's: a common lower bound $Q \le P, P'$ (Lemma 6.10, §VI.4); Corollary 6.13 to pass from $\gamma^P$ to $\gamma^{P'}$ through $Q$; and Lemma 6.21 for each chart, which turns both frames into multiples of $Q$-frames (p. 218).

**Definition 6.22, Propositions 6.23 and 6.24.** $\mathcal B$ is the collection of sets lying over the ball of some chart whose image in $\text{ball} \times \mathbb R$ is open (V6.25) ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · detBasis⟧. It is a basis of the topology of the prebundle (V6.26) ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · proposition_6_23⟧: its members are open, the charts being homeomorphisms onto $\text{ball} \times \mathbb R$, and every open set is the union of its intersections with chart domains, which are members; so the topology $\mathcal B$ generates is that one. $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ is a topological vector bundle with model fibre $\mathbb R$, and every $\gamma_{(T,P,\varepsilon)}$, read in its frame, is a trivialization (V6.27) ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · proposition_6_24⟧ (p. 218). The remark that $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ is not orientable and the classical case at the opening of §6.5 are not formalized (gap G.60; Findings, Chapter 6, item 26).

### VI.9 Orientations of line bundles, Proposition 6.26, Definition 6.27

**Orientations of line bundles** (V6.29). An orientation of a topological line bundle is a choice of rays of the fibres given near every point by a continuous nowhere-zero section ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · IsLineOrientation⟧ ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · LineOrientation⟧. Two orientations that agree on one fibre agree over a preconnected base ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · LineOrientation.eq_of_apply_eq⟧: the set where they agree is open and closed. The rays of the fibres form a two-sheeted covering ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · OrCover⟧ ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · isCoveringMap_orCover⟧, and an orientation is a continuous section of it; over a simply connected, locally path-connected base the lifting criterion extends every orientation of one fibre ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · exists_lineOrientation_apply_eq⟧, and over a nonempty such base there are exactly two orientations ⟦Chapter6/LineBundleOrientation · exists_two_lineOrientation⟧. The text gives "since the base space is contractible" as the reason, without the theorem it needs (Findings, Chapter 6, item 25) (p. 219).

**Proposition 6.26** (V6.30). Over a nonempty convex set $C$ of Fredholm operators ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · fredholmIncl⟧, the restriction $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)|_C$ ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · DetOn⟧ is a topological line bundle with exactly two orientations ⟦Chapter6/DetBundle · proposition_6_26⟧: a nonempty convex set of a normed space is contractible, hence simply connected, and locally path-connected. The proposition is stated for every nonempty convex $C$; $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ is one (§VI.1) (p. 219).

**Definition 6.27** (V6.31). At a chart point the members of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ are Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/LinOrientation · ChartPoint.isFredholm_of_mem_linSet⟧; $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ is the pull-back of $\mathrm{DET}(T_zO, K_z)$ to $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ ⟦Chapter6/LinOrientation · ChartPoint.detLin⟧, and $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ is the set of its orientations ⟦Chapter6/LinOrientation · ChartPoint.Or⟧, with exactly two elements ⟦Chapter6/LinOrientation · ChartPoint.exists_two_or⟧. For each $L \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$, $o \mapsto o(L)$ is a bijection onto the two orientations of $\det(L)$ ⟦Chapter6/LinOrientation · ChartPoint.orEquivRay⟧: injective because an orientation is determined by one value over the connected base, onto because each ray extends. The category $\mathcal O_f$ is read through its objects, the two-element sets, with bijections as morphisms; between two two-element sets there are bijections ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · nonempty_equiv_of_two⟧, each determined by one value ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · equiv_eq_of_apply_eq_of_two⟧. No negation is set up on the tensor products, so $\{o_x, -o_x\}$ is stated as "exactly two elements" (Findings, Chapter 6, item 44) (pp. 219–220). The comparison of $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ in two charts is §VI.21.

### VI.10 Proposition 6.28: the neighbourhoods of the propagation

The text: every smooth point $x$ has an open neighbourhood $U$ which (1) is sc-smoothly contractible, (2) has $\{y \in \mathrm{cl}(U) \mid f(y) = 0\}$ compact, (3) carries, for every sc-smooth path $\varphi : [0, 1] \to U$, an sc⁺-section $s : U \times [0, 1] \to Y$ with $s(\varphi(t), t) = f(\varphi(t))$, and (4) carries sc⁺-sections $q : U \times [0, 1] \to Y$ through every smooth point of every fibre over $U_\infty$, at every $t_0$. The proof takes local strong bundle coordinates, $P : K \to O$ with $x = 0$.

**The statement formalized** (V6.32) ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · proposition_6_28⟧. *With sc-smooth bump functions, every smooth $x$ has open $U \subseteq W$ in the domain of one chart of the atlas with* (1′) *any two sc-smooth paths in $U$ with the same end points are sc-smoothly homotopic in $W$ with the end points fixed* ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · IsScHomotopyRel⟧; (2) *$\{y \in \mathrm{cl}(U) \mid f(y) = 0\}$ is compact*; (3) *for every sc-smooth family $\Phi : \mathbb R^n \to X$ with $\Phi([0, 1]^n) \subseteq W$ there is an sc⁺-section $S$ of $\pi^*P \to \mathbb R^n \times X$ with $(f + S)(q, \Phi(q)) = 0$ for $q$ near $[0, 1]^n$, depending on $q \in [0, 1]^n$ only through $\Phi(q)$*; (4) *$\pi^*P$ has sc⁺-sections through all smooth fibre points*. A path "in $U$" is one with $\gamma([0, 1]) \subseteq U$.

**The neighbourhoods.** Take a chart $c$ of the atlas at $x$, $u_0 = \varphi(x)$, the retraction $r$ on $U_c \subseteq C$ with $O = r(U_c)$. Choose $\delta$ with $B_\delta \cap C \subseteq U_c$ (the domain of the retraction is relatively open); $\delta_2$ with $r(B_{\delta_2} \cap U_c) \subseteq B_\delta$ (continuity of $r$ at $u_0$ on level $0$, $r(u_0) = u_0$); a neighbourhood $N$ of $x$ whose closure meets the zeros of $f$ in a compact set ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · exists_nhds_isCompact_zeros⟧ — at a zero by the local compactness of Theorem 5.6 (§V.7), elsewhere because the zero set is closed and misses a neighbourhood of $x$; a closed neighbourhood $T \subseteq N$ of $x$ and $\delta_3$ with $\varphi^{-1}(B_{\delta_3} \cap O) \subseteq T$. With $\delta' = \min(\delta, \delta_2, \delta_3)$, $W = \varphi^{-1}(B(u_0, \delta) \cap O)$ and $U = \varphi^{-1}(B(u_0, \delta') \cap O)$.

**(1′).** Let $\gamma_0, \gamma_1$ be sc-smooth paths in $U$ with the same end points. Since paths are maps on $\mathbb R$ that lie in $U$ only for $t \in [0, 1]$, first take a $C^\infty$ map $\sigma : \mathbb R \to \mathbb R$ equal to the identity near $[0, 1]$ with values in the open set $\gamma_0^{-1}(U) \cap \gamma_1^{-1}(U)$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · exists_contDiff_eq_id_near_Icc_mapsTo⟧. Then $\Phi(\tau, t) = \varphi^{-1}\big(r\big((1 - \kappa(\tau))\,\varphi(\gamma_0(\sigma(t))) + \kappa(\tau)\,\varphi(\gamma_1(\sigma(t)))\big)\big)$. The convex combination lies in the convex set $B_{\delta'} \cap C$, hence in $U_c$; $r$ maps it into $B_\delta \cap O$, so $\Phi$ takes values in $W$; it is sc-smooth as a composite of sc-smooth maps in the chart; at $\tau = 0, 1$ it is $\gamma_0, \gamma_1$ on $[0, 1]$, because $\sigma$ is the identity there and $r$ fixes $O$; and the end points stay fixed, because $\gamma_0$ and $\gamma_1$ agree there. The text's contraction $\hat r(t, y) = r(ty)$ contracts $r(V)$ for a convex $V$; for $U = r(V')$ it needs $r(V') \subseteq V'$, which is not stated, and a convex domain of the retraction is not available in general. As we read it, (1) is not established for $U$ (gap G.61; Findings, Chapter 6, item 45). What Theorem 6.35 uses is (1′).

**(2).** $\mathrm{cl}(U) \subseteq T \subseteq \mathrm{cl}(N)$, since $U \subseteq \varphi^{-1}(B_{\delta_3} \cap O) \subseteq T$ and $T$ is closed; so the zeros in $\mathrm{cl}(U)$ are a closed subset of a compact set.

**(3), sections along families** ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · exists_isScPlusSection_pullback_of_family⟧. This is the text's $s(y) = R(y, f(x))$ made to depend on the parameter. An sc-smooth map on the finite-dimensional $\mathbb R^n$ takes values in the smooth points, and the principal part $q \mapsto \hat f(\Phi(q))$ lifts to a $C^\infty$ map into the level-$1$ fibre model. In the chart, the section over $(q, y)$ whose fibre coordinate is the projection onto $K_{\varphi(y)}$ of that lift of $-\hat f(\Phi(q))$ — after a reparametrization of the parameter, equal to the identity near $[0, 1]^n$, that keeps the family in the chart domain — is an sc⁺-section of the pull-back over the chart domain, and at $y = \Phi(q)$ it is $-f(\Phi(q))$. Cut off by an sc-smooth function on $X$ supported in the chart domain and equal to $1$ near a compact set containing $\Phi([0, 1]^n)$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · exists_isScSmoothMap_eq_one_nhdsSet⟧, it becomes a global sc⁺-section, with $f + S = 0$ at the points $(q, \Phi(q))$ where the cut-off is $1$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · exists_isScPlusSection_pullback_of_mapsTo_of_bump⟧. For $q \in [0, 1]^n$ it is the projection of $-\hat f(\Phi(q))$, so it depends on $q$ only through $\Phi(q)$. The text's (3) is for paths; it is stated for families because the homotopies of Theorem 6.35 need it (Findings, Chapter 6, item 46).

**(4)** ⟦Chapter6/OrientableNbhd · hasScPlusSectionsThrough_pullback_rn_of_bump⟧. Products of bump functions on $\mathbb R^n$ and on $X$ are bump functions on $\mathbb R^n \times X$, and they give the sections. $\mathbb R^n \times X$ ⟦Chapter2/FibredProduct · MPolyfold.paracompactSpace_prod⟧ and the total space of $\pi^*P$ ⟦Chapter2/StrongBundlePullback · paracompactSpace_pullbackSpace⟧ are paracompact, as the project's M-polyfolds and strong bundles must be. *Hidden hypotheses:* bump functions, for the global sections of (3) and (4), where the text assumes partitions of unity from §6.2 on. The construction uses neither that $x$ is smooth nor that $X$ is tame (pp. 220–221).

### VI.11 Lemma 6.29: general position along a family

The text (pp. 221–222): along a path $\varphi$ with a section $s(\cdot, t)$, the section $F(t, y, \lambda) = f(y) - s(y, t) + \sum\lambda_is_i(y, t)$ of the bundle over $[0, 1] \times \mathbb R^k \times X$; Lemma 6.29 asserts that there are $s_1, \dots, s_k$ with property (P): for every $t$, the slice $F_t$ is in general position to the boundary of $X \times \mathbb R^k$ at $(\varphi(t), 0)$. The proof is the sentence "using the results from the transversality theory".

**The statement formalized** (V6.33) ⟦Chapter6/Lemma629 · lemma_6_29⟧. *Over a tame $X$ with bump functions, for $f$ with tame germ data, an sc-smooth $\Phi : \mathbb R^n \to X$ and an sc⁺-section $S$ of $\pi^*P$ with $(f + S)(q, \Phi(q)) = 0$ near $[0, 1]^n$, there are finitely many sc⁺-sections $s_1, \dots, s_k$ of $\pi^*P$ such that $F(\lambda, (q, y)) = f(y) + S(q, y) + \sum\lambda_is_i(q, y)$ is in general position at $(0, (q, \Phi(q)))$ for all $q$ near $[0, 1]^n$.*

**The proof** is that of Theorem 5.18 (§V.20). The points $(0, (q, \Phi(q)))$ are zeros of $F$ ⟦Chapter6/Lemma629 · isZeroAt_paramSection_zero⟧, and for $q$ in a compact neighbourhood of $[0, 1]^n$ they form a compact set. At each of them finitely many sections make the parametrized section satisfy properties (i)–(ii) of §V.19; general position is open (§V.18); finitely many neighbourhoods cover the compact set, and the sections of all of them together do the job ⟦Chapter6/Lemma629 · exists_sections_isGeneralPositionGerm_of_isCompact⟧. *Hidden hypotheses:* $X$ tame, bump functions, tame germ data, the standing hypotheses of §6.5 and of Theorem 5.18. The conclusion is the general position of $F$ at the points $(t, \varphi(t), 0)$, which the text derives from (P) and which Lemmas 6.30 and 6.31 use. (P) itself, the general position of each slice $F_t$, is not stated (gap G.63); as we read it, it follows, since the tangent vectors of the family of zeros lie in $\ker F'$ and $\mathbb R^n$ has no boundary, but this chart computation is not carried out (Findings, Chapter 6, item 47).

### VI.12 Lemma 6.30: kernels as continuous families of subspaces

The text (p. 222): near $(t, \varphi(t), 0)$ the solution set of $F$ is a manifold with boundary with corners, $\pi(t, y, \lambda) = t$ restricted to it is a submersion, and the kernels $L_t$ form a smooth vector bundle $L$ over $[0, 1]$. What the propagation needs is less: the kernels form a continuous family, so that an orientation of one of them can be continued to the others.

**The kernels** (V6.34). At a zero with surjective linearization and germ data of index $d$, $\dim\ker = d$ ⟦Chapter6/KernelFamily · StrongBundle.IsSurjLinOfIndex.finrank_linKer⟧. Near a zero in good position the kernel is the tangent space of the solution set (Theorem 3.54, §III.45), the range of the derivative of an sc-retraction onto the solution set read in the chart. So along a continuous family $y_q$ of zeros in good position, read in one chart at continuously varying level-$1$ points $z_q$, near every $q_0$ the vectors $DS(z_q)b_i$, for a basis $b$ of the kernel at $q_0$ and that retraction $S$, are a continuous frame of the kernels ⟦Chapter6/KernelFamily · exists_local_frame_linKer⟧ — continuous because $(z, v) \mapsto DS(z)v$ is, independent near $q_0$ because independence is open, and spanning because the dimension is constant. The kernels form a continuous family of subspaces of the model space, of dimension the index ⟦Chapter6/KernelFamily · exists_subspaceFamily_linKer⟧. For an sc-smooth family of zeros $\mathbb R^n \to X$ read in a chart ⟦Chapter6/KernelFamily · hasFDerivAt_scDeriv_rn⟧, differentiating $\hat f(\Phi(q)) = 0$ shows that the derivative lies in the kernel of the linearization ⟦Chapter6/KernelFamily · fderiv_mem_linKer⟧. The bundle $L$ is a continuous family of subspaces; the solution set as a manifold with boundary with corners near $(t, \varphi(t), 0)$, the map $\pi$ and the smooth structure of $L$ are not formalized (gap G.62; Findings, Chapter 6, item 48).

**Continuous families of subspaces** (V6.35). A family of $n$-dimensional subspaces $L_b$ of a normed space, spanned near every point by a continuous frame ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily⟧, has the line bundle $b \mapsto \lambda(L_b)$ ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.det⟧, with the wedges of the frames as trivializations ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.Frame.pretriv⟧; the coordinate change between two frames is the determinant of the matrix expressing one in the other, continuous because that matrix solves a linear system with continuous coefficients ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.Frame.coordChange_continuousOn⟧. Families and orientations restrict along continuous maps ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.comp⟧ ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · LineOrientation.comp⟧. Over $[0, 1]$ an orientation of $\lambda(L_0)$ extends uniquely to an orientation of $\lambda(L)$ (§VI.9), and its value at $1$ is the continuation ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.transport⟧ ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.transport_eq⟧, injective ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.transport_injective⟧ and compatible with restriction ⟦Chapter6/SubspaceBundle · SubspaceFamily.transport_comp⟧; over a simply connected, locally path-connected base the continuation along a path depends only on its end points. This is the text's "an orientation of the lines … determines by continuation an orientation of all the other lines" (pp. 222–223), and the bundles $\tilde L$ of pp. 224–227. "Vector bundle" is read as a family of subspaces of one model space with continuous local frames.

**Families of kernels and their images** (V6.36). The kernels of a norm-continuous family of surjective Fredholm operators over a connected base form a continuous family ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · exists_subspaceFamily_ker⟧: their dimension is the index, and near $q_0$ the kernel of $A_q$ is the graph over $\ker A_{q_0}$ given by Lemma 6.18 with $P = 1$. The images of a continuous family under a jointly continuous family of linear maps injective on its members form one ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · SubspaceFamily.exists_map⟧, and continuous orientations are carried along ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · SubspaceFamily.isLineOrientation_map⟧. Cutting a continuous family by the kernel of a fixed $\ell$ that is onto on every member gives one ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · SubspaceFamily.exists_inf_ker⟧. "As $\tau$ varies, the bundle varies continuously" (pp. 223–226) is read in the operator norm, and for maps into a model space as joint continuity.

### VI.13 The stabilized section in a product chart, and Lemma 6.31

The text (pp. 222–223): with $T = (f - s(\cdot, t))'(\varphi(t))$, the kernel $L_t$ of $F_t'(\varphi(t), 0)$ fits into the sequence (96) $0 \to \ker T \to L_t \to \mathbb R^k \to \operatorname{coker}T \to 0$, and Lemma 6.31 says that it is exact.

**The product chart** (V6.37). The parametrized section $F$ lives on $\mathbb R^k \times (\mathbb R^n \times X)$; it is read in the product chart $(\lambda \mapsto \lambda) \times ((q \mapsto q) \times \varphi)$ at $(0, (q, z))$, whose tangent space and fibre are products ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · PullbackChartData.ofProd_scDeriv_r_apply⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · PullbackChartData.ofProd_mem_tangent_iff⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · PullbackChartData.mem_K_ofProd_iff⟧. There the linearization of $F$ is $(\lambda, (\sigma, v)) \mapsto D(\hat g_q \circ r)(z)v + \sum\lambda_i\hat s_i(q, \cdot)(z) + D_q\sigma$, with $g_q = f + S(q, \cdot)$ and $D_q$ the derivative in the parameter ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · StrongBundle.scDeriv_ofProd_slice_apply⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · StrongBundle.scDeriv_paramSection_apply⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · StrongBundleChart.paramDerivAt⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · StrongBundle.scDeriv_paramSection_ofProd_ofProd⟧. With the projection to $\sigma$ and the inclusion of the slice $\sigma = 0$ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · sliceProj⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · sliceIncl⟧, the kernel cut by $\sigma = 0$ is the image of $\ker(T \oplus \varphi)$ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · linKer_inf_ker_sliceProj_eq_map⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · exists_sliceOps⟧, where $T = g_q'(x)$ lies in $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · mem_linSet_sectionAdd_pullbackSlice⟧ and $\varphi(\lambda) = \sum\lambda_is_i(q, x)$. *$T \oplus \varphi$ is onto when $F$ is in general position at $(0, (q, \Phi(q)))$* ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · surjective_coprod_of_isLinSurjAt⟧: given $w$, the surjectivity of $F'$ gives $(\lambda, \sigma, v)$ with image $w$; the derivative of the curve of zeros, $(0, \sigma, D\Phi\,\sigma)$, lies in $\ker F'$ (§VI.12); subtracting it gives $(\lambda, 0, v - D\Phi\,\sigma)$ with the same image, a preimage under $T \oplus \varphi$. The kernel is then a closed subspace of the product with the right inclusion ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · exists_sliceKernel⟧. $\ker F_t'(\varphi(t), 0)$ is read as the kernel of the linearization of the whole $F$ cut by $\sigma = 0$ (Findings, Chapter 6, item 49) (pp. 221–223).

**Lemma 6.31** (V6.38) ⟦Chapter6/ParamKernel · lemma_6_31⟧. With these operators, (96) $0 \to \ker T \to \ker(T \oplus \varphi) \to \mathbb R^k \to K_z/R(T) \to 0$ is the stabilization sequence of $T$ and $\varphi$ (Lemma 6.14, §VI.6), hence exact. The text has $c$ onto by (P); here it is onto by the general position of $F$ (§VI.11) and the derivative of the family of zeros, which absorbs the $\mathbb R^n$-directions (p. 223).

### VI.14 Continuation, the sign, and the push-forward

The text (pp. 223–224): $\Phi_{E_t}$ of (94) identifies $\det(T_t)$ with $\lambda(L_t)$; an orientation $o_0$ of $\det(T_0)$ gives one of $\lambda(L_0)$, continuation carries it to $\lambda(L_1)$, and $\Phi_{E_1}^{-1}$ carries it to $\det(T_1)$: this defines $o_1 = \varphi_*o_0$.

**Continuation** (V6.39). Over a simply connected, locally path-connected base the continuation of a ray of $\lambda(L_{q_0})$ to $\lambda(L_{q_1})$ is the value at $q_1$ of the unique orientation extending it ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · SubspaceFamily.cont⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · SubspaceFamily.cont_eq⟧. It is the identity from a point to itself ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · SubspaceFamily.cont_self⟧, composes ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · SubspaceFamily.cont_trans⟧, is a bijection of rays ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · SubspaceFamily.contEquiv⟧, is compatible with pull-back ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · SubspaceFamily.cont_comp⟧, and along $[0, 1]$ it is the continuation of §VI.12 ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · SubspaceFamily.cont_eq_transport⟧. For a stabilization $T \oplus \varphi$ that is onto, $\det(T \oplus \varphi) \cong \lambda(\ker(T \oplus \varphi)) \otimes \lambda^*(\{0\}) \cong \lambda(\ker(T \oplus \varphi))$ ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · detEquivOfSurjective⟧, and through $\iota_\varphi$ (§VI.6) and an identification of the kernel with a member of $L$ the rays of $\det(T)$ and of $\lambda(L)$ correspond ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · stabRayEquiv⟧. The propagation is $\Phi_{E_0}$, then continuation, then $\Phi_{E_1}^{-1}$ on rays ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · propagate⟧, with the identity on a constant family ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · propagate_self⟧, composition ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · propagate_trans⟧ and pull-back ⟦Chapter6/Continuation · propagate_comp⟧. It is stated over any simply connected, locally path-connected base, so that one statement serves the paths and the squares; the fixed identification $\lambda^*(\mathbb R^k) \cong \lambda^*(\{0\})$ of (94) occurs at both ends.

**The sign** (V6.40). In a local determinant chart with projection $P$, the chart coordinate of $\iota_\psi(x) \in \det(S \oplus \psi)$ is $(-1)^{k\dim F/R(P) + \dim\operatorname{coker}S}\,D(S, \psi)$ times that of $x$ ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · coord_stabIota⟧, with $D$ ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · stabD⟧ continuous ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · continuousOn_stabD⟧ and nowhere zero ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · stabD_ne_zero⟧ near the centre. The first summand of the exponent is constant on a chart, the second is not. So where $\dim\operatorname{coker}T$ changes parity along a family, the rays carried by $\Phi_E$ jump. With $\alpha(T) = (-1)^{\dim\operatorname{coker}T}$ ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · stabSign⟧: *for a continuous orientation $o$ of $\mathrm{DET}$, a norm-continuous family $T_q$ and a continuous stabilization $\varphi_q$ with $T_q \oplus \varphi_q$ onto, the rays $\alpha(T_q)\,\Phi(o(T_q))$ of $\lambda(\ker(T_q \oplus \varphi_q))$ form an orientation* ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · isLineOrientation_stabRay⟧. Without the sign they need not ⟦Chapter6/StabilizationContinuity · not_isLineOrientation_stabRay_uncorrected⟧: $E = F = \mathbb R$, $k = 1$, $T_q = q/(1 + |q|)$ and $\varphi(r) = r_0$, where $\dim\operatorname{coker}T_q$ is $1$ at $q = 0$ and $0$ elsewhere. As we read it, the orientations carried by $\Phi_E$ of (94) along a continuous family are not continuous where $\dim\operatorname{coker}T$ changes parity, and Lemmas 6.33, 6.34 and the homotopy argument before Theorem 6.35 use that they are. The propagation uses $\alpha(T)\Phi_E$, which on each operator carries the text's orientation or its opposite (Findings, Chapter 6, item 50) (p. 212, as used on pp. 223–226).

**The push-forward** (V6.41). At a chart point $p$ of a point $y$ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · chartPt⟧, a section $S$ with $(f + S)(y) = 0$ and sections $s_1, \dots, s_k$ give $T = (f + S)'(y) \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, y)$ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · ChartPoint.stabT⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · ChartPoint.stabT_mem_linSet⟧ and $\varphi(\lambda) = \sum\lambda_i\hat s_i(z)$ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · ChartPoint.stabPhi⟧, with appended sections giving the appended stabilization ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · ChartPoint.stabPhi_finAppend⟧; $T \oplus \varphi$ is Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · isFredholm_stabCoprod⟧, and the sign is an involution ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · stabSign_inv⟧ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · toPerm_stabSign_symm⟧. A family of *stabilized kernels* ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels⟧ over a parameter space $Q$ consists of a global sc⁺-section $S$ of the pull-back with $f + S = 0$ at the points $(q, y(q))$, sections $s_1, \dots, s_k$, a continuous lift of $q \mapsto \varphi(y(q))$ to level $1$ of the chart, and a continuous family $\Lambda$ of subspaces of $E_0 \times \mathbb R^k$ such that at every chart point of $y(q)$ in the chart $T_q \oplus \varphi_q$ is onto and $\Lambda_q$ is the image of its kernel. It restricts along continuous maps ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.comp⟧. Its *push-forward* between two parameters $a, b$ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.push⟧: $o \in \mathrm{Or}^f_{y(a)}$ gives the ray $o(T_a)$, then $\alpha(T_a)\Phi_{E_a}(o(T_a))$, a ray of $\lambda(\Lambda_a)$; continuation carries it to $\lambda(\Lambda_b)$; $\alpha(T_b)\Phi_{E_b}^{-1}$ carries it to $\det(T_b)$; and $\mathrm{Or}^f_{y(b)} \cong \{\text{rays of }\det(T_b)\}$ (§VI.9) gives the image. It depends only on the data ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.push_congr⟧. With $\mathrm{orRay}_q(o)$, the ray of $\lambda(\Lambda_q)$ read from $o$ at $q$ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.orRay⟧, $\varphi_* = \mathrm{orRay}_b^{-1} \circ \mathrm{cont}_{ab} \circ \mathrm{orRay}_a$ ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.push_eq_orRay⟧. *Along a path with continuously varying data and a fixed point, continuation carries the rays read at one parameter to those read at the next* ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.cont_orRay_path⟧: the operators $T_q$, $\varphi_q$ vary continuously; their kernels form a continuous family (§VI.12); the sign makes the rays $\alpha\Phi(o(T_q))$ an orientation; and the inclusion into $E_0 \times \mathbb R^k$ carries that orientation to $\lambda(\Lambda)$. The push-forward is compatible with pull-back ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.push_comp⟧ and with concatenation ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.push_trans⟧. For given end-point operators the result differs from the text's by $\alpha(T_a)\alpha(T_b)$; the sections enter pointwise, and the continuity in the parameter is that of $\Lambda$ (Findings, Chapter 6, item 50) (p. 224).

### VI.15 The stabilized kernels exist; push-forwards along paths

**Lemma 6.30 for the push-forward** (V6.42) ⟦Chapter6/StabKernelsExist · exists_isStabKernels⟧. *For an sc-smooth $\Phi : \mathbb R^n \to X$ with $\Phi([0, 1]^n)$ in the domain of a chart, an sc⁺-section $S$ with $f + S = 0$ along $\Phi$ near $[0, 1]^n$, and sections $s_1, \dots, s_k$ as in Lemma 6.29, the stabilized kernels of the slices form a continuous family over $[0, 1]^n$.* The family $q \mapsto \varphi(\Phi(q))$ has a continuous lift to level $1$ ⟦Chapter6/StabKernelsExist · exists_continuousOn_lift_chart⟧, the values of an sc-smooth map on $\mathbb R^n$ being smooth points. The zeros $(0, (q, \Phi(q)))$ of $F$ are in general position, hence in good position; their kernels form a continuous family (§VI.12); cutting it by $\{d\sigma = 0\}$, a fixed functional onto on every member because the derivative of the family of zeros lies in the kernel, keeps it continuous (§VI.12); and §VI.13 identifies the cut with $\ker(T_q \oplus \varphi_q)$. The deviation is that of §VI.12 (gap G.62).

**Push-forwards along paths** (V6.43). The parameter points of $[0, 1]$ ⟦Chapter6/PushData · pt1_mem_Icc⟧, level-$1$ lifts at smooth points ⟦Chapter6/PushData · exists_lift_of_smooth⟧ and the chart points they give ⟦Chapter6/PushData · chartPtOf⟧ are the bookkeeping. *$e : \mathrm{Or}^f_{\gamma(0)} \to \mathrm{Or}^f_{\gamma(1)}$ is a push-forward along an sc-smooth path $\gamma$ in a chart* ⟦Chapter6/PushData · IsPush⟧ if there are global sc⁺-sections $S, s_1, \dots, s_k$ of $\pi^*P \to \mathbb R \times X$ with $(f + S)(t, \gamma(t)) = 0$ for $t$ near $[0, 1]$, and a family of stabilized kernels of their slices along $\gamma$ whose push-forward is $e$. Equal data give equal push-forwards ⟦Chapter6/PushData · IsStabKernels.push_eq_of_eq⟧. Pulled back along an affine reparametrization the sections still vanish along the reparametrized path ⟦Chapter6/PushData · isZeroAt_sectionAdd_reparamSection⟧ and give a push-forward along it ⟦Chapter6/PushData · isPush_reparam⟧; so a push-forward along $\gamma$ is the composite of push-forwards along its two halves, each reparametrized to $[0, 1]$ ⟦Chapter6/PushData · IsPush.split⟧. *Along every sc-smooth path in a set with property (3) of Proposition 6.28 there is a push-forward* ⟦Chapter6/PushData · exists_isPush⟧: (3) gives $S$, Lemma 6.29 gives $s_1, \dots, s_k$, and the stabilized kernels exist. Global sections of the pull-back stand in place of the text's sections over $U \times [0, 1]$, and (P) is used only to construct a push-forward (p. 224).

### VI.16 Lemma 6.33 and sections over families

**Lemma 6.33** (V6.45) ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.push_append⟧. *Appending sc⁺-sections $\bar s_1, \dots, \bar s_d$ after $s_1, \dots, s_k$ does not change the push-forward.* The text proves it with a homotopy $\tilde F(\tau, \cdot)$ and "one verifies by a simple computation". The computation is this. For $\ell_1, \dots, \ell_d \in \ker(T \oplus (\varphi, \psi))$ whose $\psi$-coordinates are the standard basis of $\mathbb R^d$, the map $w \mapsto (w, 0) \wedge \ell_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \ell_d$ ⟦Chapter6/AddSections · wedgeExt⟧ ⟦Chapter6/AddSections · wedgeExt_wedge⟧ does not depend on the $\ell_j$ — two choices differ by vectors of the image of $\ker(T \oplus \varphi)$, the span of the first block ⟦Chapter6/AddSections · wedgeExt_congr⟧ — and is bijective ⟦Chapter6/AddSections · wedgeExt_bijective⟧. With the appended stabilization ⟦Chapter6/AddSections · appendStab⟧ and the kernel inclusion $(v, \lambda) \mapsto (v, \lambda, 0)$ ⟦Chapter6/AddSections · kerAppend⟧, *the stabilization isomorphism of $(\varphi, \psi)$ is that of $\varphi$ followed by $w \mapsto (w, 0) \wedge \ell_1 \wedge \dots \wedge \ell_d$, exactly, with no sign* ⟦Chapter6/AddSections · detEquiv_stabIota_append⟧: a choice of Proposition 6.15 for $(\varphi, \psi)$ is one for $\varphi$ with the $\ell_j$ appended to the kernel basis and the standard basis vectors to the $r_i$, and with the appended sections last the matrix $(\bar c, r)$ becomes block triangular with an identity block, so the determinant in (94) is unchanged. Along a family the $\ell_j$ are chosen continuously ⟦Chapter6/AddSections · SubspaceFamily.exists_continuous_lifts⟧ — the larger kernels project onto $\mathbb R^d$ because $T \oplus \varphi$ is already onto — and the wedge extension carries continuous orientations along ⟦Chapter6/AddSections · isLineOrientation_wedgeExt⟧, through the kernel inclusion ⟦Chapter6/AddSections · kerEquivMap⟧. So the stabilized rays ⟦Chapter6/AddSections · stabRayEquiv_append⟧ and the propagations ⟦Chapter6/AddSections · propagate_append⟧ agree, and with them the push-forwards. The homotopy of the text's proof is not needed (Findings, Chapter 6, item 51) (pp. 224–225).

**Sections over families** (V6.46). For $g$ affine, $(q, y) \mapsto S(g(q), y)$ ⟦Chapter6/FamilySections · reparamSection⟧ is again an sc⁺-section of the pull-back ⟦Chapter6/FamilySections · StrongBundle.IsScPlusSection.reparam⟧, through the sc-smooth product map $g \times 1$ ⟦Chapter6/FamilySections · rnProdMapOp⟧, with the expected slices ⟦Chapter6/FamilySections · pullbackSlice_reparamSection⟧. Sc⁺-sections may be checked in one chart around each point ⟦Chapter6/FamilySections · StrongBundle.isScPlusSection_of_local⟧. Adding sections keeps the general position of $F$ at $(0, y)$ ⟦Chapter6/FamilySections · StrongBundle.isGeneralPositionGerm_paramSection_of_comp⟧: the linearization only gains columns, and the properties of Definition 5.17 survive. These are the sections $s(y, \tau, t)$ over a square and the text's "adding more sections, the properties will still hold" (pp. 224–226).

### VI.17 Lemma 6.34 and Proposition 6.32

**Lemma 6.34** (V6.47) ⟦Chapter6/Propagation · IsStabKernels.push_square⟧. *For a family of stabilized kernels over the square $[0, 1]^2$ with the end points $x_0$, $x_1$ fixed and the end-point operators varying continuously, the push-forwards along the edges $\tau = 0$ and $\tau = 1$ agree.* The edges are the restrictions to affine segments of the square ⟦Chapter6/PropagationWellDefined · sqEdge⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PropagationWellDefined · sqPath⟧. On the edge $t = 0$ the point is $x_0$ and the operators vary continuously, so by §VI.14 continuation along it carries $\mathrm{orRay}_{(0,0)}(o)$ to $\mathrm{orRay}_{(1,0)}(o)$; the same on $t = 1$. The square is simply connected, so continuation from $(0, 0)$ to $(1, 1)$ is the same through $(0, 1)$ and through $(1, 0)$. Writing both push-forwards as $\mathrm{orRay}^{-1} \circ \mathrm{cont} \circ \mathrm{orRay}$ gives the claim. The text's convex homotopy $s^\tau$ is part of the square of Proposition 6.32 below, and the continuity of the end-point orientations along $\tau$ is that of §VI.14, with the sign (p. 226).

**Proposition 6.32** (V6.44) ⟦Chapter6/PropagationWellDefined · proposition_6_32⟧. *Two push-forwards along the same sc-smooth path in the domain of a chart agree.* Let the data be $(S^0; s^0_1, \dots, s^0_{k^0})$ and $(S^1; s^1_1, \dots, s^1_{k^1})$. The text combines Lemma 6.33 (more sections) and Lemma 6.34 (a homotopy of the data); the formalization does both over one square (Findings, Chapter 6, item 52). *Step 1, the square.* $\Phi(\tau, t) = \gamma(t)$, constant in $\tau$, and $S^\tau = (1 - \tau)S^0 + \tau S^1$, a section of the pull-back over $\mathbb R^2 \times X$ by §VI.16; $f + S^\tau$ vanishes along $\Phi$ since both $f + S^0$ and $f + S^1$ do and the fibres are linear ⟦Chapter6/PropagationWellDefined · isZeroAt_sectionAdd_combo⟧. *Step 2, the sections.* With $\hat s^i_j = s^i_j$ for $j < k^i$ and $0$ otherwise, the sections $(1 - \tau)\hat s^0_j + \tau\hat s^1_j$, followed by the sections that Lemma 6.29 gives on the square. The parametrized section is in general position along the square — adding sections keeps it (§VI.16) — so the stabilized kernels exist over $[0, 1]^2$ (§VI.15). *Step 3, the edges $\tau = 0, 1$.* At $\tau = 0$ the sections $s^0$ are the first $k^0$ of the family and at $\tau = 1$ the sections $s^1$ are the first $k^1$, so Lemma 6.33 compares each datum with the edge of the square without reordering ⟦Chapter6/PropagationWellDefined · IsStabKernels.push_eq_of_prefix⟧, the edges being data of the same kind ⟦Chapter6/PropagationWellDefined · IsStabKernels.congr_data⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PropagationWellDefined · IsStabKernels.push_congr_data⟧. *Step 4, the edges $t = 0, 1$.* There the point is fixed and the operators are affine in $\tau$ ⟦Chapter6/PropagationWellDefined · linAt_principal_combo⟧, hence continuous ⟦Chapter6/PropagationWellDefined · continuous_principal_pullbackSlice⟧. *Step 5.* Lemma 6.34 equates the push-forwards along the edges $\tau = 0$ and $\tau = 1$, and Step 3 identifies them with the two given ones. *Hidden hypotheses:* the standing ones of §6.5 ($X$ tame, bump functions, tame germ data). "Does not depend on the choices" is read as the agreement of any two data (pp. 224–226).

### VI.18 Theorem 6.35, and paths in a chart

**Theorem 6.35** (V6.48). $U$ has the *local propagation property* in a chart $c$ ⟦Chapter6/PropagationWellDefined · HasLocalPropagation⟧ if $U$ lies in the domain of $c$, along every sc-smooth path in $U$ there is a push-forward, and any two push-forwards along paths in $U$ with the same end points agree. ⟦Chapter6/PropagationWellDefined · theorem_6_35⟧: *over a tame $X$ with bump functions, for $f$ with tame germ data, every smooth point $x$ has an open $U \ni x$ and a chart $c$ with the local propagation property.* The statement names the bundle and the point but not the section (possible omission); it is read for an sc-Fredholm section with tame germ data (Findings, Chapter 6, item 53). *Step 1.* $U \subseteq W$ and $c$ from Proposition 6.28; push-forwards exist along paths in $W$, a fortiori in $U$, by (3) (§VI.15). *Step 2, homotopy invariance* ⟦Chapter6/PropagationWellDefined · push_eq_of_homotopy⟧. For an sc-smooth $\Phi : \mathbb R^2 \to X$ with $\Phi([0, 1]^2) \subseteq W$ and the end points fixed, (3) for $n = 2$ gives $S$, Lemma 6.29 gives sections, and the stabilized kernels exist over the square. The edge $t \mapsto (\tau, t)$ is an affine map, so the restriction to it is a push-forward datum along $\Phi(\tau, \cdot)$ (§§VI.14–VI.15). Along $t = 0, 1$ the point is constant and so is the section $S(q, \cdot)$, because it depends on $q$ only through $\Phi(q)$; the end-point operators are then constant, and Lemma 6.34 applies. With Proposition 6.32, any push-forward along $\Phi(0, \cdot)$ equals any along $\Phi(1, \cdot)$. *Step 3, the reparametrization.* The homotopy of (1′) is $\gamma_0$ and $\gamma_1$ at its edges only for $t \in [0, 1]$, while a push-forward datum asks for zeros of $f + S$ for $t$ near $[0, 1]$. The proof therefore passes through $\gamma_i \circ \kappa$, which maps all of $\mathbb R$ into $\gamma_i([0, 1])$, with three homotopies whose edges are exact for all $t$: $H(\sigma, t) = \gamma_0((1 - \sigma)t + \sigma\kappa(t))$ from $\gamma_0$ to $\gamma_0 \circ \kappa$; the homotopy $(\tau, t) \mapsto \Phi(\tau, \kappa(t))$ from $\gamma_0 \circ \kappa$ to $\gamma_1 \circ \kappa$; and the analogue of $H$ for $\gamma_1$. Step 2 applied three times gives the agreement. $U$ is not shown to be sc-smoothly contractible (gap G.61); what the proof uses is (1′) (pp. 226–227).

**Paths in a chart** (V6.49). Sc-smooth maps that agree near every point of a set are sc-smooth together ⟦Chapter6/ScPaths · MPolyfold.isScSmoothMap_of_eventuallyEq⟧; $C^\infty$ maps of the parameter compose ⟦Chapter6/ScPaths · pt1_apply⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ScPaths · contDiff_pt1_comp⟧. *For an open $U$ in the domain of a chart and $x \in U$ there is an open $V \ni x$ in $U$ whose smooth points are pairwise joined by sc-smooth paths in $U$* ⟦Chapter6/ScPaths · exists_nhds_scPath⟧: in the chart, $t \mapsto \varphi^{-1}(r(u_1 + \kappa(t)(u_2 - u_1)))$, for $u_1, u_2$ in a small ball around $\varphi(x)$, as in (1′). The concatenation ⟦Chapter6/ScPaths · concatPath⟧ is $\gamma_1(\kappa(3s))$ for $s \le 1/2$ and $\gamma_2(\kappa(3s - 2))$ for $s > 1/2$ ⟦Chapter6/ScPaths · concatPath_of_le⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ScPaths · concatPath_of_gt⟧. It is constant on $[1/3, 2/3]$, with value $\gamma_1(1) = \gamma_2(0)$, so the two pieces glue sc-smoothly ⟦Chapter6/ScPaths · isScSmoothMap_concatPath⟧; it has the right end points ⟦Chapter6/ScPaths · concatPath_zero⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ScPaths · concatPath_one⟧ and halves ⟦Chapter6/ScPaths · concatPath_half₁⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ScPaths · concatPath_half₂⟧. Reparametrizing by a $C^\infty$ map keeps sc-smoothness ⟦Chapter6/ScPaths · isScSmoothMap_reparam⟧, and push-forwards compose along concatenations ⟦Chapter6/ContinuousOrientation · HasLocalPropagation.eq_trans⟧. Paths are joined only locally, inside a chart; the global facts recalled on p. 201 are not formalized (gap G.56) (pp. 227–228).

### VI.19 Definition 6.36: orientable neighbourhoods and continuous orientations

**Definition 6.36** (V6.50). The text: an orientable neighbourhood of $(f, x)$ is an open, sc-smoothly contractible $U$ with the local propagation property, and a continuous orientation over it is a choice $y \mapsto o_y$ carried into itself by the propagation. Since Proposition 6.28 gives (1′), an orientable neighbourhood is a pair $V \subseteq U$ ⟦Chapter6/SectionOrientation · IsOrientableNbhd⟧: $U$ open with the local propagation property in a chart, $V \ni x$ open with any two smooth points joined by an sc-smooth path in $U$. A *continuous orientation* is a choice $y \mapsto o_y$ on $V_\infty$, read in the chart, carried into itself by the push-forwards along the paths in $U$ ⟦Chapter6/ContinuousOrientation · IsContinuousOrientation⟧. *There are exactly two* ⟦Chapter6/ContinuousOrientation · exists_two_isContinuousOrientation⟧: given $o_x$, set $o_y$ to be the push-forward of $o_x$ along any path in $U$ from $x$ to $y$, well defined by the local propagation property; push-forwards compose along concatenations, so this is a continuous orientation; the two values of $o_x$ give two different ones; and a continuous orientation is determined by its value at $x$. *Every smooth point has an orientable neighbourhood* ⟦Chapter6/ContinuousOrientation · exists_orientableNbhd⟧ ⟦Chapter6/SectionOrientation · exists_isOrientableNbhd⟧, by Theorem 6.35 and §VI.18. *Hidden hypotheses:* the standing ones of §6.5 (Findings, Chapter 6, item 54) (p. 227).

### VI.20 The path category $PX$

**Reparametrization homotopies** (V6.51). The values of an sc-smooth path at parameters are smooth points ⟦Chapter6/ScHomotopy · mem_smoothSet_of_isScSmoothMap⟧, and $C^\infty$ maps of $\mathbb R^2$ compose ⟦Chapter6/ScHomotopy · contDiff_pt2_comp⟧. *For a $C^\infty$ $\theta$ with $\theta(0) = 0$, $\theta(1) = 1$, $\gamma \circ \theta$ is sc-smoothly homotopic to $\gamma$ with the end points fixed* ⟦Chapter6/ScHomotopy · isScHomotopyRel_reparam⟧, by $H(\tau, t) = \gamma((1 - \tau)t + \tau\theta(t))$, and inside every set containing $\gamma([0, 1])$ when $\theta([0, 1]) \subseteq [0, 1]$ ⟦Chapter6/ScHomotopy · reparam_mem⟧. With the halves of a path ⟦Chapter6/ScHomotopy · leftHalf⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ScHomotopy · rightHalf⟧, the concatenation of the two halves of $\gamma$ is such a reparametrization ⟦Chapter6/ScHomotopy · halvesReparam⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ScHomotopy · concatPath_halves⟧ (p. 228).

**The category** (V6.52). The tools are the value $\kappa(1/2)$ ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · smoothTransition_half⟧, constant maps at smooth points ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · isScSmoothMap_const_of_mem_smoothSet⟧, maps defined by cases on closed pieces that agree near the seams ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · isScSmoothMap_ite⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · isScSmoothMap_ite₃⟧ and the middle third of a concatenation ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · concatPath_of_le_two_thirds⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · concatPath_of_one_third_le⟧. Sc-smooth homotopy with the end points fixed ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScHomotopic⟧ is an equivalence relation on the sc-smooth paths from $x$ to $y$ ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScHomotopic.refl⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScHomotopic.symm⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScHomotopic.trans⟧. Transitivity needs care: a homotopy meets its edge conditions only on $[0, 1]$ (decision D2), and two homotopies glued in $\tau$ need not agree off $[0, 1]$, so all paths and homotopies are first reparametrized by $\kappa$ in $t$ (Findings, Chapter 6, item 71). The paths with smooth end points ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScPath⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScPath.source_mem_smoothSet⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScPath.target_mem_smoothSet⟧ have the constant paths ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScPath.const⟧, concatenation ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScPath.concat⟧ and reversal ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScPath.reverse⟧. Concatenation is well defined on classes ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScPath.concat_congr⟧, has the constant paths as units ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScPath.const_concat⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScPath.concat_const⟧, is associative ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScPath.concat_assoc⟧ — the two bracketings differ by an explicit reparametrization ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · assocReparam⟧, joined by a three-piece homotopy ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · isScHomotopyRel_triHomotopy⟧ — and the reversed paths are inverses ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScPath.concat_reverse⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScPath.reverse_concat⟧. The classes ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScPathClass⟧ with their composition ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · ScPathClass.comp⟧ make the smooth points a category $PX$ ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · PathCat⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · PathCat.category⟧, indeed a groupoid ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · PathCat.groupoid⟧, with the morphism of a path ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · PathCat.homMk⟧, composition and identities on representatives ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · PathCat.comp_mk⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · PathCat.id_eq_mk⟧, equality of morphisms as homotopy ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · PathCat.mk_eq_mk_iff⟧, every morphism represented ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · PathCat.exists_eq_mk⟧ and inverses by reversal ⟦Chapter6/PathCategory · PathCat.inv_mk⟧. The text does not name the identities; they are the classes of the constant paths. The second piece $\psi(\beta(s))$ of the composition on p. 228 leaves $[0, 1]$, since $\beta([1/2, 1]) = [1, 2]$; it is read as $\psi(\beta(s) - 1)$ (possible misprint; Findings, Chapter 6, item 55). ### VI.21 Comparing charts: the transfer, and $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ in a chosen chart

The proof of Theorem 6.37 carries an orientation along orientable neighbourhoods of different points of a path, which may lie in different charts. The text takes $T_xX$, $Y_x$, $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ and $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ to be the same whichever chart is used (p. 219); here they are made at chart points (§VI.1), so the charts have to be compared (Findings, Chapter 6, item 70).

**Conjugation of determinants** (V6.53). For isomorphisms $A$, $\Gamma$ with $S'A = \Gamma S$, $A$ maps $\ker S$ onto $\ker S'$ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · conjKerEquiv⟧ and $\Gamma$ induces $\operatorname{coker}S \cong \operatorname{coker}S'$ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · conjCokerEquiv⟧; together they give $\det(S) \cong \det(S')$ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · conjDet⟧, on wedges $(a \wedge \dots) \otimes (d \wedge \dots)^* \mapsto (Aa \wedge \dots) \otimes ([\Gamma d] \wedge \dots)^*$ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · conjDet_wedge_tmul⟧, compatible with composition, equal data and the identity ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · conjDet_trans⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · conjDet_congr⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · conjDet_refl⟧. Good left-projections are conjugated, $\Gamma P\Gamma^{-1} \in \Pi_{S'}$ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · IsGoodLeftProj.conj⟧, and the $\gamma^P$ commute with the conjugation ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · gammaProj_conjDet⟧; read in local determinant charts the conjugation has a continuous nowhere-zero coordinate ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · coord_conjDet_coordInv⟧, so continuous orientations of $\mathrm{DET}$ are carried along ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · isLineOrientation_conj⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · LineOrientation.conj⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · LineOrientation.conj_apply⟧, with the same rules ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · LineOrientation.conj_refl⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · LineOrientation.conj_trans⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · LineOrientation.conj_congr⟧.

**The transfer between two chart points** (V6.53). For chart points $p$, $p'$ of $x$, $A$ is the derivative at $z$ of the transition of the base charts ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.baseDeriv⟧, with the cocycle rules ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.baseDeriv_self⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.baseDeriv_trans⟧, an sc-operator ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.isScOperator_baseDeriv⟧; $\Gamma$ is the fibre part of the transition of the strong bundle charts ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.fiberMap⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.fiberMap_self⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.fiberMap_trans⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.isScOperator_fiberMap⟧. They restrict to isomorphisms $T_zO \cong T_{z'}O'$ and $K_z \cong K_{z'}$ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.transferT⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.transferK⟧, again with the cocycle rules ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.transferT_self_apply⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.transferT_trans_apply⟧. At a zero the linearizations in the two charts are related by them, the chain rule applied to the principal parts ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.scDeriv_principal_baseDeriv⟧, and sc⁺-operators conjugate to sc⁺-operators ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.IsScPlusOp.conj⟧; so $L \in \mathrm{Lin}_p(f, x)$ iff $\Gamma LA^{-1} \in \mathrm{Lin}_{p'}(f, x)$ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.mem_linSet_transfer_iff⟧. Conjugation of orientations over this bijection of the bases is the transfer $\mathrm{Or}^f_x(p) \cong \mathrm{Or}^f_x(p')$ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.orTransfer⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.orTransfer_apply⟧, with the cocycle rules ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.orTransfer_self⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ChartTransfer · ChartPoint.orTransfer_trans⟧.

**The push-forward does not depend on the chart** (V6.54). The sign is invariant, conjugation preserving $\dim\operatorname{coker}$ ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · stabSign_conj⟧; the stabilization is natural — $(\Gamma S A^{-1}) \oplus \Gamma\varphi$ is the conjugate of $S \oplus \varphi$, with the conjugated kernel, onto iff $S \oplus \varphi$ is ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · coprod_conj⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · ker_coprod_conj⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · surjective_coprod_conj⟧ — and so is its isomorphism on rays ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · conj_stab_key⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · stabRayEquiv_conjDet⟧; continuation is natural under jointly continuous families of injective linear maps ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · SubspaceFamily.cont_map⟧. The principal parts of the sections transform by $\Gamma$ ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · ChartPoint.fiberMap_principal⟧, so the operators $T$ and $\varphi$ of a datum in one chart are the conjugates of those in the other ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · ChartPoint.conj_of_linAt⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · ChartPoint.conj_of_principal⟧, and $A$ varies continuously along a path ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · continuous_baseDeriv⟧. A family of stabilized kernels in one chart is therefore carried by $A \times 1$ to one in the second chart, with the same sections ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · IsStabKernels.exists_transfer⟧, the rays read from an orientation corresponding under the transfer ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · IsStabKernels.orRay_transfer⟧; a push-forward in one chart, conjugated by the transfers at the end points, is a push-forward in the other ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · IsPush.transfer⟧, and the local propagations of two charts agree ⟦Chapter6/PushTransfer · HasLocalPropagation.push_compat⟧. The text does not compare charts (pp. 222–228).

**$\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ in a chosen chart** (V6.55). A chart of the atlas at $x$ is chosen for every $x$ ⟦Chapter6/SectionOrientation · orChart⟧ ⟦Chapter6/SectionOrientation · isChart_orChart⟧ ⟦Chapter6/SectionOrientation · mem_orChart⟧, and $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ is the set of the orientations read there ⟦Chapter6/SectionOrientation · Orx⟧, with two elements ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · exists_two_orx⟧. It is identified with the orientations read in any other chart at $x$ by the transfer ⟦Chapter6/SectionOrientation · toChartOr⟧ ⟦Chapter6/SectionOrientation · toChartOr_orChart⟧, compatibly with composition ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · toChartOr_trans⟧, and a map $y \mapsto o_y$ is read in the chart of an orientable neighbourhood through it ⟦Chapter6/SectionOrientation · restrictOr⟧. A chosen chart stands for the text's chart-free $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ (pp. 220, 228).

### VI.22 Transport along paths from local push-forwards

The proof of Theorem 6.37 (p. 228): for a path $\varphi$, "using the compactness of $[0, 1]$ and a finite covering" by orientable neighbourhoods, $\varphi_*$ is the composite of the local propagations; "by a covering argument" it depends only on $[\varphi]$; and "it is obvious that $\Gamma_f$ is unique". The formalization separates this argument from orientations: it is proved for any family of types over $X_\infty$ (Findings, Chapter 6, item 72).

**Local transport data** (V6.56) ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport⟧: a family of *good* open sets covering $X_\infty$, all fibres in bijection, and for every good set $U$ a push-forward along every sc-smooth path in $U$, such that push-forwards in one good set compose and do not depend on the good set containing the path.
