Then the push-forward along a loop in a good set is the identity ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.push_eq_refl⟧, in a good set it depends only on the end points ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.push_eq_push⟧, and only on the path on $[0, 1]$ ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.push_congr⟧.

**The dyadic transport.** At level $0$ it is the push-forward in a chosen good set containing $\gamma([0, 1])$ (an arbitrary bijection if there is none); at level $n + 1$ it is the composite of the transports at level $n$ along the two halves ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.transportN⟧. On a path in a good set every level gives the push-forward ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.transportN_eq_push⟧, by the composition rule. The pieces of level $N$ lie in good sets ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.IsFine⟧ for some $N$: the preimages of the good sets cover the compact $[0, 1]$, so there is a Lebesgue number $\delta$ ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.IsLebesgueNumber⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.exists_isLebesgueNumber⟧, and $2^N\delta > 1$ suffices ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.isFine_of_isLebesgueNumber⟧. From such an $N$ on the levels agree ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.transportN_eq_of_isFine⟧, since at the next level each piece is split inside its good set. The *transport* is the value at such a level ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.transport⟧.

**Its properties.** It is the push-forward on a path in a good set ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.transport_eq_push⟧ — property (∗) — depends only on the path on $[0, 1]$ ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.transport_congr⟧, is the identity on paths constant on $[0, 1]$ ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.transport_const⟧, and is the composite along the two halves ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.transport_halves⟧. *Homotopy invariance* ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.transport_eq_of_isScHomotopyRel⟧ is the covering argument. For a homotopy $\Phi : \mathbb R^2 \to X$ the preimages of the good sets cover $[0, 1]^2$, with a Lebesgue number $\delta$ ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.exists_isSqLebesgueNumber⟧. *The square lemma* ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.transportN_square⟧: for a rectangle of $[0, 1]^2$ with sides $< 2^n\delta$, the transports at level $n$ along its vertical, horizontal and diagonal segments ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · vSeg⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · hSeg⟧ ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · dSeg⟧ commute around its boundary — left side then top equals bottom then right side. By induction on $n$: for $n = 0$ the rectangle lies in one good set, and both composites are the push-forward along the diagonal; for $n + 1$ the rectangle is cut into four quadrants and the four commutative squares are pasted, the interior edges cancelling ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · equiv_paste_squares⟧. Applied to $[0, 1]^2$ at a level with $2^n\delta > 1$, with the sides $\tau \mapsto \Phi(\tau, 0)$, $\tau \mapsto \Phi(\tau, 1)$ constant on $[0, 1]$ and of trivial transport, it gives the invariance. The transport is invariant under reparametrization ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.transport_reparam⟧ (§VI.20) and takes concatenations to composites ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.transport_concatPath⟧, the halves of a concatenation being reparametrizations of the two paths. *Uniqueness* ⟦Chapter6/PathTransport · LocalTransport.transport_unique⟧: a family of bijections along the sc-smooth paths that is homotopy invariant, takes concatenations to composites and is the push-forward on paths in good sets, is the transport — $G(\gamma) = G(\text{left half}) \circ G(\text{right half})$ through the reparametrization, and induction on the dyadic level. Dyadic subdivisions of $[0, 1]$ and of $[0, 1]^2$ stand in place of arbitrary finite coverings (p. 228).

### VI.23 Theorem 6.37: the functor $\Gamma_f$

The text: *for a strong bundle over a tame M-polyfold and an sc-Fredholm section $f$ there is a uniquely determined functor $\Gamma_f : PX \to \mathcal O_f$, $x \mapsto \mathrm{Or}^f_x$, with (∗): for every smooth $x$, every sc-smoothly contractible open $U \ni x$ on which $f$ has the local propagation property, and every sc-smooth path $\varphi : [0, 1] \to U$, the propagation $\varphi_*$ and $\Gamma_f([\varphi])$ coincide.*

**The local data of $f$** (V6.57). $U$ is a propagation neighbourhood if it is open with the local propagation property in some chart ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · IsPropagationNbhd⟧. Along a path in such a $U$ the push-forward, read in the chosen charts of the end points through the transfer (§VI.21), is $\mathrm{orPush}$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orPush⟧; it equals every push-forward along the path in every chart in which the path lies in a set with the local propagation property ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orPush_eq⟧ — by the chart independence of §VI.21 and the cocycle rule of the transfer — it does not depend on the neighbourhood ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orPush_compat⟧, and it composes ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orPush_trans⟧. With Theorem 6.35, which makes the propagation neighbourhoods cover $X_\infty$, and §VI.9, which puts every $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ in bijection with every other, these are local transport data ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orLocalTransport⟧, and their transport satisfies (∗) ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orLocalTransport_transport_eq⟧.

**The functor.** $\Gamma_f([\varphi])$ is the transport along $\varphi$, well defined on classes by homotopy invariance ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orFunctorMap⟧ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orFunctorMap_mk⟧; it takes identities to identities ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orFunctorMap_id⟧ and compositions to composites ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orFunctorMap_comp⟧, by the constancy and concatenation rules of §VI.22; and it is a functor $PX \to \mathrm{Type}$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orFunctor⟧. Property (∗) for a family $G$ on the morphisms of $PX$, on the members of a family of open sets ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · IsStarPropertyOn⟧ and on all of them ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · IsStarProperty⟧, reads $G([\varphi]) = \mathrm{toChartOr}^{-1}_{\varphi(1)} \circ e \circ \mathrm{toChartOr}_{\varphi(0)}$ for every chart $c$, every open $U$ with the local propagation property in $c$, every sc-smooth path $\varphi$ in $U$ with smooth end points and every push-forward $e$ along $\varphi$ in $c$. $\Gamma_f$ has it ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orFunctorMap_isStarProperty⟧, so the property is satisfiable. *Uniqueness*: a family with the rules for identities and composites and with (∗) on the members of a family of such open sets covering $X_\infty$ is $\Gamma_f$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orFunctorMap_unique_of_cover⟧ — restrict the local data to the cover ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · LocalTransport.restrict⟧ and apply the uniqueness of the transport — in particular with (∗) everywhere ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · orFunctorMap_unique⟧.

**Theorem 6.37** ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · theorem_6_37⟧. *Over a tame $X$ with bump functions, for $f$ with tame germ data and $P$ with sc⁺-sections through the smooth fibre points, there is exactly one family of bijections $\Gamma_f([\varphi]) : \mathrm{Or}^f_x \to \mathrm{Or}^f_y$ on the morphisms of $PX$ taking identities to identities and compositions to composites, with property (∗).* *Hidden hypotheses:* the standing ones of §6.5, and sc⁺-sections through every smooth fibre point, so that every $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ has two elements (bump functions give them). (∗) is asked for every open set with the local propagation property, not only for sc-smoothly contractible ones (gap G.61), and the uniqueness needs it only on a covering family — for instance on the sc-smoothly contractible ones, wherever they cover $X_\infty$. $\mathcal O_f$ is read as types and bijections, and "uniquely determined" for the maps on morphisms: on objects there is no choice (p. 228).

### VI.24 Definitions 6.38–6.40: orientability and orientations

**Definition 6.38** (V6.58). *$f$ is orientable if for every pair of smooth points $x$, $y$ in the same path component, $\Gamma_f([\varphi])$ does not depend on the class $[\varphi] : x \to y$* ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · IsOrientableSection⟧. "In the same path component" is read as "joined by an sc-smooth path" ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · scPathSetoid⟧; for points not so joined there is nothing to check (Findings, Chapter 6, item 73). *Equivalently there is $y \mapsto o_y$ with $\Gamma_f([\varphi])o_x = o_y$ for every $[\varphi] : x \to y$* ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · isOrientableSection_iff_exists⟧: from left to right, choose a base point in each class of points joined by sc-smooth paths and set $o_y = \Gamma_f([\varphi])o_{\text{base}}$ for any $[\varphi]$, which does not depend on $[\varphi]$; from right to left, $\Gamma_f([\varphi])$ and $\Gamma_f([\psi])$ are bijections between two-element sets with the same value at $o_x$, hence equal (§VI.9) (p. 229).

**Definition 6.39** (V6.59). *$f$ is orientable if there is $y \mapsto o_y$ on $X_\infty$ such that every smooth point has an orientable neighbourhood over which it is one of the two continuous orientations* ⟦Chapter6/SectionOrientation · IsOrientableSection'⟧. The definition writes "$y \in U_\infty$" before any $U$ is introduced; it is read as $y \in X_\infty$ (possible misprint; Findings, Chapter 6, item 74). *This holds iff there is $y \mapsto o_y$ with $\Gamma_f([\varphi])o_x = o_y$ for all $[\varphi]$* ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · isOrientableSection'_iff_exists⟧. From right to left: on an orientable neighbourhood $V \subseteq U$ the push-forwards along paths in $U$ are values of $\Gamma_f$, by (∗), so the restriction is a continuous orientation. From left to right: elements carried into each other by the transport along the paths in the members of an open covering are carried into each other along every path ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · LocalTransport.transport_apply_eq_of_local⟧ — the transport is computed on dyadic pieces inside orientable neighbourhoods. *So Definitions 6.38 and 6.39 are equivalent* ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · isOrientableSection_iff⟧. The text calls them equivalent without proof (Findings, Chapter 6, item 73) (p. 229).

**Definition 6.40** (V6.60). *An orientation of $f$ is a map $y \mapsto o_y$ on $X_\infty$ whose restriction to every orientable neighbourhood of every smooth point is a continuous orientation* ⟦Chapter6/SectionOrientation · IsSectionOrientation⟧. Equivalently $\Gamma_f([\varphi])o_x = o_y$ for all $[\varphi] : x \to y$ ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · isSectionOrientation_iff⟧, by the argument of Definition 6.39; so $f$ has an orientation iff it is orientable ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · exists_isSectionOrientation_iff⟧, two orientations that agree at a point agree on the smooth points joined to it by sc-smooth paths ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · IsSectionOrientation.apply_eq_iff⟧, and there are exactly two on each such class ⟦Chapter6/OrientationFunctor · IsSectionOrientation.exists_two⟧. An orientable neighbourhood is the pair of §VI.19 (Findings, Chapter 6, item 75) (p. 229).

### VI.25 Theorem 6.41: the natural orientation of the solution set

The text: *over a tame $X$, let $f$ be a proper sc-Fredholm section in general position to the boundary at every zero, and $o^f$ an orientation of $f$; then $S = f^{-1}(0)$ is a smooth compact manifold with boundary with corners with a natural orientation.* The proof: $S$ is such a manifold "from the transversality discussion"; $\ker f'(x) = T_xS$ and, $f'(x)$ being onto, $T_xS$ is oriented by $o^f_x$; and "one verifies that the differential geometric local prolongation of the orientation on $S$ is the same as the Fredholm one".

**The first assertion** (V6.61) ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · theorem_6_41_solutionSet⟧. *For $X$ tame and a proper $f$ with tame germ data in general position (Definition 5.17) at every zero, $S$ is compact, a smooth submanifold in general position with the induced structure of a tame manifold with boundary with corners* — the conclusions of Theorem 5.18 (§V.20), with good position from general position by Lemma 4.19 (§IV.14) ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · MPolyfold.IsGeneralPositionAt.isGoodPositionAt⟧. In a chart, $T_xS = \ker f'(x)$ ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · tangentSpace_solutionSet_eq_linKer⟧ (§V.17). "Proper" is the text's hypothesis; the proof uses only the compactness of $S$, which for sc-Fredholm sections is equivalent to it (Theorem 5.5, §V.6), so nothing of the hypothesis is lost (Findings, Chapter 6, item 90).

**The tangent orientation.** At a zero, $f'(x)$ — the linearization of $f + s$ with $s = 0$ ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · ChartPoint.linZero⟧ — lies in $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · ChartPoint.linZero_mem_linSet⟧ and is onto ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · ChartPoint.linZero_surjective⟧, with kernel $T_xS$ in the chart ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · ChartPoint.map_ker_linZero⟧. So an element $o_x$ of $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ gives a ray of $\det f'(x) \cong \lambda(\ker f'(x)) = \lambda(T_xS)$, the *tangent orientation* ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · ChartPoint.tangentOr⟧, read in a chart at a zero ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · tangentOrAt⟧. The sign of a surjective operator is $1$ ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · stabSign_of_surjective⟧, and the stabilization by $\mathbb R^0$ of a surjective operator is $\det(T) \cong \lambda(\ker T)$ on rays ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · stabRayEquiv_zero⟧, so the tangent orientation is the stabilized ray of §VI.14 for the empty family of sections ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · ChartPoint.stabRayEquiv_eq_tangentOr⟧.

**"The local prolongation is the Fredholm one."** Along an sc-smooth path $\gamma$ of zeros in the domain of a chart, the datum $S = 0$, $k = 0$ is a family of stabilized kernels ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · isStabKernels_zero⟧, its kernels being those of $f'(\gamma_q)$ ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · SubspaceFamily.congrL⟧; they form a continuous family of subspaces, by Lemma 6.30 (§VI.12) ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · exists_tangentFamily⟧ ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · tangentFamily⟧ ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · tangentFamily_L⟧, and the rays read from an orientation are the tangent orientations ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · IsStabKernels.orRay_eq_tangentOr⟧. So along a path of zeros the push-forward is continuation between tangent orientations ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · cont_tangentOr⟧, and *the tangent orientations given by an orientation of $\mathrm{DET}$ along the path form an orientation of the line bundle $\lambda(\Lambda)$* ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · isLineOrientation_tangentOr⟧. Intermediate parameters are reached by the paths $s \mapsto \gamma(t\kappa(s))$, which stay in $\gamma([0, t])$ for all $s \in \mathbb R$. For an orientation $o$ of $f$ and an sc-smooth path of zeros in an orientable neighbourhood $V \subseteq U$, the tangent orientations of $o$ along it form an orientation of $\lambda(\Lambda)$ ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · isLineOrientation_tangentOr_of_isSectionOrientation⟧, and together this is the theorem ⟦Chapter6/SolutionOrientation · theorem_6_41⟧ (Findings, Chapter 6, item 91).

**Readings and what is left.** *Hidden hypotheses:* tame germ data, the standing hypothesis of Chapter 5; the orientation $o$ exists iff $f$ is orientable (§VI.24). "A natural orientation" is read as the tangent orientations with their continuity along the sc-smooth paths of zeros in a chart, and the prolongation sentence as the identity of continuation and push-forward along such paths. Not formalized: an orientation of $S$ as an abstract manifold, of its tangent bundle in the charts of the induced structure (gap G.67); the compatibility of the tangent orientations read in two charts at one zero (gap G.68); and the paragraph after the theorem — for $f$ not generic, a small sc⁺-perturbation $s$ supported near the zero set, the orientation of $S_{f+s}$ from $o^f$, and $\mathrm{Lin}(f + s, x) = \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ for the orientation of $\det((f + s)'(x))$ (gap G.69) (Findings, Chapter 6, items 92, 93) (pp. 229–230).

### VI.26 Remark 6.42: the orientation of $\hat f$ at a point

The text: for an oriented $(f, o)$ and an sc⁺-section $s$ of $Y \to X \times [0, 1]$, $\hat f(x, t) = f(x) + s(x, t)$ has a natural orientation from $o$ and the standard orientation of $[0, 1]$: for $L = (f - t)'(x)$ oriented by $h = (a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) \otimes (b_1 \wedge \dots \wedge b_l)^*$, orient $\tilde L(a, b) = La$ by $\tilde h = (a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n \wedge e) \otimes (b_1 \wedge \dots \wedge b_l)^*$, $e$ the standard orientation of $[0, 1]$; $\tilde L$ lies in the linearization space of $\hat f$ at $(x, t)$ (p. 230).

**The linear algebra** (V6.62). For Fredholm $L$, $\tilde L = L \oplus 0 : E \times \mathbb R \to F$ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · extOp⟧ is Fredholm ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · isFredholm_extOp⟧ with $\ker\tilde L = \ker L \times \mathbb R$ — one dimension more ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · finrank_ker_extOp⟧, the new direction $e = (0, 1)$ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · extE⟧ — and the same range ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · range_extOp⟧ and cokernel ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · extCoker⟧. The map $h \mapsto \tilde h$, $(a_1 \wedge \dots \wedge a_n) \otimes d^* \mapsto ((a_1, 0) \wedge \dots \wedge (a_n, 0) \wedge e) \otimes d^*$, is an isomorphism $\det(L) \cong \det(\tilde L)$ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · extDet⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · extDet_wedge_tmul⟧, the wedge extension of §VI.16 with one vector. In local determinant charts its coordinate is $(-1)^{\dim F/R(P) + \dim\operatorname{coker}L}$ times a continuous nowhere-zero function ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · coord_extDet⟧. Over the convex $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$, where $\dim\operatorname{coker}L$ can change parity, the orientation defined by $\tilde h$ at one $L$ could therefore differ from the one defined at another, as we read it. With the sign of §VI.14, $(-1)^{\dim\operatorname{coker}L}\,h \mapsto \tilde h$ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · extDetN⟧ has a coordinate continuous up to a sign constant on a chart ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · coord_extDetN⟧, agrees with the text's map when $L$ is onto ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · extDetN_eq_of_surjective⟧, and pulls continuous orientations back along $L \mapsto \tilde L$ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · isLineOrientation_extPull⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · LineOrientation.extPull⟧ (Findings, Chapter 6, item 95). Transported along isomorphisms $A$, $\Gamma$, $\hat L = \Gamma^{-1}(L \oplus 0)A$ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · extConjOp⟧ gets the isomorphism $h \mapsto \tilde h$ followed by the conjugation of §VI.21 ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · extConjDet⟧; and for a preconnected $C$ and a simply connected, locally path-connected $\hat C$ containing the $\hat L$, an orientation $o$ of $\mathrm{DET}$ over a nonempty $C$ gives exactly one orientation $\hat o$ over $\hat C$ with $\hat o(\hat L)$ the image of $o(L)$ for every $L \in C$ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · existsUnique_extConjOr⟧.

**In charts.** $X \times [0, 1]$ is read as $\mathbb R \times X$ (decision D2), with the parameter first; $s$ is an sc⁺-section $S$ of $\pi^*P$, and $\hat f = \tilde f + S$ with $\tilde f(t, y) = f(y)$. At the product chart point $(t, z)$ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · ChartPoint.prodPt⟧ the tangent space is $\mathbb R \times T_zO$ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · ChartPoint.mem_prodPt_T_iff⟧ and the fibre $K_z$ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · ChartPoint.mem_prodPt_K_iff⟧. The text's $\tilde L(a, b) = La$ puts the $\mathbb R$-factor second, so $\hat L = \Gamma^{-1}(L \oplus 0)A$ with $A$ the swap of the factors and $\Gamma = 1$ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · ChartPoint.prodT⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · ChartPoint.prodK⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · ChartPoint.prodLin⟧. Sc⁺-operators lift to the product ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · ChartPoint.IsScPlusOp.prodPt⟧, sections of $P$ lift to $t$-constant sections of $\pi^*P$ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · constLift⟧, and so $\hat L \in \mathrm{Lin}(\hat f, (t, x))$ for every $L \in \mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · ChartPoint.prodLin_mem_linSet⟧ — the derivative in $t$ of a $t$-constant lift vanishes, and $S$ only contributes an sc⁺-operator. *An orientation $o$ of $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ gives exactly one orientation $\hat o$ of $\mathrm{DET}(\hat f, (t, x))$ with $\hat o(\hat L)$ the image of $o(L)$ for every $L$* ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · ChartPoint.existsUnique_prodOr⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · ChartPoint.prodOr⟧ ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · ChartPoint.prodOr_apply⟧, and $o \mapsto \hat o$ is injective ⟦Chapter6/ProductOrientation · ChartPoint.prodOr_injective⟧ (Findings, Chapter 6, item 96). *Hidden hypotheses:* $x$ smooth and $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ nonempty (bump functions give it, §VI.1); only the orientation of $\mathrm{DET}(f, x)$ at the one point is used, not an orientation of $f$. That $(t, y) \mapsto \hat o$ is an orientation of $\hat f$ in the sense of Definition 6.40 — continuity over the orientable neighbourhoods of $\mathbb R \times X$, independence of the chart of the pull-back bundle — built from an orientation of $f$, is not formalized (gap G.66; Findings, Chapter 6, item 97).

### VI.27 §6.6 and Theorem 6.43: not formalized

§6.6 (p. 230) recalls, for a proper oriented $(f, o)$ over a tame $X$ with sc-smooth bump functions and an auxiliary norm $N$, the neighbourhood $U$ of $S$ of Theorem 5.18 and the sc⁺-perturbations $s$ supported in $U$ with $N(s) \le 1$ for which $f + s$ is in general position at its zeros; it calls them *admissible for the pair $(N, U)$*. Theorem 5.18 is formalized (§V.20) and the orientation of $S_{f+s}$ is the subject of §VI.25, but the notion itself, used only in Theorem 6.43, is not formalized (gap G.55; Findings, Chapter 6, item 101).

**Theorem 6.43** (p. 231): a well-defined linear map $\Psi_{(f,o)} : H^*_{dR}(X, \partial X) \to \mathbb R$, $\Psi_{(f,o)}([\omega, \tau]) = \int_{S_{f+s}}\omega - \int_{\partial S_{f+s}}\tau$ for every admissible $s$, with its proof (pp. 231–233) and the case $\partial X = \emptyset$ (p. 233). It is not formalized (gap G.54): it needs the sc-differential forms and their cohomology of §4.4 (gaps G.37–G.40), and integration over oriented compact manifolds with boundary with corners with Stokes' theorem, which Mathlib does not have (decision D1). What the theorem rests on is formalized: the perturbations of Theorem 5.18 (Part V) and the tangent orientations of Theorem 6.41 (§VI.25) (Findings, Chapter 6, item 100).

### VI.28 Appendix §6.7.1: the proof of Lemma 6.5

**The text's proof** (pp. 234–235) has three steps: a change of the basis of the complement of $\alpha(A)$ multiplies both wedges of (91) by its determinant; a change of the bases of $A$ and $D$ multiplies the source by $\det(\tau)/\det(\varepsilon)$; and a change of complements adds to the basis of the complement of $\alpha(A)$ vectors of $\alpha(A)$, and to the $\gamma$-preimages vectors of $\beta(B)$, which leaves the wedges unchanged.

**The formalized proof** (V6.63) does the three steps at once. For two choices $\chi$, $\chi'$ there is a scalar $\mu$ with $\text{source}(\chi') = \mu\,\text{source}(\chi)$ and $\text{value}(\chi') = \mu\,\text{value}(\chi)$ ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.Choice.exists_smul_source_value⟧. *Step 1.* Project the basis $b''$ of the new complement $Z'$ onto $Z$ along $\alpha(A)$; the projections form a basis of $Z$, related to $b'$ by some $\sigma$, and since $\beta \circ \alpha = 0$ they have the same $\beta$-images as $b''$. *Step 2.* In $B$, $\alpha(a') \wedge b'' = \alpha(a') \wedge p(b'')$, adding vectors of the span of the first block; with $a' = \tau a$ this is $\det\tau\,\det\sigma\;\alpha(a) \wedge b'$. *Step 3.* In $C$, the $\gamma$-preimages $c'$ of $d' = \varepsilon d$ in $V'$ differ from the $\gamma$-preimages in $V$ by vectors of $\ker\gamma = \beta(B)$, the span of the second block, so the wedge of the basis of $C$ ⟦Chapter6/ExactSequence · FourTermExact.Choice.wedgeC⟧ is $\det\varepsilon\,\det\sigma$ times that of $\chi$. *Step 4.* So the value scales by $\det\tau\,\det\sigma/(\det\varepsilon\,\det\sigma) = \det\tau/\det\varepsilon$, as the source does, and Lemma 6.5 follows from the fixed choice that defines $\Phi_E$. The step "independent of the choices of the basis if and only if $\det(\tau) = \det(\varepsilon)$" is read as this homogeneity of (91) in the bases of $A$ and $D$, $\tau$ being the $\sigma$ just introduced; the corrections $p_i$ lie in $\beta(B)$, written $\beta(C)$, and are combinations of the $\beta$-images, whose names are exchanged with those of the $\gamma$-preimages in the last step (possible misprints; Findings, Chapter 6, item 1).

### VI.29 Appendix §6.7.2: the proof of Proposition 6.12

(V6.64.) Let $P \le Q$ in $\Pi_T$. *Step 1, adapted bases.* Take a basis $a$ of $\ker T$ and classes $[d_i]$ forming a basis of $\operatorname{coker}T$ with $d_i \in \ker Q$, possible because $R(QT) = R(Q)$; complete $a$ by $b$ to a basis of $\ker(QT)$, and $(a, b)$ by $\tilde b$ to a basis of $\ker(PQT) = \ker(PT)$. *Step 2, the three values.* By (91) with these choices (Lemma 6.5, §VI.3), $\gamma^Q_T(h_0) = (a \wedge b) \otimes ([d]_Q \wedge [Tb]_Q)^*$; $\gamma^P_{QT}\gamma^Q_T(h_0) = (a \wedge b \wedge \tilde b) \otimes ([d]_P \wedge [Tb]_P \wedge [QT\tilde b]_P)^*$, the classes $[d]_P$, $[Tb]_P$ being preimages of $[d]_Q$, $[Tb]_Q$ because $Pd_i = PQd_i = 0$ and $PTb \in R(P) \subseteq R(Q)$; and $\gamma^P_T(h_0) = (a \wedge b \wedge \tilde b) \otimes ([d]_P \wedge [Tb]_P \wedge [T\tilde b]_P)^*$ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · gammaProj_wedge_tmul⟧. *Step 3, the spanning.* $[T\tilde b]_P - [QT\tilde b]_P = [(I - Q)T\tilde b]_P$, and $(I - Q)T\tilde b \in \ker Q$. If $Qg = 0$, then $g = \sum c_id_i + Tx$ with $x \in \ker(QT)$ — write $[g] = \sum c_i[d_i]$ in $\operatorname{coker}T$ and use $Qd_i = 0$ — so the classes of the $d_i$ and of the $Tb_j$ span what the text calls $\ker\tilde Q$ ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · mem_span_append_of_ker⟧. *Step 4.* The last block of the third value differs from that of the second by vectors of the span of the first two blocks, which does not change the wedge (§VI.2), and with the identification of $\det(P(QT))$ with $\det(PT)$ the two values agree ⟦Chapter6/ProjectionSequence · comp_comp_eq_of_projLE⟧. The spanning is proved directly in $F$; the name $\alpha_q$ in the last part is read as $\alpha^P$ (possible misprint; Findings, Chapter 6, items 6, 7) (pp. 235–237).

### VI.30 What is not formalized

- **Theorem 6.43** (gap G.54): the invariant $\Psi_{(f,o)}$, its proof and the case $\partial X = \emptyset$ need the forms and cohomology of §4.4 (gaps G.37–G.40), integration and Stokes' theorem (decision D1) (§VI.27). **The admissible sections of §6.6** (gap G.55), used only there.
- **The facts on paths of p. 201** (gap G.56): local path connectedness and sc⁺-smooth paths within a path component; only the local form inside a chart is formalized (§VI.18), and "in the same path component" is read as "joined by an sc-smooth path" (§VI.24).
- **§§6.2–6.4 remarks**: the alternative determinant $\lambda(\ker T) \otimes \lambda(\operatorname{coker}(T)^*)$ (gap G.57, §VI.4); the identification (95) and the maps after Proposition 6.15 (gap G.58, §VI.6); Lemma 6.19 in general, applied only to trivial bundles (gap G.59, §VI.7); the non-orientability of $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ and the classical case at the opening of §6.5 (gap G.60, §VI.8).
- **Proposition 6.28 (1)** (gap G.61): the sc-smooth contractibility of $U$, and with it the word "contractible" in Theorem 6.35, Definition 6.36 and (∗) of Theorem 6.37; (1′) is proved instead and is what the proofs use (§§VI.10, VI.18, VI.19, VI.23).
- **Lemma 6.30 as a statement about manifolds** (gap G.62): the solution set near $(t, \varphi(t), 0)$, the submersion $\pi$ and the smooth bundle $L$; the kernels are a continuous family of subspaces (§§VI.12, VI.15). **Property (P) for the slices** (gap G.63); the general position of $F$ that the text derives from it is proved (§VI.11).
- **Lin on every level** (gap G.64): the members of $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$ are Fredholm on level $0$, not shown sc-Fredholm on every level (§VI.1).
- **Paths on $[0, 1]$** (gap G.65): paths, homotopies and families sc-smooth on $[0, 1]$, $[0, 1]^2$, $[0, 1]^n$ only, and $X \times [0, 1]$ as an M-polyfold with boundary; they are read on $\mathbb R$, $\mathbb R^2$, $\mathbb R^n$ and $\mathbb R^n \times X$ (decision D2), and a path that does not extend sc-smoothly to $\mathbb R$ is not covered.
- **Remark 6.42 beyond a point** (gap G.66, §VI.26).
- **Theorem 6.41, the global parts** (§VI.25): the orientation of $S$ as an abstract manifold (gap G.67), the compatibility of the tangent orientations read in two charts (gap G.68), and the perturbation paragraph after the theorem (gap G.69).
- **The chart-free objects** $T_xX$, $Y_x$, $\mathrm{Lin}(f, x)$, $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ (gaps G.6, G.7, G.13 of Chapter 2): they are made in chart points and identified between charts (§VI.21).

### VI.31 What the formalization taught us

**The sign of (94).** The main change of substance is a sign. The coordinate of $\Phi_E$ in a local determinant chart carries the factor $(-1)^{\dim\operatorname{coker}S}$, which jumps where the parity of the cokernel dimension changes; the orientations it carries along a continuous family are then not continuous, as we read it, and an example on $\mathbb R$ shows it (§VI.14). The continuity statements of pp. 223–226 are not written in coordinates in the text, and it is in coordinates that the sign appears. The normalized $\alpha(T)\Phi_E$ at both ends of every propagation changes nothing on surjective operators — the tangent orientations of Theorem 6.41 are the text's — and the same sign is used in Remark 6.42 (§VI.26).

**Lemma 6.10 and the 2017 remark.** The common lower bound of two good left-projections exists, but not with the range $R(P) \cap R(P')$: a projection onto a smaller, finite-codimensional piece of it, along a complement containing both kernels, is below both (§VI.4). This keeps the preprint's construction of $\mathrm{DET}(E, F)$ — one lower bound, Corollary 6.13, Lemma 6.21 — intact.

**Contractibility was never needed.** Proposition 6.28 (1) is not established for the neighbourhood its proof builds, as we read it, but every later use of contractibility is a use of (1′): two paths in $U$ with the same end points are homotopic in a larger region where sections along families exist. Orientable neighbourhoods become pairs $V \subseteq U$, and property (∗) of Theorem 6.37 holds on every set with the local propagation property (§§VI.10, VI.19, VI.23).

**Paths on $\mathbb R$ cost reparametrizations.** With paths and homotopies on $\mathbb R$ whose conditions hold on $[0, 1]$ (decision D2), the homotopy of (1′) has the right edges only on $[0, 1]$ while push-forward data need zeros near $[0, 1]$; transitivity of homotopy, associativity of concatenation and Theorem 6.35 all pass through the smooth transition function $\kappa$ (§§VI.18, VI.20).

**Charts must be compared.** The text's chart-free $\mathrm{Or}^f_x$ becomes a set read in a chosen chart, and the invariance of the local propagation under a change of chart — the naturality of the stabilization isomorphism, of the sign and of continuation — is a file of its own (§VI.21).

**"By a covering argument" and "one verifies".** The covering argument of Theorem 6.37 is a dyadic transport with a square lemma, proved for any family of types (§VI.22); the "simple computation" of Lemma 6.33 is an exact identity of stabilization isomorphisms, with no sign, once the appended sections come last (§VI.16); and the equivalence of Definitions 6.38 and 6.39, stated without proof, needs the transport computed on dyadic pieces inside orientable neighbourhoods (§VI.24).

## Part VII. Ep-groupoids (HWZ Chapter 7, §§7.1–7.5)

Chapter 7 opens Part II of the book. Part II has no 2014 preprint, so its numbers and pages are those of the 2017 text (pp. 225–256). The chapter introduces ep-groupoids, the sc-smooth version of étale proper Lie groupoids. §7.1 defines groupoids, isotropy groups and ep-groupoids (Definitions 7.1–7.3), the local sc-diffeomorphism $\hat\varphi$ of a morphism and its tangent (Definition 7.4), the levels and the degeneracy index of the orbit space (Definition 7.5), tame ep-groupoids and the category $\mathcal{EP}$ (Definitions 7.6, 7.7). It proves that $\pi$ is open, that $|X|$ has countable bases of neighbourhoods, the local closure relation and the finiteness of the isotropy groups (Propositions 7.1–7.4, Lemma 7.1). It states the natural representation of $G_x$ (Theorem 7.1), discusses the translation groupoid $G_x \ltimes U(x)$ and the action $\hat\Phi$ (pp. 231–233), extends the natural representation to finite sets of isomorphic objects (Proposition 7.5, Definition 7.8), identifies $|U(x)|$ with $G_x\backslash U(x)$ (Proposition 7.6) and defines local uniformizers and ep-subgroupoids (Definitions 7.9, 7.10, Proposition 7.7). §7.2 treats effective ep-groupoids, the subgroups $T_x$, the reduced morphism space $\mathbf X^R$ and the reduced ep-groupoid $X_R$ (Definitions 7.11–7.13, Lemmas 7.2, 7.3, Propositions 7.8–7.10). §7.3 proves that $|X|$ is locally metrizable, regular and Hausdorff (Theorem 7.2, Lemmas 7.4–7.7, Corollaries 7.1, 7.2, Definition 7.14) and lifts ep-groupoids to level $1$ (Proposition 7.11). §7.4 defines paracompact orbit spaces and sc-smooth partitions of unity (Definitions 7.15, 7.16, Remarks 7.1, 7.2), proves Proposition 7.12 and Theorems 7.3, 7.4, and characterizes the closed subsets of $|X|$ (Definition 7.17, Propositions 7.13, 7.14). The appendix §7.5 proves Theorem 7.1 as Theorem 7.5 (Lemmas 7.8, 7.9) and Theorem 7.4 as Theorem 7.6 (Lemma 7.10), and ends with Corollary 7.3. This Part retells §7.1 in §§VII.1–VII.12 — Definitions 7.1, 7.2 (§VII.1), Definition 7.3 and properness (§VII.2), Definitions 7.4–7.6 (§VII.3), Definition 7.7 and the remark after it (§VII.4), Propositions 7.1–7.3 (§VII.5), Lemma 7.1 and Proposition 7.4 (§VII.6), Theorem 7.1 (§VII.7), pp. 231–233 (§VII.8), the uniqueness of natural representations (§VII.9), Proposition 7.5 and Definition 7.8 (§VII.10), Proposition 7.6 and Definition 7.9 (§VII.11), Definition 7.10 and Proposition 7.7 (§VII.12); §7.2 in §§VII.13–VII.17 — Definition 7.11 and Lemmas 7.2, 7.3 (§VII.13), Proposition 7.8 (§VII.14), $T_x$ and Definition 7.12 (§VII.15), Proposition 7.9 (§VII.16), $X_R$, Proposition 7.10 and Definition 7.13 (§VII.17); §7.3 in §§VII.18–VII.22 — Theorem 7.2 and Lemmas 7.4, 7.5 (§VII.18), Lemmas 7.6, 7.7 and Corollary 7.1 (§VII.19), Michael's theorem of Part I (§VII.20), Definition 7.14 and Corollary 7.2 (§VII.21), Proposition 7.11 (§VII.22); §7.4 in §§VII.23–VII.25 — Definition 7.15, Remark 7.1 and Proposition 7.12 (§VII.23), Theorem 7.3, Definition 7.16, Remark 7.2 and the statement of Theorem 7.4 (§VII.24), Definition 7.17 and Propositions 7.13, 7.14 (§VII.25); the appendix in §§VII.26–VII.29 — the proof of Theorem 7.1 (§VII.26), Lemma 7.10 (§VII.27), the proof of Theorem 7.4 (§VII.28) and Corollary 7.3 (§VII.29); the witnesses and counterexamples (§VII.30); what is not formalized (§VII.31); and what the formalization taught us (§VII.32). Each item carries the number of its comparison item (V7.1–V7.68) in `Exposition/verification/ch07.md`.

**What is proved, and what is not.** Theorems 7.1–7.6 are proved, and so are Propositions 7.1–7.8 and 7.11–7.14, Propositions 7.9 and 7.10 under the hypothesis that $\mathbf X^R$ is Hausdorff and paracompact, Lemmas 7.1–7.10 and Corollaries 7.1–7.3, Corollary 7.3 with the theorem of Godefroy–Troyanski–Whitfield–Zizler as an explicit hypothesis, as in Part I. Every definition of the chapter is formalized; the tangent $T\varphi$ of Definition 7.4 is a definition only. Five places needed more than a reading. The remark after Definition 7.7, that a functor sc-smooth on objects is sc-smooth on morphisms, does not hold as we read it, and a counterexample on the trivial $\mathbb Z/3$-action on $\mathbb R$ shows it; it holds for functors continuous on morphisms, which is what its argument uses (§VII.4). The proof of Proposition 7.9 gives the charts of $\mathbf X^R$ and their sc-smooth transitions but, as we read it, neither Hausdorffness nor paracompactness, which become hypotheses, discharged for effective ep-groupoids (§VII.16). The natural representation of Theorem 7.1 is taken on a connected neighbourhood, which the text chooses on p. 231 but does not put in the statement; connectedness makes $\Phi$ a homomorphism and $\Gamma$ a functor, and the local path connectedness of M-polyfolds that supplies it is proved (§VII.7). The tameness of $X^1$ in Proposition 7.11 needs that the index lift of a tame retraction is tame, which Part I left open; it is proved (§VII.22). And several omitted steps are supplied: the uniqueness of natural representations behind "adapting restrictions" (§VII.9), the conjugation $\varphi T_x\varphi^{-1} = T_y$ that the composition of $X_R$ needs (§VII.15), the passage from compact to component compact sets in Corollary 7.2 (§VII.21), the support bound that makes the sum in the proof of Theorem 7.4 locally finite (§§VII.27–VII.28) and Michael's theorem on unions of closed paracompact sets (§VII.20). Proposition 7.5 is proved by a construction without induction (§VII.10), Proposition 7.12 by Smirnov's theorem pulled back to $|X^1|$ (§VII.23), Proposition 7.14 (2) without Lemma 2.7 (§VII.25), Lemma 7.6 from the closedness of points and regularity (§VII.19), and the normalization of Theorem 7.4 by bump coverings (§VII.28). Not formalized: the properties of $T\varphi$ (gap G.70), the set $|X_\infty|$ of the filtration of $|X|$ (gap G.72), the tangent facts (3), (4) recalled before Proposition 7.7, the Hausdorff and paracompact properties of $\mathbf X^R$ for a general ep-groupoid (gap G.71), and the open question of p. 249 (§VII.31).

**Seven structural choices.** (1) *A groupoid is a structure of maps.* Objects and morphisms are types; $s, t, u, \iota$ are maps and the composition $m$ is a total map whose value on a non-composable pair is a junk value never used; the groupoid laws are required on composable pairs. A bridge to Mathlib's groupoids makes "full" and "faithful" Mathlib's. (2) *Properness is Mathlib's.* Definition 7.3 (3) is the properness, in Mathlib's sense, of $t$ restricted to $s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X V)$, for some open $V \ni x$, per point; on metrizable spaces it is equivalent to the sequential form the text uses (§VII.2). (3) *Condition (4) in two forms.* It is stated literally, on the fibred product of Part I's Proposition 2.15 (§II.17, there Proposition 2.46), and used in the equivalent *sheet form*: for every local inverse $\sigma$ of $s$, the map $\psi \mapsto m(\sigma(t\psi), \psi)$ is sc-smooth. (4) *Natural representations are data.* "An open neighbourhood $U(x)$ equipped with the natural $G_x$-action" is always a datum $(U, \Phi, \Gamma)$ with $U$ open, connected and containing $x$, never a hypothesis "for every such $U(x)$". (5) *$G \times U$ is a product with a discrete M-polyfold*, the finite disjoint union of copies of $U$, on which sc-smoothness is sc-smoothness on each slice (§VII.8). (6) *The reduced morphisms* $\mathbf X^R$ are a quotient whose M-polyfold structure is built under the hypotheses that it is Hausdorff and paracompact (§VII.16). (7) *Michael's theorem without Hausdorff.* Part I's Lemma 2.7 and Proposition 2.17 (gap G.15 there) are proved for regular spaces, and Mathlib's paracompactness, like Definition 7.15, does not include Hausdorff (§VII.20).

**Map.**

- `Chapter7/Groupoid`: Definitions 7.1, 7.2; the orbit space, saturations, the conjugation of isotropy groups, regular objects, full subcategories, translation groupoids, functors and the bridge to Mathlib.
- `Chapter7/EpGroupoid`: Definition 7.3 with the fibred-product and sheet forms of (4), Definition 7.4, the levels, Definitions 7.5–7.17 as structures and predicates, the trivial ep-groupoid and its witnesses.
- `Chapter7/ProperMaps`: proper maps between metrizable spaces, the sequential criterion, proper restrictions $t : s^{-1}(Q) \to X$.
- `Chapter7/LocalDiffeo`: local sc-diffeomorphisms, their levels, degeneracy index and tameness; Part I's partitions of unity on $\mathbb R^n$.
- `Chapter7/Basic`: the remark after Definition 7.7, Propositions 7.1–7.4, Lemma 7.1, the conjugation $G_x \cong G_y$.
- `Chapter7/Discrete`: finiteness from proper locally injective maps, discrete M-polyfolds, $G \times X$ and its sheets.
- `Chapter7/LocConnected`: local path connectedness of retracts and M-polyfolds, uniqueness of sections on connected sets.
- `Chapter7/NaturalRep`: Theorem 7.1 = Theorem 7.5 with Lemmas 7.8, 7.9.
- `Chapter7/NaturalAction`: the consequences of Theorem 7.1 on pp. 231–233 and the uniqueness of natural representations.
- `Chapter7/NaturalRepFinite`: Proposition 7.5 by the star construction, Definition 7.8.
- `Chapter7/Uniformizer`: Proposition 7.6, Definition 7.9 and the claims after it.
- `Chapter7/SubGroupoid`: Definition 7.10, the M-polyfold $\mathbf A$, Proposition 7.7.
- `Chapter7/Effective`: Definition 7.11's consequences, Lemmas 7.2, 7.3, Proposition 7.8, $T_x$.
- `Chapter7/Reduced`: Definition 7.12 made precise, Propositions 7.9, 7.10, Definition 7.13.
- `Chapter7/OrbitTopology`: Theorem 7.2, Lemmas 7.4–7.7, Corollaries 7.1, 7.2.
- `Chapter7/Michael`: Part I's Lemma 2.7 and Proposition 2.17, unions of closed paracompact sets.
- `Chapter7/Lift`: Proposition 7.11, the map $|X^1| \to |X|$, Definition 7.15's consequences, Remark 7.1, Proposition 7.12.
- `Chapter7/ProperSubsets`: Propositions 7.13, 7.14.
- `Chapter7/PartitionsOfUnity`: Theorem 7.3, Lemma 7.10, Theorem 7.4 = Theorem 7.6, Corollary 7.3.
- `Chapter7/NonVacuity`: the translation groupoid of a finite group action, $\mathbb Z/2 \ltimes \mathbb R$ by reflection, the trivial $\mathbb Z/3$-action, the counterexamples.

Throughout, $X = (X, \mathbf X)$ is an ep-groupoid: $X$ is the object M-polyfold and $\mathbf X$ the morphism M-polyfold, both Hausdorff and paracompact, as every M-polyfold of the project (Definition 2.8, §II.5); $s, t : \mathbf X \to X$ are source and target, $m(\varphi, \psi) = \varphi \circ \psi$ the composition, $u(x) = 1_x$ the unit and $\iota(\varphi) = \varphi^{-1}$ the inverse. $|X|$ is the orbit space with the quotient topology and $\pi : X \to |X|$ the projection; $G_x$ is the isotropy group of $x$, $\mathrm{cl}_X$ the closure in $X$, and $\mathbf U(x)$ the set of morphisms with source and target in $U(x)$. For a natural representation $(U, \Phi, \Gamma)$ at $x$, $g \ast y = \Phi(g)(y)$. A *sheet* is an open set $\mathbf W \subseteq \mathbf X$ on which $s$ is an sc-diffeomorphism onto an open set, its inverse a *local inverse* of $s$. Part I results are cited by their 2017 numbers; the Lean names and the earlier Parts carry the preprint numbers (Theorem 2.2 of 2017 is Theorem 2.16 in §II.7, Lemma 2.7 and Proposition 2.17 are `lemma_2_56` and `proposition_2_57`, Theorem 5.12 is Theorem 5.37 in §V.25). Findings are those of `Exposition/Findings.md`, "Chapter 7".

### VII.1 Definitions 7.1 and 7.2: groupoids, the orbit space, isotropy

**Definition 7.1** (V7.1). A groupoid is a structure of maps $s, t, m, u, \iota$ on a type of objects and a type of morphisms ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr⟧, with associativity, units and inverses required on composable pairs; the morphisms $x \to y$ are a set ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.mor⟧, and so are the morphisms between points of a set $A$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.morOn⟧. The composition of a non-composable pair is a junk value; no statement uses it. The text's list of consequences — $(\varphi^{-1})^{-1} = \varphi$, $1_x^{-1} = 1_x$, $(\varphi \circ \psi)^{-1} = \psi^{-1} \circ \varphi^{-1}$, uniqueness of inverses — is derived from the laws ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.inv_inv⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.inv_unit⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.inv_comp_rev⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.eq_inv_of_comp_eq_unit⟧. Objects are isomorphic if there is a morphism between them ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.Isomorphic⟧, an equivalence relation ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.orbitSetoid⟧ whose quotient is $|X|$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.OrbitSpace⟧ with projection $\pi$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.π⟧; $\pi(x) = \pi(y)$ iff $x \cong y$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.π_eq_π_iff⟧, $\pi(s\varphi) = \pi(t\varphi)$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.π_src_eq_π_tgt⟧ and $\pi$ is onto ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.surjective_π⟧. The saturation $\pi^{-1}(\pi(A))$, used from Definition 7.10 on, is defined here ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.saturation⟧, with saturated sets ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.IsSaturated⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.isSaturated_iff⟧. The bridge to Mathlib's groupoids is a type synonym of the objects ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.Ob⟧ with the groupoid instance ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.instGroupoid⟧, whose isomorphism classes are those of the orbit relation ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.orbitSetoid_eq⟧ (Findings, Chapter 7, item 1) (pp. 225–226).

**Definition 7.2** (V7.2). $G_x$, the morphisms $x \to x$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.Isotropy⟧, is a group under composition with $gh = g \circ h$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.Isotropy.val_mul⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.Isotropy.val_one⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.Isotropy.val_inv⟧, the text's order. Mathlib's vertex group multiplies in the other order; it is identified with the opposite group ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.isotropyEquivVertexGroup⟧, and $G_x$ with the automorphisms of $x$ in the bridge ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.isotropyEquivAut⟧ (Findings, Chapter 7, item 2) (p. 226).

### VII.2 Definition 7.3, and properness

**Definition 7.3** (V7.3) ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid⟧. An ep-groupoid is a groupoid with M-polyfold structures on the objects and on the morphisms such that (1) $s$ and $t$ are local sc-diffeomorphisms, (2) $u$ and $\iota$ are sc-smooth, (3) every $x$ has an open neighbourhood $V(x)$ with $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X V(x)) \to X$ proper, and (4) $m$ is sc-smooth on $\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X$. "In particular all structure maps are sc-smooth": $s$ and $t$ are ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.isScSmoothMap_src⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.isScSmoothMap_tgt⟧, and continuous ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.continuous_src⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.continuous_tgt⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.continuous_unit⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.continuous_inv⟧ (pp. 226–227).

*Condition (3).* It is existential, one open $V(x)$ per point, as the text writes it. The universal reading, "for every open $V \ni x$", fails: in the pair groupoid of $\mathbb Z$ (objects $\mathbb Z$, one morphism between any two objects) $t$ is proper over $s^{-1}(\{x\})$ but not over $s^{-1}(\mathbb Z)$ ⟦Chapter7/NonVacuity · Examples.pair_isProperMap⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NonVacuity · Examples.pair_not_isProperMap_univ⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NonVacuity · Examples.pair_not_forall_isProperMap⟧; every smaller open neighbourhood of $x$ works as soon as one does (§VII.25) (Findings, Chapter 7, items 3, 103).

*Condition (4).* The text cites "Lemma 2.8 in [38]" for the M-polyfold structure of the fibred product; this is an external reference, and the statement used is Part I's Proposition 2.15 (§II.17): since $s$ is a local sc-diffeomorphism, $\mathbf X\,{}_s{\times}_t\,\mathbf X$ is a sub-M-polyfold of $\mathbf X \times \mathbf X$ ⟦Chapter2/FibredProduct · MPolyfold.isSubMPolyfold_fibredProduct⟧, and (4) is stated on it ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · IsScSmoothComp⟧. The proofs use an equivalent *sheet form* ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · IsScSmoothCompSheet⟧: for every sc-diffeomorphism $s : \mathbf W \to V$ with inverse $\sigma$, the map $\psi \mapsto m(\sigma(t\psi), \psi)$ is sc-smooth on $t^{-1}(V)$. *Step 1.* The graph of $\sigma \circ t$ over $t^{-1}(V)$ is an open piece of the fibred product, and the second projection is an sc-diffeomorphism from it onto $t^{-1}(V)$, with inverse $\psi \mapsto (\sigma(t\psi), \psi)$. *Step 2.* So the literal (4) gives the sheet form by composition, and conversely the fibred product is covered by such graphs ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · isScSmoothComp_iff_sheet⟧. Every ep-groupoid satisfies the sheet form ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.isScSmoothCompSheet⟧. The "for every $\sigma$" of the sheet form carries no vacuity risk, being equivalent to the literal condition (Findings, Chapter 7, item 4).

**Properness in sequential form** (V7.4). The text uses properness through sequences: in Proposition 7.3, Lemma 7.1, Proposition 7.7, Proposition 7.11, Proposition 7.13 and Lemma 7.8. For a continuous map between metrizable spaces, properness is equivalent to: every sequence whose images converge has a convergent subsequence ⟦Chapter7/ProperMaps · isProperMap_iff_exists_tendsto_subseq⟧. *Step 1, from properness.* The images and their limit form a compact set, whose preimage is compact, hence sequentially compact ⟦Chapter7/ProperMaps · exists_tendsto_subseq_of_isProperMap⟧. *Step 2, to properness.* Preimages of compact sets are sequentially compact, hence compact in a metrizable space, and a continuous map with compact fibres of compacta into a compactly generated space is proper (Mathlib's characterization) ⟦Chapter7/ProperMaps · isProperMap_of_exists_tendsto_subseq⟧. For the restriction of $t$ to $s^{-1}(Q)$ the criterion reads: every sequence with $s(\varphi_k) \in Q$ and $t(\varphi_k)$ convergent has a subsequence converging to a morphism over $Q$ ⟦Chapter7/ProperMaps · isProperMap_domRestrict_iff⟧, over $\mathrm{cl}\,Q$ when $Q$ is closed ⟦Chapter7/ProperMaps · isProperMap_domRestrict_iff_of_isClosed⟧ ⟦Chapter7/ProperMaps · MPolyfold.isProperMap_domRestrict_iff⟧, and it is the compactness of $s^{-1}(Q) \cap t^{-1}(K)$ for compact $K$ ⟦Chapter7/ProperMaps · MPolyfold.isProperMap_domRestrict_iff_isCompact_preimage⟧. Three consequences recur. Properness passes to smaller closures, so any open $V' \subseteq V(x)$ around $x$ will do ⟦Chapter7/ProperMaps · isProperMap_domRestrict_closure_mono⟧; the image $t(s^{-1}(Q))$ is closed for closed $Q$, a proper map being closed ⟦Chapter7/ProperMaps · isClosed_image_preimage_of_isProperMap_domRestrict⟧; and the fibres over points are finite when $t$ is locally injective ⟦Chapter7/ProperMaps · finite_setOf_of_isProperMap_domRestrict⟧. If $t$ is proper over $s^{-1}(Q)$ and the units exist, $Q$ is closed: a limit $x$ of $x_n \in Q$ is the source of a limit of a subsequence of the units $1_{x_n}$ ⟦Chapter7/ProperMaps · isClosed_of_isProperMap_domRestrict⟧. The hidden hypothesis is metrizability, which M-polyfolds have (Theorem 2.2, §II.7) (Findings, Chapter 7, item 3).

### VII.3 Definition 7.4, the levels, Definitions 7.5 and 7.6

**Definition 7.4** (V7.5). For a morphism $\varphi : x \to y$ the text takes open $\mathbf U(\varphi)$, $U(x)$, $U(y)$ with $s : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to U(x)$ and $t : \mathbf U(\varphi) \to U(y)$ sc-diffeomorphisms and sets $\hat\varphi = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\varphi))^{-1} : U(x) \to U(y)$. Such a sheet exists at every morphism ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.Sheet⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.exists_sheet⟧: (1) gives open neighbourhoods of $\varphi$ on which $s$, resp. $t$, is an sc-diffeomorphism onto an open set, and on their intersection both are, an sc-diffeomorphism restricting to one on every open subset. A sheet is chosen at every morphism ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.sheetAt⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.mem_sheetAt⟧, and $\hat\varphi$ is defined from it ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.Sheet.hat⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.hat⟧: an sc-diffeomorphism ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.Sheet.isScDiffeoOn_hat⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.isScDiffeoOn_hat⟧, a composite of sc-diffeomorphisms, with $\hat\varphi(x) = y$ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.hat_src⟧. It depends on the sheet only as a germ. $T\varphi = T\hat\varphi(x)$ is read through the chain rule as $Tt \circ (Ts|_{T_\varphi\mathbf X})^{-1}$ with Part I's tangent maps ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.tangentMor⟧; that it is a linear isomorphism on level $0$ for $\varphi$ on level $1$, and an sc-isomorphism for smooth $\varphi$, is not proved: $T_xX$ carries no linear structure in Part I (gaps G.7, G.70). The display "$\hat\varphi = t \circ (s|\mathbf U(\varphi))^{-1} \circ U(x) \to U(y)$" is read with $:$ for the last $\circ$, and "$T\varphi : T_{s(\varphi)}X \to T_{t(\varphi)}$" with the missing $X$ (possible misprints; Findings, Chapter 7, items 5, 110) (p. 227).

**The levels and the degeneracy index** (V7.6). A local sc-diffeomorphism preserves the levels and the degeneracy index: in a sheet it is an sc-diffeomorphism, and Part I's Proposition 2.7 (§II.11) applies ⟦Chapter7/LocalDiffeo · MPolyfold.IsLocalScDiffeo.mem_levelSet_iff⟧ ⟦Chapter7/LocalDiffeo · MPolyfold.IsLocalScDiffeo.degIndex_eq⟧. Hence $\varphi \in \mathbf X_m$ iff $s(\varphi) \in X_m$ iff $t(\varphi) \in X_m$ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.mem_levelSet_src_iff⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.mem_levelSet_tgt_iff⟧, and $d_X(s\varphi) = d_{\mathbf X}(\varphi) = d_X(t\varphi)$ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.degIndex_src⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.degIndex_tgt⟧. The text's $ml(x)$, the largest $m$ with $x \in X_m$, is the maximal level ⟦Chapter7/LocalDiffeo · MPolyfold.maxLevel⟧, preserved too ⟦Chapter7/LocalDiffeo · MPolyfold.IsLocalScDiffeo.maxLevel_eq⟧. $|X_k| = \pi(X_k)$ is defined ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.orbitLevel⟧; the set $|X_\infty|$ and the identity $|X_\infty| = \bigcap_k|X_k|$ are not stated (gap G.72; Findings, Chapter 7, items 6, 112) (pp. 227–228).

**Definition 7.5** (V7.7). $d_{|X|}(|x|) = d_X(x)$ is well defined by the previous paragraph ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.degIndexOrbit⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.degIndexOrbit_π⟧ (p. 228).

**Definition 7.6** (V7.8). $X$ is tame if the object M-polyfold is tame ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.IsTame⟧, "tame" being the existence of an equivalent tame atlas (Definition 2.19, §II.14) ⟦Chapter2/Tame · MPolyfold.IsTame⟧ — not "every chart is tame", which would be unsatisfiable. *Then $\mathbf X$ is tame.* At a morphism, a sheet $s : \mathbf W \to V$ composed with a tame chart of $X$ around $s(\varphi)$ is a tame chart of $\mathbf X$, since tameness is carried by sc-diffeomorphisms (§III.27) ⟦Chapter7/LocalDiffeo · MPolyfold.IsScDiffeoOn.exists_tame_chart⟧; these charts are compatible with the atlas of $\mathbf X$ and form a tame atlas ⟦Chapter7/LocalDiffeo · MPolyfold.IsLocalScDiffeo.isTame⟧; conversely a surjective local sc-diffeomorphism transfers tameness down ⟦Chapter7/LocalDiffeo · MPolyfold.IsLocalScDiffeo.isTame_iff_of_surjective⟧. The witnesses are the trivial ep-groupoid of $\mathbb R^n$ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.isTame_trivial_rn⟧ and the reflection groupoid of §VII.30 (Findings, Chapter 7, items 7, 106) (p. 228).

### VII.4 Definition 7.7, and the remark after it

**Definition 7.7** (V7.9). A functor between groupoids is a pair of maps commuting with $s$, $t$, $m$ on composable pairs and $u$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidFunctor⟧; it commutes with $\iota$, by the uniqueness of inverses ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidFunctor.mor_inv⟧, has identities and composites ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidFunctor.id⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidFunctor.comp⟧, a Mathlib functor ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidFunctor.toFunctor⟧ and a map of orbit spaces ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidFunctor.orbitMap⟧. An ep-functor is sc-smooth on objects and on morphisms ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpFunctor⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpFunctor.id⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpFunctor.comp⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpFunctor.ext⟧, and $\mathcal{EP}$ is the category of bundled ep-groupoids and ep-functors ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EP⟧ (Findings, Chapter 7, item 8) (p. 228).

**The remark after Definition 7.7** (V7.10). The text says that it suffices to ask sc-smoothness between the object spaces, because near $\varphi$ one has $f(\gamma) = (s|\mathbf U(\psi))^{-1}(f(s(\gamma)))$ for $\gamma$ in a neighbourhood $\mathbf U(\varphi)$ with $f(\mathbf U(\varphi)) \subseteq \mathbf U(\psi)$, $\psi = f(\varphi)$. Choosing that neighbourhood uses the continuity of $f$ on morphisms, and without it the claim does not hold as we read it. *The counterexample.* On the trivial action of $\mathbb Z/3$ on $\mathbb R$ (objects $\mathbb R$, morphisms $\mathbb Z/3 \times \mathbb R$, $s = t$ the projection), let $f$ be the identity on objects and $(g, y) \mapsto (g, y)$ for $y \le 0$, $(g, y) \mapsto (g^2, y)$ for $y > 0$ ⟦Chapter7/NonVacuity · Examples.remarkFunctor⟧. Since $g \mapsto g^2$ is an automorphism of $\mathbb Z/3$, this is a functor; it is sc-smooth on objects ⟦Chapter7/NonVacuity · Examples.isScSmoothMap_remarkFunctor_obj⟧ but not continuous on morphisms, jumping at $(g, 0)$ for $g \ne 1$ ⟦Chapter7/NonVacuity · Examples.not_continuous_remarkFunctor_mor⟧, hence not sc-smooth there ⟦Chapter7/NonVacuity · Examples.not_isScSmoothMap_remarkFunctor_mor⟧, and no ep-functor has these components ⟦Chapter7/NonVacuity · Examples.not_exists_epFunctor_remarkFunctor⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NonVacuity · Examples.remark_definition_7_7_counterexample⟧. *The remark for functors continuous on morphisms.* Take a sheet $\mathbf U(\psi)$ of $s$ at $\psi = f(\varphi)$, with inverse $\sigma$, and $\mathbf U(\varphi) = f^{-1}(\mathbf U(\psi))$, open by continuity. For $\gamma \in \mathbf U(\varphi)$, $f(\gamma)$ lies in $\mathbf U(\psi)$ and has source $f(s\gamma)$, so $f(\gamma) = \sigma(f(s\gamma))$ ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.mor_eq_srcInv_obj_src⟧, a composite of sc-smooth maps ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.isScSmoothMap_mor_of_continuous⟧. The sheet at $\varphi$ and the neighbourhoods $U(s\varphi)$, $U(s\psi)$ of the text are not used. Since every ep-functor is continuous on morphisms ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpFunctor.continuous_mor⟧, the remark becomes an equivalence for functors sc-smooth on objects ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.isScSmoothMap_mor_iff_continuous⟧, and a functor sc-smooth on objects and continuous on morphisms is an ep-functor ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpFunctor.ofContinuous⟧ (Findings, Chapter 7, items 9, 104) (pp. 228–229).

### VII.5 Propositions 7.1–7.3: the topology of $|X|$

**Proposition 7.1** (V7.11) ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.proposition_7_1⟧. *$\pi$ is open.* $|X|$ carries the quotient topology, so $\pi$ is continuous ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.continuous_π⟧, and $\pi(U)$ is open iff its saturation $\pi^{-1}(\pi(U))$ is. *Step 1.* The saturation of $U$ is $t(s^{-1}(U))$: $y \cong x \in U$ iff some $\varphi$ has $s\varphi \in U$ and $t\varphi = y$ ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.preimage_π_image_eq⟧. *Step 2.* $s^{-1}(U)$ is open since $s$ is continuous, and $t$ is an open map, being a local sc-diffeomorphism ⟦Chapter7/LocalDiffeo · MPolyfold.IsLocalScDiffeo.isOpenMap⟧. The text argues with the sheets $V(\varphi)$, which is the openness of $t$ unpacked. So $\pi$ is an open quotient map ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.proposition_7_1_isOpenQuotientMap⟧ and carries neighbourhood filters to neighbourhood filters ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.proposition_7_1_map_nhds⟧ (Findings, Chapter 7, item 10) (p. 229).

**Proposition 7.2** (V7.12) ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.proposition_7_2⟧. *Every $z \in |X|$ has a countable basis of open neighbourhoods, chosen monotone.* $X$ is metrizable (Theorem 2.2); for $z = \pi(x)$ the images of the balls $B(x, 1/(k + 1))$ are open by Proposition 7.1 and decreasing, and they form a basis because $\pi$ maps the neighbourhood filter of $x$ onto that of $z$ ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.proposition_7_2_of_hasAntitoneBasis⟧. The statement is Mathlib's antitone basis indexed by $\mathbb N$ (radii $1/(k + 1)$, the index starting at $0$), and $|X|$ is first countable ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.proposition_7_2_firstCountableTopology⟧ (Findings, Chapter 7, item 10) (p. 229).

**Proposition 7.3** (V7.13) ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.proposition_7_3⟧. *Every $x$ has an open $U$ with $\pi(\mathrm{cl}_XA) = \mathrm{cl}_{|X|}\pi(A)$ for every $A \subseteq U$.* The text proves "$\supseteq$" with a sequence $\varphi_k : a_k \to b_k$, $b_k \to b$, $a_k \in A$, of which properness extracts a convergent subsequence. The formalization proves more, for every $U$ with $t$ proper over $s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_XU)$ and every $A \subseteq \mathrm{cl}_XU$, and without sequences ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.proposition_7_3_of_isProperMap⟧. *Step 1.* Since $\pi$ is open and continuous, $\pi^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}\,\pi(A)) = \mathrm{cl}\,\pi^{-1}(\pi(A)) = \mathrm{cl}\,t(s^{-1}(A))$. *Step 2.* $t(s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}A))$ is closed, as the image of the closed $s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}A) \subseteq s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}U)$ under a proper, hence closed, map (§VII.2), and contains $t(s^{-1}(A))$; so $\mathrm{cl}\,\pi(A) \subseteq \pi(t(s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}A))) = \pi(\mathrm{cl}A)$. *Step 3.* "$\subseteq$" is the continuity of $\pi$. "For every $z$ and every representative $x$" is "for every $x$" (Findings, Chapter 7, item 11) (pp. 229–230).

### VII.6 Lemma 7.1, Proposition 7.4, and the conjugation $G_x \cong G_y$

**Lemma 7.1** (V7.14) ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.lemma_7_1⟧. *If $t : s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_XU(x_0)) \to X$ is proper, only finitely many $\psi$ have $s(\psi) = x$ and $t(\psi) \in U(x_0)$.* **The text's proof** argues by contradiction with distinct $\psi_n : s(\psi_n) \to x$, $s(\psi_n) \in U(x_0)$; properness gives a convergent subsequence, $t$ is a local sc-diffeomorphism near the limit, and $t(\psi_n) = t(\psi_m) = x$ forces $\psi_n = \psi_m$. The proof thus treats the inverses of the morphisms of the statement, with $s$ and $t$ exchanged, and writes "$t : V(\psi) \to V(y)$" for $V(x)$ and "$s(\psi) \in s^{-1}(\mathrm{cl}_X(U(x_0)))$"; parentheses are unbalanced in the statement and the proof (possible misprints; Findings, Chapter 7, items 12, 96). **The formalized proof** does the proof's form first and has no sequences. *Step 1.* The fibre of the proper restriction of $t$ over $x$ is compact. *Step 2.* It is discrete, $t$ being locally injective as a local sc-diffeomorphism ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · MPolyfold.IsLocalScDiffeo.isLocallyInjective⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · IsLocallyInjective.isDiscrete_preimage_singleton⟧. *Step 3.* A compact discrete set is finite ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · IsProperMap.finite_preimage_singleton_of_isLocallyInjective⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · finite_setOf_mem_of_isProperMap_domRestrict⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · MPolyfold.finite_setOf_mem_of_isLocalScDiffeo⟧. This gives the finiteness of $\{\psi \mid s\psi \in \mathrm{cl}_XU(x_0),\ t\psi = x\}$ ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.lemma_7_1_swap_of_isProperMap⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.lemma_7_1_swap⟧. *Step 4.* The statement's form follows by $\iota$, which exchanges $s$ and $t$ and is injective, and holds even for targets in $\mathrm{cl}_XU(x_0)$ ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.lemma_7_1_of_isProperMap⟧. The openness of $U(x_0)$ and $x_0 \in U(x_0)$ are kept as hypotheses but not used (p. 230).

**Proposition 7.4** (V7.15) ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.proposition_7_4⟧. *$G_x$ is finite.* Lemma 7.1 with $x_0 = x$ and $U(x_0) = V(x)$ of Definition 7.3 (3): $G_x$ is contained in the finite set of morphisms with source $x$ and target in $V(x)$ ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · MPolyfold.finite_isotropy_of_isLocalScDiffeo⟧. The proposition is an instance, so the cardinality of $G_x$ is its order as a finite group (Findings, Chapter 7, item 13) (p. 230).

**The conjugation** (V7.16). For $\varphi : x \to y$, $g \mapsto \varphi \circ g \circ \varphi^{-1}$ is an isomorphism $G_x \to G_y$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.isotropyConj⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.isotropyConj_val⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.conjIsotropy⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.conjIsotropy_val⟧, so isomorphic objects have isomorphic isotropy groups of the same order ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.nonempty_isotropy_mulEquiv⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.nat_card_isotropy_eq⟧. "There is no canonical identification" is given its content: two choices $\varphi, \varphi'$ give isomorphisms that differ by conjugation with $\varphi'\varphi^{-1} \in G_y$, an inner automorphism ⟦Chapter7/Basic · EpGroupoid.isotropyConj_eq_isotropyConj_conj⟧ (Findings, Chapter 7, item 13) (p. 230).

### VII.7 Theorem 7.1, and local path connectedness

**Theorem 7.1** (V7.17) ⟦Chapter7/NaturalRep · EpGroupoid.theorem_7_1⟧. *For every object $x$ and every open $V \ni x$ there are an open neighbourhood $U \subseteq V$ of $x$, a homomorphism $\Phi : G_x \to \mathrm{Diff}_{sc}(U)$ and an sc-smooth $\Gamma : G_x \times U \to \mathbf X$ with (1) $\Gamma(g, x) = g$, (2) $s(\Gamma(g, y)) = y$ and $t(\Gamma(g, y)) = \Phi(g)(y)$, (3) every morphism $h : y \to z$ between points of $U$ is $\Gamma(g, y)$ for a unique $g$.* The data form a *natural representation* at $x$ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep⟧: $U$ open, connected and containing $x$; $\Phi(g)$ an sc-diffeomorphism of $U$ with inverse $\Phi(g^{-1})$ and $\Phi(gh) = \Phi(g) \circ \Phi(h)$ on $U$; $\Gamma$ sc-smooth on each slice $\{g\} \times U$, which is sc-smoothness on $G_x \times U$ (§VII.8), with (1)–(3). The first consequences: $\Phi(g)$ maps $U$ into $U$ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.mapsTo_Φ⟧, $\Phi(1)$ is the identity on $U$ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Φ_one⟧, every $\Phi(g)$ fixes $x$ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Φ_self⟧, $\Gamma(g, y)$ is a morphism between points of $U$ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Γ_mem_morOn⟧, $\Phi(g^{-1})\Phi(g) = 1$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Φ_inv_Φ⟧, and (3) is a bijection $G_x \times U \to \mathbf U(x)$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.bijOn_Γ⟧. The action $g \ast y = \Phi(g)(y)$ is a group action on $U$ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.smul_val⟧. The proof is the text's Theorem 7.5 in the appendix (§VII.26). *Hidden hypothesis:* $U$ connected. The text chooses "the connected open neighborhood $U(x)$" on p. 231 but does not put it into the statement; as we read it, the homomorphism property of $\Phi$, the functoriality of $\Gamma$ and the uniqueness of $(\Phi, \Gamma)$ all need it (Findings, Chapter 7, item 20) (p. 231).

**Local path connectedness** (V7.18). Connected neighbourhoods exist because M-polyfolds are locally path connected, which the text uses without statement (p. 231, Lemma 7.9, Corollary 7.2). *Step 1, a retract.* For $o \in O = r(U)$, $U$ open in a partial quadrant $C$, and a neighbourhood $W$ of $o$, there is $\varepsilon > 0$ such that every $p \in O$ with $\|p - o\| < \varepsilon$ is joined to $o$ inside $O \cap W$ by the path $\tau \mapsto r(o + \tau(p - o))$: the segment lies in the convex set $B_\varepsilon(o) \cap C \subseteq U$, $r$ is continuous on level $0$ and fixes $o$ and $p$ ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · ScRetraction.exists_ball_joinedIn⟧. So an sc-smooth retract is locally path connected ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · IsScRetract.locallyPathConnectedSpace⟧. *Step 2, an M-polyfold.* Through any chart around a point, path components of open sets are neighbourhoods ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · MChart.pathComponentIn_mem_nhds⟧, and $X$ is locally path connected ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · MPolyfold.locallyPathConnectedSpace⟧, hence locally connected ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · MPolyfold.locallyConnectedSpace⟧. *Step 3, consequences.* Open connected neighbourhoods form a basis ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · MPolyfold.hasBasis_isOpen_isConnected⟧ ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · MPolyfold.hasBasis_isOpen_isPathConnected⟧ ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · MPolyfold.exists_isOpen_isConnected_subset⟧; components, also of open sets, are open ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · MPolyfold.isOpen_connectedComponent⟧ ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · MPolyfold.isOpen_connectedComponentIn⟧; an open set is connected iff path connected ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · MPolyfold.isConnected_iff_isPathConnected⟧; every quotient of $X$, in particular $|X|$, is locally path connected ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · MPolyfold.locallyPathConnectedSpace_quotient⟧; and finitely many points of a Hausdorff locally connected space have pairwise disjoint connected open neighbourhoods inside a given open set ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · exists_pairwiseDisjoint_isOpen_isConnected⟧. *Step 4, the tool for connectedness.* Two continuous sections of a locally injective map into a Hausdorff space that agree at one point of a preconnected set agree on all of it ⟦Chapter7/LocConnected · eqOn_sections_of_isPreconnected⟧, by Mathlib's statement for separated maps ⟦Mathlib/Topology/SeparatedMap · eqOn_of_comp_eqOn⟧. For $s$ this says that a local inverse of $s$ on a connected $U$ is determined by one value; it is what makes $\Phi$ a homomorphism (§VII.26) and $\Gamma$ a functor (§VII.8). The paths are continuous on level $0$; sc-smooth paths between smooth points are Chapter 6's (§VI.18). This is the first fact of gap G.56 of Part I, now formalized (Findings, Chapter 7, items 21, 114).

### VII.8 Pages 231–233: the sheets $\mathbf U(g)$, $G_x \ltimes U(x)$, the functor $\Gamma$, and $\hat\Phi$

Everything on these pages is derived from one natural representation $(U, \Phi, \Gamma)$; the text's "using the proof of Theorem 7.1 one verifies" is not needed. No possible misprint was found on pp. 231–233 (Findings, Chapter 7, item 22).

**The splitting $\mathbf U(x) = \bigsqcup_g \mathbf U(g)$** (V7.19). Put $\mathbf U(g) = \Gamma(g, U)$. *Step 1, open.* The image of a continuous section of a local homeomorphism over an open set is open ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · isOpen_image_of_section⟧; $\Gamma(g, \cdot)$ is a section of $s$ by (2) ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.isOpen_image_Γ⟧. *Step 2, connected, disjoint, covering.* $\mathbf U(g)$ is connected as a continuous image of $U$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.isConnected_image_Γ⟧; two sheets are disjoint by the uniqueness in (3) ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Γ_inj⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.pairwise_disjoint_image_Γ⟧; they cover $\mathbf U(x)$ by the existence in (3) ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.iUnion_image_Γ⟧, which is therefore open ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.isOpen_morOn⟧. *Step 3, components.* Open, connected, disjoint and covering, they are the connected components of $\mathbf U(x)$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.connectedComponentIn_morOn⟧, and there are $\#G_x$ of them ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.injective_image_Γ⟧. *Step 4.* $s, t : \mathbf U(g) \to U$ are sc-diffeomorphisms, with inverses $\Gamma(g, \cdot)$ and $\Gamma(g, \cdot) \circ \Phi(g)^{-1}$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.isScDiffeoOn_src_image⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.isScDiffeoOn_tgt_image⟧. Every $\varphi \in \mathbf U(x)$ has a sheet index $h$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.index⟧ with $\varphi = \Gamma(h, s\varphi)$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Γ_index⟧ and $t\varphi = \Phi(h)(s\varphi)$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.tgt_eq_Φ_index⟧, locally constant on $\mathbf U(x)$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.eventually_index_eq⟧. Once $U$ is connected, the text's "choose $U(x)$ so small that $\mathbf U(x)$ splits into $\#G_x$-many components" needs no shrinking. "$\mathbf U(x)$ fits into an arbitrarily small open neighbourhood of $G_x$" belongs to the construction: Lemma 7.8 holds for arbitrary open $N_g \ni g$ (§VII.26) ⟦Chapter7/NaturalRep · EpGroupoid.lemma_7_8⟧ (p. 231).

**The M-polyfold $G \times U$** (V7.20). "A natural M-polyfold structure as the finite disjoint union of copies of $U$" is the product with a discrete M-polyfold. *Step 1.* A discrete space is an M-polyfold with the charts $\{g\} \to \mathbb R^0$ ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · discreteChart⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · discretePolyfold⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · isChart_discreteChart⟧, pairwise compatible because their transitions are the identity of the one-point space or the empty map ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · discreteChart_compatible⟧; every point is smooth ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · discretePolyfold_smoothSet⟧, and a map into it is sc-smooth iff continuous ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · isScSmoothMap_discrete_iff⟧. *Step 2.* In $G \times X$ the slices $\{g\} \times X$ are open ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · isOpen_sheet⟧, $x \mapsto (g, x)$ is sc-smooth ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · isScSmoothMap_sheet⟧ and the projection of a slice is an sc-diffeomorphism ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · isScDiffeoOn_snd_sheet⟧, with $d_{G \times X}(g, x) = d_X(x)$ ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · degIndex_prod_discrete⟧. *Step 3.* Hence a map on $G \times U$ is sc-smooth iff it is on each slice ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · isScSmoothOn_prod_discrete_iff⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · isScSmoothOn_univ_prod_discrete_iff⟧ ⟦Chapter7/Discrete · isScSmoothMap_prod_discrete_iff⟧, the text's sheet-by-sheet reading of "$\Gamma$ sc-smooth on $G \times U$". For a natural representation the objects are the open-subset M-polyfold $U$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.objPolyfold⟧, the morphisms $G_x \times U$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.morPolyfold⟧, and $(g, y) \mapsto g \ast y$ is sc-smooth ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.isScSmoothMap_smul⟧ (Findings, Chapter 7, item 23) (p. 232).

**The translation groupoid $G_x \ltimes U(x)$ is an ep-groupoid** (V7.21). The groupoid has objects $U$, morphisms $G \times U$, $s(g, y) = y$, $t(g, y) = g \ast y$, $(g, h \ast z) \circ (h, z) = (gh, z)$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.translation⟧ ⟦Chapter7/EpGroupoid · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.translationGroupoid⟧. *(1).* $s$ is the projection, a local sc-diffeomorphism by Step 2 above ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.translation_isLocalScDiffeo_src⟧; $t$ is the projection after the shear $(g, y) \mapsto (g, g \ast y)$, an sc-diffeomorphism with inverse $(g, y) \mapsto (g, g^{-1} \ast y)$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.shearHomeomorph⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.translation_isLocalScDiffeo_tgt⟧. *(3), for every $V$.* $t$ is the shear followed by the projection $G \times U \to U$, proper because $G_x$ is finite ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.translation_isProperMap⟧. *(4), sheet form.* For a local inverse $\sigma$ of $s$, $\sigma(t\psi) \circ \psi = (k(\psi)\psi_1, \psi_2)$ with $k$ locally constant, sc-smooth on each slice ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.translation_isScSmoothCompSheet⟧. So $G_x \ltimes U(x)$ is an ep-groupoid ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.translationEpGroupoid⟧, built from $(\Phi, \Gamma)$ alone (p. 232).

**The functor $\Gamma : G_x \ltimes U(x) \to X$** (V7.22). *Step 1, composition.* $y \mapsto \Gamma(g, h \ast y) \circ \Gamma(h, y)$ and $y \mapsto \Gamma(gh, y)$ are continuous sections of $s$ over $U$ — the first by (4) in the sheet form, for the sheet $\mathbf U(g)$ — with the same value $g \circ h$ at $x$ by (1); on the connected $U$ they agree (§VII.7) ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Γ_mul⟧. *Step 2.* In the same way $\Gamma(1, y) = 1_y$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Γ_one⟧, and $\Gamma(g^{-1}, g \ast y) = \Gamma(g, y)^{-1}$ by the uniqueness of inverses ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Γ_inv⟧. *Step 3.* So $\Gamma$, the inclusion on objects, is a functor ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.functor⟧, full and faithful by (3) ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.full⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.faithful⟧, onto the full subcategory on $U$ ⟦Chapter7/Groupoid · GroupoidStr.fullSub⟧, and an ep-functor ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.epFunctor⟧. *Hidden hypothesis:* $U$ connected, without which the sheet index of $\Gamma(g, h \ast y) \circ \Gamma(h, y)$ is only locally constant (p. 232).

**The action $\hat\Phi$ on $\mathbf U(x)$** (V7.23). The text defines $\hat\Phi(g)(\varphi) = \Gamma(ghg^{-1}, g \ast s(\varphi))$ for $\varphi \in \mathbf U(h)$. The formalization defines the total map $\hat\Phi(g)(\varphi) = \Gamma(g, t\varphi) \circ \varphi \circ \Gamma(g, s\varphi)^{-1}$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Φhat⟧ and recovers the text's formula from $\Gamma_{\mathrm{mul}}$ and $\Gamma_{\mathrm{inv}}$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Φhat_Γ⟧, together with $\Phi(g)\Phi(h)\Phi(g)^{-1} = \Phi(ghg^{-1})$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Φ_conj⟧. Then $\hat\Phi(g)$ maps $\mathbf U(h)$ onto $\mathbf U(ghg^{-1})$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Φhat_mem_image⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.image_Φhat⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.index_Φhat⟧; the two diagrams are $s \circ \hat\Phi(g) = \Phi(g) \circ s$ and $t \circ \hat\Phi(g) = \Phi(g) \circ t$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.src_Φhat⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.tgt_Φhat⟧; $\hat\Phi(1) = 1$ and $\hat\Phi(gh) = \hat\Phi(g)\hat\Phi(h)$ on $\mathbf U(x)$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Φhat_one⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Φhat_mul⟧; and $\hat\Phi(g)$ is an sc-diffeomorphism of $\mathbf U(x)$ with inverse $\hat\Phi(g^{-1})$, sc-smooth by (4) in the sheet form and the sc-smoothness of $\iota$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.isScDiffeoOn_Φhat⟧ (pp. 232–233).

### VII.9 Uniqueness and restriction of natural representations

(V7.24.) The text uses without statement that natural representations can be shrunk and compared: "adapting the corresponding restrictions" (Lemma 7.3), "$U(x)$ can be chosen so small" ($T_x$, p. 241). Let $R = (U, \Phi, \Gamma)$ and $R' = (U', \Phi', \Gamma')$ be natural representations at $x$ and $C$ the connected component of $x$ in $U \cap U'$, open and connected (§VII.7) ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.isOpen_connectedComponentIn_inter⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.isConnected_connectedComponentIn_inter⟧. *Step 1.* $\Gamma(g, \cdot)$ and $\Gamma'(g, \cdot)$ are continuous sections of $s$ over $C$ with the value $g$ at $x$, so they agree on $C$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Γ_eqOn⟧; applying $t$, $\Phi(g) = \Phi'(g)$ on $C$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.Φ_eqOn⟧. *Step 2.* $C$ is invariant: $\Phi(g)(C)$ is connected, contains $x$ and lies in $U \cap U'$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.mapsTo_Φ_connectedComponentIn⟧. *Step 3.* So a natural representation restricts to every invariant connected open neighbourhood of $x$ inside $U$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.restrict⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalRep · EpGroupoid.NatRepConstruction.restrict⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalRep · EpGroupoid.exists_naturalRep_restrict⟧, in particular to $C$, where the restrictions of $R$ and $R'$ coincide ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.restrictInter⟧ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.restrictInter_eq⟧, and natural representations exist inside every open $V \ni x$ ⟦Chapter7/NaturalRep · EpGroupoid.exists_naturalRep_shrink⟧. *Step 4.* If $\Phi(g) = 1$ for one natural representation, then $\Phi'(g) = 1$ near $x$ for every one ⟦Chapter7/NaturalAction · EpGroupoid.NaturalRep.eventually_Φ_eq_of_actsTrivially⟧. Uniqueness holds on the component $C$; $U \cap U'$ itself need not be connected (Findings, Chapter 7, item 24).

### VII.10 Proposition 7.5 and Definition 7.8: the star construction
